en: Vālmīki: Rāmāyaṇa, 7. Uttarakāṇḍa 7.001.001a When Rāma had obtained the kingdom and the slaughter of the rākṣasas was accomplished...
All the sages came to congratulate Rāghava:
Kauśika, Yavakrīta, Raibhya, Cyavana,
and Kaṇva— the son of Medhātithi— and those who dwell in the eastern quarter.
The venerable Svastyātreya, Namuci, and Pramuci likewise arrived,
along with Agastya and those who resided in the southern quarter;
as did Pṛṣadgu, Kavaṣa, Dhaumya, and the great Ṛṣi Raudreya.
Those who had taken refuge in the western direction also arrived with their disciples—
Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Atri, Viśvāmitra, Gautama,
Jamadagni, and Bharadvāja; these were the seven great ṛṣis.
Having reached the residence of Rāghava, those high-souled ones, whose splendor was equal to that of the fire-god, stood ready at the entrance. Then,
by the word of Agastya, the gatekeeper quickly [informed him].
He quickly entered the presence of the high-souled Rāghava. Seeing Rāma, who possessed a splendor like that of the full moon,
he immediately announced Agastya’s arrival along with the other sages.
Having heard that those sages, who possessed a radiance like the rising sun,
had arrived, the king then said to the gatekeeper, "Let them enter at their pleasure. Upon seeing that the sages had arrived, he rose to meet them with his hands joined in reverence.
Having offered his salutations, Rāma, with a composed mind, assigned seats to them.
Those bulls among sages sat upon those comfortable seats, which were variegated with gold and well-spread with rugs, each according to his rank.
Questioned by Rāma regarding their welfare, those great seers— learned in the Vedas, accompanied by their disciples and leaders— spoke these words to Rāma:
"O mighty-armed descendant of Raghu, we are well in every respect."
7.001.013c By good fortune, we see you safe and sound, having slain your enemies.
7.001.014a For that Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, was no burden for you, O Rāma; 7.001.014c indeed, with your bow, you could have conquered the three worlds without a doubt.
"By good fortune, O Rāma, you have slain Rāvaṇa along with his sons and grandsons.
By good fortune, we behold you today victorious together with your wife.
By good fortune, Prahasta, Vikaṭa, Virūpākṣa, and Mahodara [have been slain]."

Unshakable and invincible, those night-stalkers have been slain— those whose vast proportions find no equal here in this world. By good fortune, O Rāma, Kumbhakarṇa has been struck down by you in battle.
"By good fortune, you have entered into a duel with the lord of the rākṣasas;
you have achieved victory over one who is invincible even to the gods. Yet, in that battle, there was not the slightest defeat for Rāvaṇa."
"By good fortune, having entered into this duel, the son of Rāvaṇa has been slain by you.
By good fortune, O mighty-armed hero, you have escaped from that enemy of the gods who was rushing toward you like Time itself, and victory has been attained by you."
"O gentle one, this is indeed a source of wonder for us, having heard that Indrajit has been slain—
he who was invincible to all beings in battle and a master of great illusion.
O hero, you have bestowed upon us this auspicious and gentle gift of safety."
"By good fortune you prosper, O descendant of Kakutstha, through victory, O crusher of enemies!
Having heard these words of those sages of purified souls,
Rāma was filled with supreme wonder and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
"O sirs, passing over Kumbhakarṇa and Rāvaṇa,
the night-stalker of great prowess, why do you praise the son of Rāvaṇa?
[Why not praise] Mahodara, Prahasta, and the Rākṣasa Virūpākṣa?"
"7.001.025c Having bypassed those of great heroism, why do you praise the son of Rāvaṇa? 7.001.026a Of what nature is his power, what is his strength, and what is his prowess?
7.001.026c For what reason does he surpass Rāvaṇa?"
"If it is possible for me to hear, I certainly do not command you; if it is not a secret and can be spoken, I wish to hear it—so please tell me:
how was Śakra defeated by him, and how did he obtain the boon?"
Having heard those words of the high-souled Rāghava,
the pot-born sage of great splendor spoke these words:
"Listen, O King, to how it happened, and of what his great power and strength consist."
He slew his enemies in battle, yet he himself could not be slain by his foes. O Rāghava, I shall tell you of this lineage and birth of Rāvaṇa,
as well as the boon that was granted to him.
Long ago in the Kṛta age, O Rāma, there was a powerful lord, a son of Prajāpati,
a Brahman-sage named Pulastya, who was like the Grandfather Brahmā himself. His virtues, both in righteousness and in character, cannot be fully recounted.
Indeed, he could have been called "the son of Prajāpati" by name; however,
out of devotion to dharma, that bull among sages went to the hermitage of Tṛṇabindu on the side of the great mountain Meru and dwelt there.
That righteous-souled one, with his senses restrained through the study of the Vedas, performed austerities. When he went to his hermitage, certain maidens created obstacles for him—
maidens who were daughters of gods, of *pannagas*, and of royal sages.
And playing, the Apsarases also arrived at that place;
because that forest was enjoyable in all seasons and so delightful,
those maidens would constantly go to that place and play there.
Then the great sage, possessed of immense splendor, being enraged, declared:
"Whosoever shall come into my sight, she shall conceive a child.
Having heard these words of the high-souled one, they all departed.

Fearing the dread of a Brahmin’s curse, they did not venture into that region. But the daughter of the royal seer Tṛṇabindu did not hear of this; having gone to his hermitage, she roamed about quite fearlessly.
At that very time, that great sage Prājāpatya,
his splendor illuminated by asceticism, was engaged in the private recitation of the Vedas there.
Having heard the sound of the Veda and having seen that one whose wealth is penance, she [approached].
Her body became pale, and the signs of pregnancy were clearly manifested.
Seeing her own form, she was deeply distressed;
realizing, "What is this that has happened to me?", she went before her father and stood there.
Seeing her in such a state, Tṛṇabindu then said:
"Why do you maintain this form so unbecoming of yourself? The maiden, distressed, joined her palms in reverence and spoke to the one whose wealth is asceticism.

"I do not know, dear father, the cause by which my form has become such as this. However, previously I went alone to the divine hermitage of the great seer Pulastya, whose soul is purified, in order to search for my companions."
"I did not see any of my friends there who had come;
rather, having observed a transformation in their appearance, I have come here.
For the royal sage Tṛṇabindu has his splendor illuminated by asceticism."
He entered that meditation and beheld there the fruit born of the rishi’s ascetic power.
Having realized that curse of the great rishi of purified soul,
he took his daughter, went to Pulastya, and spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, O Great Sage, please accept this daughter of mine as alms, offered by myself and adorned with her own virtues;
for you who are engaged in the practice of austerity and whose senses are weary."

"She will be constantly devoted to service; of this there is no doubt. When the righteous royal sage had spoken these words, that twice-born man, desiring to accept her, said "So be it" to the maiden.
Having given her away, the king then departed for his own hermitage;
that maiden also remained there, pleasing her husband with her virtues.
And he, of great splendor, being delighted, spoke these words.

"I am well-pleased; may prosperity be yours, for you are exceedingly rich in virtues. Therefore, I shall now desist from [granting] a son equal to myself in qualities—one who will be the founder of both lineages and renowned as Paulastya."
"Since the Veda has become renowned (*viśruta*) here through you as I practice it, therefore he shall be named Viśravas; of this there is no doubt.
Having been addressed thus, that maiden was filled with joy in her innermost heart.
In no long time at all, the Sūtas gave birth to a son, Viśravas.
He was renowned throughout the three worlds and endowed with purity and righteousness; that bull among sages, Viśravas, was possessed of ascetic power just like his father.
Then Pulastya’s son, Viśravas, the bull among sages,
in a short time became established in asceticism just like his father;
he was truthful, virtuous, capable, devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas, and pure.
Unattached to all enjoyments and eternally devoted to dharma—
having learned of his conduct, the great seer Bharadvāja gave his own daughter, Devavarṇinī, as a wife to Viśravas.
Having then rightfully accepted the daughter of Bharadvāja, Viśravas,
the bull among sages, was filled with supreme joy. He begot upon her a most wonderful offspring, endowed with great prowess.
The righteous-souled one begot [a son] endowed with all the qualities of a Brahmin.
When he was born, the Grandfather (Brahmā) became exceedingly joyful;
pleased, he then bestowed a name upon him together with the celestial sages.
"Because he is the offspring of Viśravas and resembles Viśravas,
he shall therefore become famous by the name Vaiśravaṇa. Then Vaiśravaṇa went there to the forest of asceticism.
7.003.008c He, possessed of great splendor, grew like a fire fed with oblations.
7.003.009a While that high-souled one was staying in his hermitage, this thought arose in him:
7.003.009c "I shall practice dharma with self-restraint, for dharma is the supreme goal."
Having performed austerities in the great forest for thousands of years,
when a full thousand years had passed, he engaged in various disciplines:
subsisting on water, subsisting on air, and likewise remaining without food.
7.003.011c Thus those thousands of years passed away as if they were but a single year.
7.003.012a Then the one of great splendor, being pleased along with the hosts of gods led by Indra,
went to his hermitage and spoke these words, O Brahmā:
"O child of noble vows, I am well-pleased with this deed of yours. Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—for in my view, you are worthy of a boon.
Then Vaiśravaṇa spoke to the Grandfather who stood before him.
"O Blessed One, I desire the status of a world-protector and the guardianship of wealth.
Then Brahmā, together with the hosts of gods, spoke to Vaiśravaṇa with a highly pleased mind, joyfully saying, "So be it!"

"For I am indeed intent on creating a fourth among the world-protectors— Yama, Indra, and Varuṇa— for that station which you desire has been established. Go, O knower of dharma, and attain the status of Lord of Wealth."
"For today you shall indeed become the fourth among Yama, Indra, and Varuṇa.
Accept this celestial chariot named Puṣpaka, which resembles the sun, for the purpose of travel; thus attain equality with the gods."
"May it be well with you; we shall all depart just as we came. We have accomplished our purpose, dear one, having granted you this great boon.
When the gods, headed by Brahmā, had thus departed into the sky, [the world was left behind].
7.003.020c Bowing low with humility, the Lord of Wealth spoke these words to his father:
7.003.021a "O Blessed One, I have obtained a boon from the Lotus-born One;
however, that Lord Prajāpati has not yet assigned a dwelling for me."
"O Blessed One, O Lord, look for some place for us to dwell where no living being whatsoever shall suffer harm. Thus addressed by his son, Viśravas, the bull among sages, [replied:]
The knower of dharma spoke these words: "O knower of dharma, listen!
There is a beautiful city named Laṅkā, built by Viśvakarman for the residence of the Rākṣasas, just as Amarāvatī is for Indra."
For that city was indeed delightful, with its gateways of gold and lapis lazuli;
it had been abandoned by the Rākṣasas in former times, who were tormented by the fear of Viṣṇu,
and it was now empty of all the hosts of Rakṣasas, who had gone to the depths of the netherworld.
"Therefore, set your mind on dwelling there;
your residence there shall be free from harm, and no one shall cause you any distress.
Having heard these righteous words of his father, the virtuous-souled [Rāma]—
Then, by his command, he established Laṅkā upon the mountain peak;
in a short time, it was filled with thousands of delighted and ever-joyful Nairṛtas.
Then the righteous-souled lord of the Nairṛtas, the son of Viśravas, dwelt there joyfully in Laṅkā, which has the ocean for its garment;
from time to time, that self-disciplined lord of wealth would travel by means of the Puṣpaka chariot.
7.003.030c He approached his father and mother with great joy. 7.003.031a He was praised by hosts of gods and Gandharvas, as well as by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Surrounded by splendor like the sun enveloped in its rays with majesty, he proceeded to his father’s presence.
Having heard the words uttered by Agastya, Rāma was filled with wonder.
7.004.001c Previously, there was this origin of the *rākṣasa*s in Laṅkā.
7.004.002a Then, shaking his head, and looking repeatedly at Agastya— who possessed a form like the three sacrificial fires— he spoke with a smile:
"O Blessed One, even in the past this Laṅkā belonged to the flesh-eaters;
hearing this from you, wonder has been born within me.
We have heard that the Rākṣasas originated from the lineage of Pulastya."
7.004.004c Now you have also described their origin from others:
7.004.005a From Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Prahasta, and even Vikaṭa;
7.004.005c And from the sons of Rāvaṇa—were they perhaps more powerful than you?

7.004.006a O Brahmin, who was the first among them, what were their names, and what was the power of their asceticism? 7.004.006c And having committed what offense were they driven away by Viṣṇu in the past?
7.004.007a Tell me all of this in detail, O sinless one.
"Curiosity has been aroused in me; dispel it as the sun dispels the darkness.
Having heard those words of Rāghava, which were refined and adorned with eloquence, Agastya, feeling a slight sense of wonder, spoke to that descendant of Raghu.
In the past, Prajāpati, who was born from the waters, created the waters;
then the one born from the lotus created living beings for their protection. Those beings approached the creator of beings with humility.
"Alas, what shall we do? they cried, afflicted by the fear of hunger and thirst.
But Prajāpati, the bestower of honor, as if smiling, addressed those beings with a careful voice, saying, "Protect [one another]."
"Let us protect," said some there; "let us sacrifice," said others. To those who had eaten and those who had not eaten, the Creator of Beings then spoke:
"Those by whom it was said, 'Let us protect,' let them become Rākṣasas for you."
"May those by whom it was said, 'We shall sacrifice' (yakṣāma), indeed become Yakṣas for you.
There, Heti and Praheti, two brothers who were bulls among Rākṣasas and subduers of enemies,
became like Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
The righteous Heti did not desire a wife there;
however, for the sake of marriage, he then made a supreme effort. He [sought] a maiden named Bhayā, the sister of Kāla, who was terrifying and inspired fear.
The great-minded one of immeasurable soul married her of his own accord. That bull among Rākṣasas begot upon her a son known as Vidyutkeśa, the best among those who possess sons.

Vidyutkeśa, the son of Heti, possessing a radiance equal to a blazing fire and endowed with great splendor, grew like a lotus in the midst of water. When that night-stalker had reached auspicious youth, [he became even more radiant].

Then his father resolved to perform the marriage ceremony for him; he, Heti, the bull among Rākṣasas, sought the hand of Sandhyā’s daughter— equal to Sandhyā herself in power— for the sake of his son.
"Sandhyā reflected, 'She must certainly be given away to another,' and so, O Rāghava, she gave her daughter to Vidyutkeśa.
Having obtained Sandhyā’s daughter, the night-stalker Vidyutkeśa— "
He took his pleasure with her, just as Maghavan does with Paulomī.
Then, after some time had passed, O Rāma, Sālakaṭaṅkaṭā conceived a child from Vidyutkeśa, as a row of clouds receives moisture from the ocean.
Then that Rākṣasī, having gone to Mount Mandara, gave birth to an embryo with a luster like the interior of a rain cloud— just as the Gaṅgā brought forth the fire-born Skanda—
and desiring sexual pleasure, she abandoned that embryo for Vidyutkeśa.
7.004.025c She took her pleasure with her husband, having forgotten her own son.
7.004.026a Abandoned by her, that infant, possessing a radiance like the autumn sun,
7.004.026c placed his hand to his mouth and wept like the king of clouds.
Then, traveling upward while seated upon his bull,
the Lord Hara beheld the son of the Rākṣasa weeping together with Umā.
Thereupon, Bhava, the destroyer of Tripura, was moved by Pārvatī’s state of compassion.
He made that son of the Rākṣasa equal in age to his mother;
and having rendered him immortal, the imperishable and immutable Mahādeva bestowed upon him a city that travels through the sky, out of a desire to please Pārvatī.
O prince, Umā also granted a boon to the rākṣasīs:
that there should be the immediate conception of a fetus and birth immediately thereafter;
and that they should attain maturity at the very same time as their mother’s own maturity.
Then Sukeśa, arrogant because of the granting of the boon,
having obtained glory from the presence of Lord Hara,
that great-minded bird roamed everywhere.
Having reached the city of Khaga like Indra reaching his own city,
and seeing the righteous Rākṣasa Sukeśa who had obtained boons,
there was a Gandharva named Grāmaṇī, whose splendor was equal to that of Viśvāvasu.
He had a second daughter named Devavatī, who was like the goddess Śrī herself.
Dakṣa gave her to Sukeśa according to dharma, just as he had given Śrī [to Viṣṇu].
Having obtained that beloved husband, she attained sovereignty through the granting of boons.
She was as delighted as a poor man who has acquired wealth;
united with her, that night-stalker shone like a great elephant emerged from the *añjana* forest accompanied by a female elephant.
O Rāghava, Sukeśa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, begot upon Devavatī three sons who were equal to the three-eyed god;
they were Mālyavān, Sumālī, and Mālī, the foremost among the powerful.
They were like the three worlds remaining undisturbed, like the three sacrificial fires,
like the three most formidable mantras, and like the three terrible diseases;
they were the three sons of Sukeśa, possessing a splendor equal to the three sacred fires.
There they grew in power, like diseases that have been neglected. But having learned of their father’s attainment of the boon and his great sovereignty,
those brothers, firm in their resolve, went to Mount Meru to perform austerities.
O best of kings, having undertaken formidable vows, those Rākṣasas practiced severe asceticism that struck fear into all living beings;
they did so through austerities difficult to perform on earth, which were endowed with truth, uprightness, and self-restraint.
Scorching the three worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans,
the omnipresent four-faced Lord, seated upon his excellent celestial chariot,
addressed the sons of Sukeśa and said, "I am here to grant a boon."
7.005.012 Knowing Brahmā, the giver of boons, to be surrounded by the hosts of gods led by Indra,
they all spoke with palms joined in reverence, like trembling trees. 7.005.013 "O God, if you, who have been propitiated by our ascetic penance, grant us a boon..."
"May we be invincible, slayers of our enemies, long-lived,
and powerful," they said, each devoted to the other.
Having said, "It shall be so," the Lord [spoke] to the sons of Sukeśa.

7.005.014c Brahmā, who is affectionate toward brahmins, departed for the world of Brahmā. 7.005.015a Having then obtained that boon, O Rāma, all those night-stalkers, rendered utterly fearless by the granting of the boon, began to oppress the gods and asuras.
Being slaughtered by them, the thirty gods, along with the hosts of sages and the cāraṇas,
found no protector, just like men dwelling in hell.
Then they [sought] Viśvakarman, the imperishable best of artisans.
7.005.017c Having gathered together, the delighted Rākṣasas said, O best of the Raghus:
7.005.018a "You alone are the builder of the dwellings desired by the hearts of the gods; therefore, O high-minded one, build a house for us as well."
"Taking refuge on the Himavat, or Meru, or even Mandara,
let a great house be built for us, resembling the abode of Maheśvara. Then Viśvakarman, the mighty-armed one, [acted] for those Rākṣasas.
He described his dwelling as being like Amarāvatī, the city of Śakra.
On the shore of the southern ocean stands a mountain named Trikūṭa;
on its central peak, which resembles a mass of clouds, [is my abode].
Even for birds, it is difficult to reach, with its four directions cut away by chisels;
thirty yojanas in extent, with golden walls and gateways—
that city called Laṅkā was built by me at the command of Śakra.
Dwelling in that city, those invincible and most excellent of Rākṣasas were like the gods with Indra when they have reached Amarāvatī;
having reached the fortress of Laṅkā, they were surrounded by many Rākṣasas.

"You shall become invincible to your enemies, O slayers of foes. Having heard the words of Viśvakarman, O Rāma, those rākṣasas then departed with their thousands of followers and dwelt in that city of Laṅkā.

Having reached Laṅkā, which is surrounded by firm walls and moats and filled with hundreds of golden houses, those night-rangers dwell there joyfully. There is a Gandharva woman named Narmadā, who has been nurtured by various religious duties.
She had three daughters whose splendor was equal to Wisdom (Dhī), Fortune (Śrī),
and Fame (Kīrti). With a face like the full moon, she joyfully gave those maidens to those Rākṣasas in order of their seniority, though she herself was not a Rākṣasī.

To the three lords of the Rākṣasas, O illustrious one, three Gandharva maidens were given by their mother under the constellation presided over by Bhaga. Having taken wives, O Lord Rāma, they became the sons of Sukeśa.
Together with their wives, they sported like immortals with apsarases.
There, Mālyavat’s wife was named Sundarī, truly beautiful;
learn now of the offspring he begot upon her.
Vajramuṣṭi, Virūpākṣa, and the Rākṣasa Durmukha; Suptaghna, Yajñakopa, as well as Matta and Unmatta;
and a daughter named Anala was born, O Rāma, who was more beautiful than Sundarī.
Sumāli also had a wife whose face resembled the full moon;
named Ketumatī, she was dearer to him than his own life. Sumāli, the night-stalker, begot offspring from her.
7.005.034c O great king, learn now in due order concerning those born of Ketumatī: 7.005.035a Prahasta, Akampana, Vikaṭa, Kālakārmuka,
7.005.035c Dhūmrākṣa, Daṇḍa, and the exceedingly powerful Supārśva.
Saṃhrādi, Praghasa, and the Rākṣasa Bhāsakarṇa;
Rākā, Puṣpotkaṭā, Kaikasī of the radiant smile,
and Kumbhīnasī— these are remembered as the offspring of Sumālī.
Māli had a wife named Vasudā, a Gandharvī endowed with great beauty; she was lotus-petal-eyed, fair-limbed, and resembled the most excellent Yakṣīs.
O Lord, Sumāli’s younger brother begot a son upon her.
"O Rāghava, listen as I describe that offspring to you.
Anala, Anila, Hara, and Saṃpāti—these are the ministers of Vibhīṣaṇa; they are the Māleyas, those night-rangers."
Then those three bull-like Rākṣasas,
surrounded by their hundred sons who were night-stalkers,
[attacked] the gods led by Indra, as well as the sages, nāgas, and dānavas.
Proud of their strength and heroism,
they harassed the world as they wandered about like the wind, difficult to approach;
in battle they were like Death itself, remaining focused and resolute.

7.005.041c Exceedingly arrogant because of the granting of the boon, they constantly brought an end to the performance of sacrifices; 7.006.001a by them were the gods and the sages rich in asceticism being slaughtered.
Afflicted by fear, they sought refuge with Maheśvara, the God of gods.
Having assembled before the enemy of Kāma, the foe of Tripura, the three-eyed Lord,
the gods, their voices faltering with fear, spoke with palms joined in reverence.

"O Blessed One, O Lord of Creatures, O Subduer of Enemies, all our subjects are being oppressed by the sons of Sukeśa, who have been emboldened by the boon of the Grandfather. Our hermitages, which were once places of refuge, have been rendered defenseless."
Śakra has been cast down from heaven, yet they sport in heaven like Śakra himself.
"I am Viṣṇu, I am Rudra, I am Brahmā, I am the King of the Gods;
I am Yama, I am Varuṇa, I am the Moon, and I am the Sun as well."
"Thus, O God, those Rākṣasas, arrogant because of the granting of the boon,
and those who are their vanguard, exulting in battle, are causing oppression. Therefore, you ought to grant fearlessness to us who are afflicted by the fear of the gods."
"Assuming an inauspicious form, slay the thorns of the gods. Thus addressed by all the deities, the Lord Kapardin, who is blue-and-red (Nīlalohita),
spoke with concern for Sukeśa to the hosts of gods:
"I shall not slay them, for those asuras are not to be killed by me;
however, I will grant a mantra that will indeed destroy them. Having thus set forth their resolve, O bulls among the gods, they proceeded.
"Let them go for refuge to Viṣṇu; that Lord will slay them. Then, having greeted Maheśvara with shouts of victory, they, afflicted by the fear of the night-stalkers, approached the presence of Viṣṇu.
Having bowed down to and paid great honor to the god who bears the conch and the discus,
those who were tormented by the sons of Sukeśa spoke these words in agitation: "O Lord,
we have been attacked by the three sons of Sukeśa, who resemble the three sacrificial fires."
7.006.013c By means of a boon, he has seized our territories after attacking them.
7.006.014a There is a fortress city named Laṅkā situated on the peak of Mount Trikūṭa;
7.006.014c Residing there, those night-stalkers oppress us all.

Therefore, O Madhusūdana, for the sake of our pleasure, slay them; present to Yama those whose lotus-faces have been severed by your discus. Among those who grant us fearlessness in times of danger, there is none other equal to you.
"O God, dispel our fear as the sun dispels the mist.
Thus addressed by the deities, Janārdana, the God of gods,
who grants fearlessness even to his enemies, spoke to the gods after bestowing that security upon them.
I know the Rākṣasa Sukeśa, who was arrogant due to the boon granted by Īśāna;
I also know his sons, of whom Mālyavān is the eldest. Those lowest of Rākṣasas have transgressed all bounds of propriety.
"I shall slay you in battle; O gods, be free from anxiety.
Thus addressed by the powerful Viṣṇu, all those gods went to their respective abodes, joyful and pacifying Janārdana.
Having heard of the mobilization of the gods, that night-stalker Mālyavān spoke these words to his two heroic brothers:
"It is said that the immortals and the sages, having united, [approached] Śaṅkara."
Desiring our destruction, they spoke thus to the Three-eyed Lord:
"O God, the daughters of Sukeśa, arrogant due to the power of the boon they have received,
are harassing us with their fierce forms at every step as they exert themselves against us."
"O Lord of Umā, we have been overwhelmed by the Rākṣasas; out of fear of those evil-minded ones, we are unable to remain even in our own dwellings.
Therefore, for our benefit, O Three-eyed One, do you slay them."
"O best of burners, consume the Rākṣasas with a mere roar!"—
having been addressed thus by the gods, the slayer of Andhaka heard them and,
shaking his head and hand, spoke these words.
"Those gods, the sons of Sukeśa, are not to be slain by me in battle;
however, I shall grant you a mantra that will indeed slay them. That Janārdana, who holds the discus and mace in his hands and is clad in yellow garments—"

"He will slay them in battle; go to him for refuge. Having obtained their desire from Hara and having paid homage to the Enemy of Kāma (Śiva), they reached the abode of Nārāyaṇa and reported everything to him.

Then Nārāyaṇa spoke to the gods, headed by Indra: "O gods, I shall slay the enemies of the gods; be free from your feverish anxiety. To the gods who were terrified with fear, Hari [spoke] regarding those two bulls among the Rākṣasas.

7.006.031c Our execution has been promised; therefore, consider what is appropriate. 7.006.032a The death of Hiraṇyakaśipu and of other enemies of the gods occurred because he desired to slay us, who were unable to conquer Nārāyaṇa.
Then Sumālī and Mālī, having heard the words of Mālyavat,
spoke to their eldest brother, who was like Vāsava to the two portions of Bhaga: "We have studied, we have given gifts, we have performed sacrifices, and we have protected our sovereignty."

Long life free from disease has been attained, and our own dharma has been established. Having plunged into the unshakeable ocean of the gods with floods of weapons, we have eternally conquered the gods in battle; we have no fear caused by death.
Nārāyaṇa, Rudra, Śakra, and Yama as well—all of them indeed fear to stand before us. O Lord of Rākṣasas, there is no fault on Viṣṇu’s part; this is simply the cause.
"By the very fault of the gods, Viṣṇu’s mind has been provoked.
Therefore, prepared today and surrounded by our entire army,
we shall seek to slay those very gods from whom this offense has arisen."
Thus Mālin, Sumālin, and their elder brother, the lord Mālyavat—
having then proclaimed a call to arms— all those Rākṣasas set forth for battle in a rage, like Jambha, Vṛtra, and Bala.
With chariots, lordly elephants, and horses resembling mountains;
with donkeys, cattle, and camels;
and with porpoises, serpents, crocodiles, tortoises, fish, and birds like Garuḍas.
Accompanied by lions, tigers, boars, sṛmaras, and even camaras,
all those Rākṣasas, proud of their strength, then abandoned Laṅkā and set out for the world of the gods to fight the enemies of the deities.

Having seen the reversal of Laṅkā, all the beings dwelling in Laṅkā then became fearful and despondent in every respect; likewise, the terrestrial and atmospheric beings, portending danger as if by the decree of Time, were struck with fear.
Portents have swiftly arisen for the destruction of the lords of the Rākṣasas:
the clouds rain down bones and even hot blood;
the ocean has overstepped its shore, and the greatest mountains are shaking.
Letting out loud bursts of laughter with sounds like the roar of thunderclouds,
thousands of spirits fell about, dancing;
and there was also a great circle of vultures with mouths vomiting flames.
It indeed revolves above the Rākṣasas like the wheel of time.
Those Rākṣasas, arrogant in their strength, do not turn back from those inconceivable and great portents; bound by the noose of death, they simply go on.
Mālyavān, Sumālī, and Mālī were the night-rangers who served as their precursors,
like sacrificial fires at the forefront of rituals.
And they all [followed] Mālyavān, who was like Mount Mālyavān itself.
The night-stalkers took refuge [in him] as embodied beings take refuge in the Creator.
That army of the lords of the Rākṣasas, resounding like the roar of massive clouds,
marched toward the world of the gods with a desire for victory, while Māli remained under their command.

But the Lord Nārāyaṇa, having heard from the messenger of the gods about that mobilization of the Rākṣasas, then set his mind upon battle. He [was accompanied] by gods, Siddhas, Ṛṣis, and great serpents;
Accompanied by songs from the chief Gandharvas and Apsarases, he approached the army of the enemies of the gods,
bearing a discus, sword, plowshare, and other excellent weapons.
With its wings fanned by the wind from the wings of the *suparṇas*,
with its banners whirling and its weapons scattered,
that army of the king of the *rākṣasas* trembled.
Moving like a restless mountain peak, he was like Mount Nīla;
likewise, with his limbs smeared with blood and flesh and resembling the fire at the end of an eon, his form was terrifying.
The night-stalkers, having completely surrounded Mādhava,
pierced him by the thousands with their excellent weapons.
Those Rākṣasa-clouds, however, roared at the mountain that was Nārāyaṇa.
They rained down a shower of arrows, like clouds raining upon a mountain.
Surrounded by those foremost night-stalkers, who were dark as collyrium and yet possessed of a fair complexion, Viṣṇu appeared like Mount Añjana enveloped by pouring rain-clouds.
Just as locusts [overwhelm] a field, as gnats [assail] a mountain,
as living beings [seek] a jar of nectar, or as crocodiles [enter] the ocean—
so too were those arrows released from the Rākṣasa’s bow, swift as the thunderbolt, the wind, or thought.
7.007.004c Arrows entered Hari as living beings enter [the sun] at the end of an eon.
7.007.005a Those mounted on chariots [entered him] with their chariots, those in the vanguard of elephants with their elephants,
7.007.005c horsemen with their fine horses, and foot soldiers who moved through the sky.
The lords of the *rākṣasas*, resembling mountains, rendered Hari breathless with arrows, spears, double-edged swords,
and javelins, as if performing a yogic breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*) upon a twice-born man.
Being tormented by the night-stalkers like a great whale by small fish, he was struck down.
Drawing his Śārṅga bow in that great battle,
Viṣṇu cut the limbs of the Rākṣasas into hundreds and thousands of pieces as small as sesame seeds with arrows released from a fully drawn bow— arrows with diamond-hard tips and the speed of thought.
Having dispersed that shower of arrows which had arisen like a storm of rain,
Puruṣottama blew his great conch, Pāñcajanya.
That king of conchs, born from the waters, was blown by Hari with all his might.
It roared with a terrifying sound like a rain-cloud at the end of an eon;
then that sound of the king of conchs struck terror into the rākṣasas,
as a lion in the forest terrifies rutting elephants.

The horses were unable to stand their ground, and the elephants lost their vigor; warriors, weakened by the blare of conchs, fell from their chariots. Arrows released from the Śārṅga bow, with tips like thunderbolts, [rained down].
Having torn through those *rākṣasas*, those well-feathered arrows entered the earth.
Others, being pierced by the arrows released from Nārāyaṇa’s bow, fell down—
terrible *rākṣasas* like mountains struck by thunderbolts.
7.007.015 With wounds inflicted by the arrows of Adhokṣaja, which are the enemies of all that causes wounds,
they bled in streams like mountains discharging torrents of liquid gold.
7.007.016 There was also the sound of the king of conchs, as well as the resonance of the Śārṅga bow.
The roar of Viṣṇu indeed swallows even the cries of the Rākṣasas,
just as fierce rays [emanate] from the sun, as waves from the ocean,
as lordly elephants from a mountain, and as torrents of water from a cloud.
Likewise, the arrows released from the Śārṅga bow by Nārāyaṇa rushed forth swiftly by the hundreds and thousands,
like lions driven by a śarabha or elephants by a lion.
Just as tigers are [overpowered] by an elephant, as leopards by a tiger,
as dogs by a leopard, as cats by a dog,
as snakes by a cat, and as mice by a snake; so too [were they overpowered].
7.007.021a Thus those Rākṣasas in battle were driven away and even laid low upon the surface of the earth by the powerful Viṣṇu.
7.007.022a Having slain thousands of Rākṣasas, Madhusūdana—

Like the king of the gods making the clouds roar with his thunderbolt, he caused the water-born [conch] to resound. The Rakshasa army, overwhelmed by Narayana’s arrow and utterly distressed by the blast of the conch, fled broken toward Lanka.
When the Rākṣasa army was shattered, struck by Nārāyaṇa’s arrows,
Sumālī covered Hari in battle with a shower of shafts,
raising his hand adorned with golden ornaments like an elephant raises its trunk.
The Rākṣasa roared with joy like a rain-cloud flashing with lightning.
As that Sumālī was roaring, [Hanumān] severed his head, adorned with flaming earrings;
and the horses of that Rākṣasa’s charioteer bolted away.
7.007.027a Sumāli, the lord of the Rākṣasas, was whirled about by those wandering horses,
just as a man lacking self-control is whirled about by his wandering senses.
7.007.028a And Māli rushed forward in the battle, grasping his bow with an arrow fixed upon it.
The arrows released from Mālin’s bow, adorned with gold,
entered Hari upon reaching him, like birds entering Mount Krauñca.
Then, he was afflicted by those thousands of arrows discharged by Mālin.

Viṣṇu was not agitated in the battle, like one who has conquered his senses is unperturbed by mental afflictions. Then the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, wielding sword and mace, made the twang of his bowstring and discharged floods of arrows at Mālin.
7.007.031a Having reached Mālin’s body, those arrows, radiant as lightning and a thunderbolt,
7.007.031c drank his blood, just as serpents drink the nectar of old.
7.007.032a Having forcibly turned Mālin away and deprived him of his crown, Hari—
He struck down the chariot along with its banner, the bow, and the horses. Deprived of his chariot, Mālin, the foremost of night-stalkers, seized a mace and,
with mace in hand, leapt up like a lion from a mountain peak.
In that battle, he struck Garuḍa on the forehead with his mace, as Antaka strikes Īśāna, or as Indra strikes a mountain with his thunderbolt. Struck violently by Mālin with that mace, Garuḍa—
Afflicted by pain, he caused the god to turn his back on the battle. When the god had been turned away by Mālin with Garuḍa,
a great roar arose from the shouting rākṣasas.
Hearing the roar of the shouting Rākṣasas, the younger brother of Indra (Viṣṇu),
though turning his back, hurled his discus with the intent to slay Māli.
That [discus], shining like the solar orb, illuminated the sky with its own radiance.
A wheel resembling the wheel of time struck off the head of Māli. That terrifying head of the lord of the Rākṣasas, severed by the wheel,
fell dripping with blood like the head of Rāhu in ancient times.
Then, by the gods who were greatly rejoiced, a lion’s roar was let forth, impelled by all their vital breaths, as they cried out, "Well done, O God!
Seeing Mālin slain, Sumālī and Mālyavān also [were overcome].
Overwhelmed by grief and tormented by sorrow, the two powerful ones rushed toward Laṅkā;
but the high-minded Garuḍa, having regained his composure and turned back,
being enraged, put the Rākṣasas to flight with the wind from his wings.
Nārāyaṇa, moreover,
tore apart the night-stalkers— whose hair was disheveled as they were struck— with excellent arrows and thunderbolts released from his bow.
Like the great Indra with his thunderbolts and lightning,
he [struck] him whose parasol was shattered, whose weapons were falling,
and whose body was struck down and mangled by arrows.
With entrails protruding and eyes rolling in fear,
that army became like a host of elephants tormented by lions.
The roars and the charges of the night-stalkers together with their elephants became equal [in intensity],
as they were being crushed by that ancient lion.
Being covered by the nets of Hari’s arrows,
yet discharging their own nets of arrows,
the night-stalking clouds rushed forward.
Like dark clouds driven by the wind,
their heads were severed by blows from the discus and their limbs crushed by blows from the mace.
Split in many ways by blows from swords,
the lords of the Rākṣasas fell like mountains;
their lotus-like faces were severed by discuses, and their chests were crushed by maces.
With their necks crushed by plows and their heads split by maces,
some cut by swords and others struck by arrows,
the rākṣasas fell swiftly from the sky into the waters of the ocean.
Then the sky was seen to be filled without interval by night-stalkers, who resembled dark clouds and had their necklaces and earrings fallen away, as they were being struck down.
While that army was being struck from behind by Padmanābha, as if by blue mountains being cast down,
Mālyavat then turned back like an ocean overflowing its shores.
With bloodshot eyes and his crown shaking in rage,
the night-stalker then spoke these harsh words to Padmanābha:
"O Nārāyaṇa, you do not know the eternal dharma of the Kṣatriyas."

"O Lord of the Gods, you who slay us like any other when we are broken and have no heart for battle— O Lord of the Gods, he who commits the sin of killing those with their backs turned does not go to the heaven attained by those of meritorious deeds."
"O wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, do you have a desire for battle?
I stand here; behold and show me whatever strength you possess.
Thus spoke the powerful younger brother of the king of the gods to that lord of the rākṣasas.

"Out of fear of you, I granted the gods freedom from fear; that promise, which included the destruction of the Rākṣasas, is now being fulfilled. Indeed, I must always do what is pleasing to the gods, even at the cost of my own life."
"Therefore, I shall slay you all, even if you have gone to the subterranean realm (rasātala).
As the god, whose eyes were like red lotuses, was speaking thus,
the enraged lord of the rākṣasas pierced him with a spear and let out a roar.
Released from the arm of Mālyavat, the spear, sounding with the ring of its bells,
shone upon the chest of Hari like lightning amidst the clouds.
Then, drawing back that very spear, he who is dear to the wielder of the spear [replied].
Aiming at Mālyavat, the lotus-eyed one hurled it. Released from Govinda’s hand like a spear cast by Skanda, it sped toward the Rākṣasa like a great meteor toward a mountain of collyrium.
7.008.012a It fell upon the broad chest of that lord of the Rākṣasas, which was illuminated by the luster of his necklace; 7.008.012c it struck like a thunderbolt upon the peak of a mountain.
7.008.013a With its armor shattered by that [weapon], he entered into a vast darkness.
7.008.013c Mālyavat, having regained his composure, stood firm like an immovable mountain.
7.008.014a Then, seizing an iron spear bristling with many spikes,
he struck the god firmly between the breasts.
In that very manner, the night-stalker, bloodied by the battle, struck the younger brother of Vāsava with his fist and retreated a distance of a bow's length.
Then, a great sound arose in the sky, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!"

Having struck Viṣṇu, the Rākṣasa then assailed Garuḍa as well. Thereupon, the powerful son of Vinatā, filled with rage, blew the Rākṣasa away with the wind from his wings, just as a strong gale scatters a heap of dry leaves.
Seeing his elder brother driven away by the wind from the wings of the lord of birds,
Sumālī, together with his own forces, fled toward Laṅkā; and the Rākṣasa Mālyavān also, tossed by the force of the wind from the wings, departed.
Having encountered his own forces, he departed for Laṅkā, overcome with shame. Thus, O lotus-eyed Rāma, those Rākṣasas were repeatedly broken in battle by the monkey, their foremost leaders slain.
Unable to fight against Viṣṇu and afflicted by fear,
they abandoned Laṅkā and went to dwell in the netherworld (pātāla) along with their wives,
O descendant of Raghu, having approached the Rākṣasa Sumālin.
Those of renowned prowess who stood in the lineage of Sālakaṭaṅkaṭa—
those Rākṣasas known as the Paulastyas who were indeed slain by you,
including Sumālī, Mālyavān, Mālī, and those who were their leaders.
"O highly fortunate one, all of these are stronger than Rāvaṇa;
and there is no other slayer of the Rākṣasas even among the gods, O conqueror of cities,
except for the divine Nārāyaṇa, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace."
"You are the god Nārāyaṇa, the four-armed, eternal,
invincible, and imperishable Lord, born for the purpose of slaying the Rākṣasas. Then, after some time had passed, there was a Rākṣasa named Sumālī.
7.009.001 He indeed wandered through the entire mortal world from the subterranean realm (rasātala).
7.009.002 Resembling a dark blue cloud and wearing earrings of refined gold,
he took his daughter as a maiden, like the goddess Śrī without her lotus.
Then he saw the Lord of Wealth departing on the Puṣpaka chariot.
Seeing him, who resembled an immortal and was like a blazing fire as he went along,
the Rākṣasa then spoke to his daughter, Kaikasī by name.
"O daughter, this is the time for your giving away; your youth is passing by. For your sake, we have all been restrained by our sense of dharma.
For you, my daughter, are endowed with every virtue, like the goddess Śrī with her lotus."
"Because they fear rejection, you are not being accepted by suitors. Indeed, for all those who desire honor, the state of being a daughter's father is a source of sorrow.
And it is not known, O daughter, which suitor might choose you."

The mother’s family, the father’s family, and the family into which she is given— these three families always remain in a state of uncertainty because of a daughter. Therefore, you [should give me] to that best of the foremost sages, born from the lineage of Prajāpati.
"Go, daughter, and choose Viśravas, the descendant of Pulastya, yourself.
Such sons as these, O daughter, will be yours, without a doubt—
equal in splendor to the sun, just like this Lord of Wealth."
In the meantime, O Rāma, the twice-born son of Pulastya approached his *agnihotra* fire like a fourth sacrificial flame.
But she, disregarding that terrible hour out of reverence for her father, [proceeded].
Approaching before him, she stood with her face cast down toward his feet.
But he, beholding that woman of beautiful hips whose face resembled the full moon,
spoke, most noble and as if blazing with spiritual power.
"O blessed lady, whose daughter are you? Or from where have you come here? What is your purpose, and for what reason? Tell me the truth, O beautiful one.
Thus addressed, the maiden then spoke with her palms joined in reverence.
"O Sage, by your own power, you ought to know my intention.
But know this, O Brahmin: I have come here at the command of my father.
I am Kaikasī by name; you ought to know the rest."
Having entered into meditation, that sage spoke these words:
"O blessed lady, I have understood the reason that is in your mind,
as to why you approached me at such a dreadful hour."
"Therefore, listen, O blessed lady, to the kind of sons you will give birth to:
cruel, of cruel appearance, and fond of a cruel lineage; O fair-hipped one, you shall bring forth Rākṣasas of fierce deeds."
Having heard those words, she bowed down and spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, sons such as these are not worthy of you, who are born from the womb of Brahmā.
Then the sage said there: "That which is your last-born son..."
"He shall be worthy of my lineage and righteous in soul.
Having been addressed thus, O Rāma, after some time that maiden gave birth to a loathsome and most dreadful being in the form of a *rākṣasa*.
Ten-headed, with great tusks, resembling a heap of black collyrium,
with copper-colored lips, twenty arms, a massive mouth, and blazing hair—
just as he was born, jackals with flaming morsels in their mouths [howled].
Flesh-eating beasts performed counter-clockwise circles,
the sky-god rained down blood, and the clouds thundered with harsh sounds.
The sun did not shine in the sky, and great meteors fell upon the earth.
Then his father, who was equal to his grandfather, gave him a name:
"Since he was born with ten heads, he shall be known as Daśagrīva (Ten-necked).
Immediately after him was born the exceedingly powerful Kumbhakarṇa.
From her, whose proportions were so vast that no further measure could be found here on earth,
was born Śūrpaṇakhā, who had a deformed face;
and the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa was the youngest son of Kaikasī.
7.009.028a They grew up there in that great forest, possessing immense power.
7.009.028c Among them, the cruel Daśagrīva became a source of terror to the world. 7.009.029a But Kumbhakarṇa, being intoxicated, [harassed] the great seers who were devoted to dharma.

The wicked one roamed about, terrifying the three worlds and devouring [beings]. But the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, ever established on the path of dharma, dwelt there with his senses restrained, fixed in self-study and moderation in food.
Then, after some time, the god Kubera,
the lord of wealth, arrived there in his Puṣpaka chariot to see his father of great luster.
Seeing him there, blazing as if with splendor, Kaikasī—
Adopting a demonic mindset, she said to the Ten-necked one:
"Look at your brother Vaiśravaṇa, who is endowed with splendor;
even though your status as brothers is equal, look at yourself in such a state."
"O Daśagrīva of immeasurable prowess, exert yourself in such a way that you may quickly become my son, equal to Vaiśravaṇa.
Having heard those words of his mother, the powerful Daśagrīva—
He felt incomparable indignation and then made a vow:
"I promise you truly, O Mother, that before long I shall become equal to or even superior to my brother; cast away the grief dwelling in your heart."
Then, out of that very anger, Daśagrīva, together with his younger brothers, resolved,
"I shall obtain my desire through ascetic penance," and departed for the auspicious hermitage of Gokarṇa in order to achieve his own purpose.
Then Rāma said to the twice-born man: "How were your brothers in the forest?
And what kind of asceticism, O Brahmin, did those of great vows practice then?
Agastya, with a disciplined mind, replied to Rāma there:
There, those brothers engaged in various religious observances;
at that time, Kumbhakarṇa, ever diligent and devoted to dharma,
performed austerities during the summer season while standing amidst five fires.
In the rainy season, drenched by the waters of the clouds, he practiced the *vīrāsana* posture; and during the winter season, he constantly took his shelter in the midst of water.
In this manner, ten thousand years passed for him.
7.010.005c For one striving in dharma and established on the path of the righteous, 7.010.006a Vibhīṣaṇa, however— righteous-souled, eternally devoted to dharma, and pure—
7.010.006c stood for five thousand years upon a single foot.
When his vow was completed, throngs of Apsarases danced;
a rain of flowers fell, and even the gods were stirred with joy.
For five thousand years, he followed after the sun.

With his head and arms held erect, he remained with his mind fixed upon the study of the Vedas. In this manner, ten thousand years passed for Vibhīṣaṇa as well, who was self-restrained, like one dwelling in heaven within the Nandana grove.
For ten thousand years, the ten-faced one remained without food;
when each full thousand years had passed, he offered his head as an oblation into the fire.
In this manner, nine thousand years elapsed for him.
9.10.011c Furthermore, nine of his heads had entered the sacrificial fire.
9.10.012a Then, in the tenth thousandth year, that righteous-souled one, desiring to cut off the tenth head, was approached there by the Grandfather (Brahmā).
But the Grandfather (Brahmā), well-pleased and attended by the gods, addressed him: "Child, child, O Ten-necked One, I am pleased. "Quickly choose, O knower of dharma, whatever boon you desire."
"What desire of yours shall I fulfill today? Your exertion must not be in vain.
Then the Ten-necked one, with a joyful inner soul, bowed his head to the god and spoke with a voice faltering with joy.
"O Blessed One, for living beings there is no fear constant other than death;
there is no enemy equal to death, therefore I choose immortality. [He said:
"Of the Suparṇas, Nāgas, Yakṣas, Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas..."
"O Overseer of Creatures, may I be eternally invulnerable even to the gods.
O you who are worshipped by the immortals, I have no concern for other living beings;
for all creatures, from humans downward, are as mere blades of grass to me."
Thus addressed by the ten-necked Rākṣasa,
O Rāma, the righteous-souled Grandfather, together with the gods, spoke these words:
"O bull among Rākṣasas, it shall indeed be exactly so for you."
7.010.020c Listen further to my auspicious words, spoken here out of affection for you.
7.010.021a O sinless Rākṣasa, those heads which were previously offered by you into the fire shall become yours again exactly as they were before.

"Thus, O Rāma, those heads of the ten-necked Rākṣasa Daśagrīva, which had been offered into the fire as prescribed by his grandfather Prajāpati, indeed rose up again. Having spoken thus to Daśagrīva, Prajāpati—
Then the Grandfather of the World spoke these words to Vibhīṣaṇa:
"O child Vibhīṣaṇa, O knower of dharma, O observer of noble vows, I am well-pleased with you whose intellect is fixed upon righteousness; choose a boon."
But the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, ever endowed with all virtues like the moon with its rays, spoke these words with palms joined in reverence:
"O Blessed One, I have accomplished my purpose, since the Teacher of the World himself [has appeared] before me."
"O you of noble vows, if you are pleased, listen to the boon I must have granted:
whatever thought arises in my mind while I am in whichever stage of life (āśrama) here, let that thought be most righteous, and may I uphold that particular dharma."
"This is considered by me to be the most noble and supreme boon;
for indeed, nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain in this world for those who are devoted to righteousness.
Then Prajāpati, being pleased, spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa.

"O child, since you are so righteous, this shall indeed come to pass. O crusher of foes, because your mind does not turn toward unrighteousness even though you are born from a Rākṣasa womb, I grant you immortality."
7.010.031a O subduer of enemies, as Prajāpati was granting a boon to Kumbhakarṇa, all the gods, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words:
7.010.032a "You must not grant this boon to Kumbhakarṇa for the time being."
For you know how this evil-minded one terrifies the worlds:
seven Apsarases in the Nandana grove and ten followers of Mahendra have been devoured by him, O Brahmin, as have sages and human beings alike.
"O you of immeasurable splendor, let delusion be given to him under the guise of a boon;
thus may there be well-being for the worlds, and he shall be brought to submission.
When the gods had spoken thus, Brahmā, who was born from the lotus, reflected.
As soon as she was thought of, the goddess Sarasvatī appeared by his side.
Standing at his side with palms joined in reverence, Sarasvatī spoke these words: "O Lord, here I am; what task shall I perform for you?"
But Prajāpati spoke these words to Sarasvatī as she arrived:
"O Vāṇī, become the desired deity for the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Having said, "So be it," she entered; then Prajāpati spoke.
"O mighty-armed Kumbhakarṇa, choose whatever boon you desire.
Hearing those words, Kumbhakarṇa spoke this speech:
"O God of gods, it is my wish to sleep for many years."
Having said "So be it" to him, the Grandfather (Brahmā), together with the gods,
and the goddess Sarasvatī likewise, departed for heaven after releasing him.
But the evil-minded Kumbhakarṇa, filled with sorrow, began to reflect.
"What kind of speech was this that has just issued from my mouth today?
Thus, all those brothers of radiant splendor, having obtained their boons,
went to the Śleṣmātaka forest and dwelt there in happiness."
7.011.001a But Sumālī, realizing that those night-stalkers had indeed obtained boons, rose up from the netherworld (rasātala) with his followers, casting aside his fear.
7.011.002a Mārīca, Prahasta, Virūpākṣa, and Mahodara—
7.011.002c The ministers of that Rākṣasa rose up, highly agitated.
7.011.003a Sumālī, surrounded by all those bulls among the Rākṣasas,
approached the Ten-necked one, embraced him, and spoke as follows.
"By good fortune, this long-cherished desire has been fulfilled for you,
that you have obtained such a boon from the most excellent being in the three worlds—
for whose sake we abandoned Laṅkā and went to the subterranean realm."
"O mighty-armed one, that great fear caused by Viṣṇu has now passed for us. For we have been repeatedly defeated by him and, abandoning our own abode,
we all fled together and entered the subterranean realm (rasātala)."
"And this city of Laṅkā belongs to us; it is inhabited by Rākṣasas and was established here by your wise brother, the Lord of Wealth.
O sinless one, if it were possible here through conciliation or through gifts..."
"Or rather, O mighty-armed one, it would be better to bring her back by force;
for you, dear brother, will undoubtedly become the Lord of Laṅkā and the sovereign of us all, O one of great strength."
Then the ten-necked one spoke to his maternal grandfather who stood before him:
"The Lord of Wealth is our elder; you ought not to speak in such a manner.
To Daśagrīva, who had spoken these words, the night-stalker replied:
7.011.011c Prahasta spoke these humble words, full of reason: 7.011.012a "O ten-necked one, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to speak in such a manner.
There is no brotherly affection among heroes; hear these words of mine."
Aditi and Diti were indeed sisters who lived together; they were both wives of Kaśyapa Prajāpati and possessed supreme beauty. Aditi gave birth to the gods, the lords of the three worlds.

Diti, however, gave birth to the Daityas as the offspring of Kaśyapa. O knower of dharma, O hero, in former times this earth— with its forests, oceans, and mountains— belonged to those Daityas, who were exceedingly powerful.
Having slain them in battle by means of the powerful Viṣṇu,
this imperishable triple world was brought under the control of the gods.
You alone shall not bring about a reversal of this state.
"Perform this which was practiced by the gods in the past; carry out these words of mine.
Thus addressed by the evil-minded Prahasta, the ten-necked Rāvaṇa reflected for a moment and said, "So be it."
Filled with that very same joy, on that day the valiant Ten-necked one went to the forest together with those night-rangers. Then,
that night-stalker, the Ten-necked one, remained stationed upon Mount Trikūṭa.
7.011.020c He dispatched Prahasta, who was skilled in speech, on a mission as an envoy.
7.011.021a "O Prahasta, go quickly and speak these words to the bull among the Nairṛtas, the Lord of Wealth, in my name, beginning with words of conciliation."
"O King, this city of Laṅkā belongs to the high-souled Rākṣasas;
it has been settled by you, O gentle one, yet this is not fitting for you, O sinless one.
Therefore, if you are inclined toward conciliation, O you of incomparable prowess, you should give it back."
"By this, my pleasure shall be attained and righteousness itself will be upheld. Having been addressed thus, Prahasta, who was skilled in speech,
went and reported all of Daśagrīva’s words to the Lord of Wealth.
Having heard these words from Prahasta as well, the god Vaiśravaṇa,
who is skilled in speech, replied to Prahasta with these words:
"Go and say to the Ten-necked one that my city and my kingdom [are his]."
"O mighty-armed one, you too shall enjoy this world with its thorns destroyed;
I shall accomplish all this for you, O Lord of Rākṣasas—may prosperity be yours—without delay. However, wait a moment until I announce this to my father."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Wealth went into the presence of his father;
having saluted his elder, he reported what Rāvaṇa desired:
"O Father, this Ten-necked one has dispatched me as a messenger."
"Let the city of Laṅkā, formerly inhabited by the hosts of Rākṣasas, be given [to you].
O you of noble vows, tell me what I must perform here for you.
Thus addressed, that Brahmarṣi Viśravas, the bull among sages, [replied].
He spoke these words to the Giver of Wealth: "Listen, my son, to my words.
The mighty-armed Daśagrīva spoke in my presence;
that evil-minded one was rebuked by me and addressed with many harsh words."
7.011.032a Out of anger, I told him again and again, "Perish! 7.011.032c But listen, my son, to my words which are beneficial and righteous.
7.011.033a Deluded by the granting of the boon, that evil-minded one [failed to distinguish] between those worthy of honor and those unworthy.
Due to my curse, he has become cruel by nature and no longer recognizes me.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, go to Mount Kailāsa, the upholder of the earth;
establish your residence there and abandon Laṅkā along with your followers.
There flows the delightful Mandākinī, the most excellent of rivers,
its waters covered with golden lotuses that shine like the sun. Indeed,
it is not fitting for you to harbor enmity toward that Rākṣasa, the giver of wealth (Kubera).
"For you know how he obtained that supreme boon.
Thus addressed, having accepted those words out of respect for his father,
he departed with his wife, his citizens, his ministers, his vehicles, and his wealth.
Prahasta, having gone to the Ten-necked One, reported everything:
"That city of Laṅkā, thirty yojanas in extent, is empty;
enter it with us and maintain your own dharma there."
Thus addressed by Prahasta, Rāvaṇa the Rākṣasa then entered the city of Laṅkā together with his brother, his army, and his followers.
And he was then consecrated by the night-stalkers.
Daśānana established his city there,
and that city became completely filled with night-stalkers who resembled dark clouds.
Then Dhaneśvara, out of respect for his father’s words,
established his city on the mountain as bright as the moon,
adorned with excellent, well-decorated palaces.
Then, like Amarāvatī belonging to Purandara,
the lord of the Rākṣasas, having been consecrated together with his two brothers,
reflected upon the bestowal of his Rākṣasa sister.

He gave that Rākṣasī sister, named Śūrpaṇakhā, to the lord of the Dānavas, Kālakeya, who was known by the name Vidyujjihva. Then, having given away his sister, the king went out wandering for the hunt.

There, Rāma then beheld a son of Diti named Maya. Seeing him accompanied by a maiden, the night-stalker Daśagrīva asked: "Who are you, standing alone in this forest of wild beasts where no humans dwell?"
Then, O Rāma, Maya spoke to that questioning night-stalker:
"Listen, I shall relate to you everything exactly as it happened.
My dear, there was an Apsaras named Hemā, whom you may have heard of before."
7.012.006c She was given to me by the gods, like Paulomī to Śatakratu.
7.012.007a With my mind attached to her, dear one, I remained for five hundred years;
7.012.007c and she, on account of a divine mission, departed for fourteen years.
And for the sake of that Hemā, I then created by means of my power of illusion the entire city of Hemapura, variegated with diamonds and lapis lazuli; yet,
being deprived of her, I found no pleasure there and was deeply distressed.
"Taking my daughter from that city, I have come to the forest.
O King, this is my own daughter, who grew in her mother's womb;
I have come here together with her to search for her husband."
7.012.011a For the fatherhood of a daughter is indeed a source of sorrow for men who desire honor;
7.012.011c for a daughter always causes two families to remain in a state of uncertainty.
7.012.012a But two sons were born to me from this wife.
"O dear one, Māyāvī was the first, and Dundubhi immediately after him.
All this has been told to you exactly as it happened, since you asked.
Now, O dear one, how may I know you? Who are you?"
Thus addressed, the lord of the Rākṣasas spoke these humble words:
"I am the son of Paulastya, known by the name Daśagrīva. Knowing you to be the son of a Brahmarṣi, O Maya, I have been filled with joy."
7.012.015c He indeed took pleasure there in giving his daughter to him.
7.012.016a Laughing, the lord of the Daityas spoke these words to the lord of the Rākṣasas: 7.012.016c "O King, this daughter of mine was borne by the Apsaras Hema."
"Let this maiden named Mandodarī be accepted as your wife.
"Very well," Rāma replied to the ten-necked one,
and having kindled a fire there, he performed the ceremony of joining hands.
"O Rāma, Maya was indeed not unaware of the curse from that one whose wealth is asceticism;
having learned of it, he gave her to him because of his lineage on his father's side,
and he also bestowed upon him an exceedingly wonderful spear that is never-failing."
By means of that very power obtained through supreme asceticism, he slew Lakṣmaṇa;
thus, having taken a wife, that lord and sovereign went to Laṅkā and brought his two wives from his brothers' city.
Rāvaṇa married as his wife the granddaughter of Vairocana, known by the name Vajrajvālā;
she was the daughter of the high-souled Śailūṣa, the king of the Gandharvas.
7.012.022c Vibhīṣaṇa, who knew the dharma, obtained a wife named Saramā. 7.012.023a She was indeed born upon the shore of Lake Mānasa;
7.012.023c And Lake Mānasa, O dear one, swelled with water at the arrival of the rainy season.
But because her mother had spoken the affectionate and lamenting words,
"Do not grow," she therefore became Saramā.
Thus, having taken wives, those Rākṣasas indeed took their pleasure there.
Taking each their own wife, like Gandharvas in the Nandana grove,
Mandodarī then gave birth to my son Meghanāda;
he is this one who is called Indrajit by you.
Indeed, as soon as he was born long ago, that son of a Rākṣasa let out a great cry while weeping, resembling the roar of a rain-cloud; by that cry of his,
Lankā was truly rendered motionless.
His father himself gave him the name Meghanāda.
O Rāma, he then grew up in the auspicious inner apartments of Rāvaṇa,
protected by excellent women like a fire concealed by logs of wood.
Then, at a certain time, a powerful sleep, sent by Lokeśvara, took bodily form and fell upon Kumbhakarṇa. Thereupon,
Kumbhakarṇa spoke these words to his brother who was seated there.

"O King, sleep afflicts me; please have a dwelling built for me. Thereupon, craftsmen as skilled as Viśvakarman were appointed by the king, and they constructed for Kumbhakarṇa a residence equal to Mount Kailāsa.
They constructed for Kumbhakarṇa a dwelling that was one yojana wide, twice as long, beautiful to behold, and free from all affliction;
it was adorned everywhere with pillars made of crystal, gold, and various other precious materials.
It was adorned with the beauty of lapis lazuli and likewise possessed a network of tinkling bells;
it featured ivory archways and a pedestal of diamond and crystal,
providing constant pleasure in all seasons like a holy cave on Mount Meru.
There, the night-stalker Kumbhakarṇa, having entered into sleep,
did not awaken even while lying for many thousands of years.
But when Kumbhakarṇa was thus overcome by sleep, the Ten-faced one—

He constantly harassed the celestial sages, yakṣas, and gandharvas. Having gone to the various wonderful gardens, such as Nandana and others, the ten-faced one, filled with great rage, would destroy them.
Like an elephant playing in a river, like the wind uprooting trees,
or like a thunderbolt hurled at mountains, he constantly destroys them.
Having learned that the Ten-necked one had behaved in such a manner, the Lord of Wealth [acted].
"O knower of dharma, remembering your own conduct which is worthy of your lineage,
Vaiśravaṇa then dispatched a messenger to Laṅkā for the sake of demonstrating brotherly affection and for the benefit of the Ten-necked one."
Having gone to the city of Laṅkā, he approached Vibhīṣaṇa.
Honored by him according to dharma, he was questioned regarding his arrival. And having inquired after the welfare of the king, as well as his kinsmen and relatives, [he proceeded].

In the assembly hall, he showed him, the ten-faced one, as he sat there. Having seen the king blazing with his own splendor and having honored him with cries of victory, he remained silent for a moment.
When a couch covered with excellent rugs had been brought for him,
the messenger sat down before the Ten-necked one and spoke these words:
"O King, I shall tell you everything that your brother said."
“O gentle one, this is worthy of both your conduct and your lineage.
It is well; this much is sufficient, for you have maintained your integrity. Now, if possible, let a firm commitment to dharma be made.”
"I have seen the Nandana grove destroyed; I have heard that the sages have been slain.
O King, I have also heard of the mobilization of the gods against you.
And yet, O Lord of Rākṣasas, I have been repeatedly rejected by you."
"For one's own kinsmen, even if they have erred through childishness, must be protected.
I, however, have gone to the slopes of the Himalayas to practice dharma,
having undertaken the fierce vow, self-restrained and with senses subdued."
There I beheld the Lord, the God, together with his Goddess Umā.
And there my left eye fell upon the Goddess, thinking, "Who indeed might this beautiful lady be? Surely not for any other reason."
Having assumed an incomparable form, Pārvatī sports there.
Then, by the power of the Goddess, my left eye was scorched;
like a light covered in dust, it turned a tawny color.
Then, having gone to another broad slope of that mountain,
I completed the great vow for eight hundred years.
When that observance was concluded, the god Maheśvara appeared there.
7.013.026c Delighted, with a joyful mind, the Lord spoke these words:
7.013.027a "I am pleased with you, O knower of dharma, because of this austerity, O observer of noble vows;
7.013.027c This very vow was performed by me, and it has been performed by you as well, O Lord of Wealth."
"There is no third person who could observe such a vow;
for this vow is exceedingly difficult to perform, having been established by me alone in the past.
Therefore, O Lord of Wealth, take pleasure in friendship with me."
"O sinless one, because you have been conquered by my ascetic power, become my friend.
Since your left eye has been burnt by the power of the Goddess,
it shall remain forever known by the name 'the one-eyed, tawny one' (Ekākṣi Piṅgalā)."
7.013.031a Thus, having obtained friendship and permission from Śaṅkara,
and having returned, this determination of yours toward evil was heard by me. 7.013.032a Therefore, O defiler of your lineage, desist from this association with the most unrighteous.
"For the gods together with the hosts of sages are indeed contemplating a means for your destruction.
Thus addressed, the ten-necked one became enraged, his eyes bloodshot;
gnashing his teeth and clenching his fists, he spoke these words.
"O messenger, I have understood the words you speak. Neither you nor he by whom you were sent are truly real;
for that guardian of wealth does not speak what is beneficial to me."
"O fool, you are indeed proclaiming your friendship with Maheśvara!
He thinks, 'This elder brother of mine must not be killed.
But having now heard my words, he has formed this resolve."
Relying on the strength of my arms, I shall conquer even the three worlds. For this single moment, for his sake alone,
I shall indeed send those four world-protectors to the abode of Yama.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Laṅkā struck the messenger with his sword and gave him to the evil-minded Rākṣasas to devour. Then,
having performed rites for his own welfare, Rāvaṇa mounted his chariot.
7.013.039c Desiring victory over the three worlds, the Lord of Wealth went there.
7.014.001a Then, together with six ministers who were ever-exceedingly powerful— Mahodara and Prahasta, as well as Mārīca, Śuka, and Sāraṇa— [he departed].
Accompanied by the heroic Dhūmrākṣa, who was ever eager for battle,
the illustrious one set forth, as if burning the worlds with his wrath, [passing] over cities,
rivers, mountains, forests, and groves.
Having passed over [the way] in a moment, he entered Mount Kailāsa.
Perceiving that lord of the Rākṣasas settled upon that mountain,
she said, "This is the king's brother," and went to where the Lord of Wealth was.
Having gone, they reported everything regarding their brother’s resolve;
permitted by the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), they set out for battle. Then, the agitation of the army increased like that of the swelling ocean.
He became like the king of the Nairṛtas shaking the very mountain.
Then a battle ensued, crowded with Yakṣas and Rākṣasas,
and the ministers of that Rākṣasa were distressed there.

Seeing that army in such a state, the night-stalker Daśagrīva let out a roar out of joy and then advanced with fury. As for those ministers of the lord of the Rākṣasas, who possessed terrible prowess—
They fought each one against a thousand times a thousand [demons].
Then, being struck by maces, iron clubs, swords, spears, and javelins,
the ten-necked Rāvaṇa plunged into that army.
Being struck there by them as if he were breathless, the Ten-faced one was hemmed in by the lords of the Yakṣas, who were like raining clouds;
that evil-souled one, raising his mace which resembled the staff of Death, [attacked].
Then he entered the army, sending the yakṣas to the abode of Yama. Like a fire driven by the wind burning a vast thicket filled with dry fuel, he consumed that most dreadful host.
But by those ministers of his, Mahodara, Śuka, and the others,
the Yakṣas were reduced in battle to a small remnant, like clouds scattered by the winds. Some, with their limbs shattered by weapons, fell upon the battlefield.

Biting their own lips with their sharp teeth, they were cast down upon the earth; out of fear, those yakṣas on the field of battle, their weapons fallen, sat huddled together like riverbanks eroded by the waters.
7.014.017 While those who had fallen and were established in heaven watched from the surface of the earth as they fought, there was no space left in the sky for the throngs of seers looking on.
7.014.018 In the meantime, O Rāma, he whose army and vehicles were vast—
A very great yakṣa named Saṃyodhakaṇṭaka arrived;
by that yakṣa, Mārīca was struck down as if by Viṣṇu,
and he fell to the earth like one whose merit is exhausted falling from the sky.
Having regained consciousness after a moment and having rested, the night-stalker fought that yakṣa; and he, being defeated, fled away.
Then [he saw] one whose limbs were variegated with gold and inlaid with beryl and silver.
7.014.021c It entered that gateway, which was the boundary of the gatekeepers.
7.014.022a Then, O Rāma, as the ten-necked night-stalker was entering,
the gatekeeper known as Sūryabhānu stopped him.
Then, having uprooted a gateway, he was struck by that Yakṣa;
the Rākṣasa, hit by the gateway hurled by the Yakṣa,
did not fall to the earth, O Rāma, because of the boon granted by the one born from the waters.
With that very same gateway, he struck the yakṣa;
at that moment, the yakṣa was no longer seen, for he had been reduced to ashes by it.
Then, seeing his prowess, all the yakṣas fled.
7.014.025c Then, afflicted by fear, they entered rivers and caves.
7.015.001a Then, seeing those hundreds of thousands of yakṣas fleeing,
the Lord of Wealth himself went forth toward the battle.
There, a yakṣa named Māṇicāra, who was exceedingly difficult to conquer,
fought together with four thousand yakṣas.
They [attacked] with maces, clubs, spears, javelins, lances, and hammers.
Striking them in battle, the yakṣas rushed against the rākṣasas.
Then, a thousand were slain in that combat by Prahasta,
and another thousand were killed by Mahodara with his mace.
And then, O Rāma, by the enraged and evil-minded Mārīca,
two thousand [demons] were struck down in the mere twinkling of an eye. Having encountered Dhūmrākṣa in that great battle, Māṇibhadra—
Struck on the chest with a mace by Māṇibhadra out of anger, he did not tremble;
then, having brandished a club, the Rākṣasa Dhūmrākṣa was struck on the head by Māṇibhadra and fell down overwhelmed.
Seeing Dhūmrākṣa struck down and fallen, drenched in blood,
the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa), highly incensed, rushed toward Maṇibhadra.
As he charged forward in fury like the fire rising at the end of an eon—
The bull among Yakṣas struck him with three spears.
Then, struck in battle by the king of the Rākṣasas with a mace,
his crown was knocked to one side by that blow.
From that time forth, that Yakṣa has been known as Pārśvamauli.
But when that high-souled Yakṣa Māṇibhadra turned his face away,
O Rāma, a tremendous clamor arose on that mountain.
Then, from afar, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), the wielder of the mace, was seen;
his two feet were marked with white lotuses and surrounded by conch shells.
Seeing his brother in battle, his dignity diminished by the curse, he [approached].
The wise one spoke words appropriate for the lineage of the Grandfather:
"O evil-minded one, though you were being restrained by me, you did not understand;
later, having reached the fruit of this [action] and gone to hell, you will know."

For that man who, having drunk poison out of delusion, does not realize it at first, will later, in its full effect, understand the fruit of his action as a fool. Indeed, the deities rejoice when someone is endowed with righteousness.
And you do not realize that by which you have been brought to such a state.
For he who treats his mothers, fathers, brothers, and teachers with contempt—
having fallen under the power of the King of the Dead— he beholds the fruit of that action.
For he who does not practice the acquisition of austerity while the body is unstable,
that fool suffers later, having seen his own fate after death. Indeed,
the intellect of any foolish person does not arise according to their own will.

Whatever kind of action one performs, such is the fruit one reaps. Men obtain intelligence, beauty, strength, wealth, sons, and even greatness— all of these through their own previously performed deeds.
"Thus you are destined for hell, since your mind is such as this. I will not speak further with you; this is the verdict for one of evil conduct.
Having spoken thus, he then summoned his ministers.

Led by Mārīca, they all turned their faces away and fled in all directions. Then, though struck on the head with a mace by that high-souled lord of the Yakṣas, the Ten-necked one did not waver from his place.
Then, O Rāma, as those two were striking each other in that supreme combat,
they did not become overwhelmed nor exhausted due to their indignation.
Thereupon, Dhanada released the Āgneya weapon in the battle.

The ten-necked one warded off that weapon with a *vāruṇa* [missile]. Then, having entered into a *rākṣasa* illusion, the lord of the *rākṣasas* brandished a massive club and struck Dhanada on the head.
Thus struck by him,
the Lord of Wealth, overwhelmed and drenched in blood, fell down like an *aśoka* tree whose roots have been severed.
Then, there, that Lord of Wealth [was surrounded] by the treasures, Padma and the others.
Having brought him to the Nandana grove, the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) then consoled him.
Then, O Rāma, having defeated that Giver of Wealth, the lord of the rākṣasas seized his Puṣpaka chariot, the very emblem of victory.
Enveloped by golden pillars, with archways of lapis lazuli gems,
covered with nets of pearls, and filled with trees that yield the fruits of all desires— the king ascended that chariot which moves at will and was won through his own prowess.

Having defeated the god Vaiśravaṇa, he descended from Kailāsa. O Rāma, having thus conquered his brother, the giver of wealth, that lord of the rākṣasas then went to the Śaravaṇa forest, the birthplace of Mahāsena.
Then the Ten-necked One beheld a golden forest of reeds,
enveloped by a network of rays like a second sun;
