having reached that mountain with its somewhat lovely interior of woods.
7.016.003c There he saw the Puṣpaka chariot suspended in the sky.
7.016.004a Seeing the Puṣpaka— capable of going anywhere at will— rendered motionless,
the Rākṣasa, surrounded by his ministers, began to reflect.
"Why is it that this Puṣpaka does not move for my sake? While I am stationed atop the mountain, whose deed could this be?
Then Mārīca, skilled in discernment, spoke to the Ten-necked One:

"O King, it is not for no reason that this Puṣpaka does not proceed. Then, approaching the side of Bhava, the powerful attendant Nandīśvara spoke these words to the lord of the Rākṣasas without hesitation.
"Turn back, O Ten-necked One! Śaṅkara is sporting upon this mountain.
This mountain has been made inaccessible to all living beings—suparṇas, nāgas, yakṣas, daityas, dānavas, and rākṣasas."
With eyes copper-red from rage, he descended from the Puṣpaka chariot and,
saying "Who is this Śaṅkara?", approached the foot of the mountain.
Then he beheld the lord Nandīśvara standing nearby.
Grasping his blazing trident like a second Śaṅkara,
that Rākṣasa, seeing the monkey-faced one, disregarded him and,
out of folly, let out a roar of laughter like a water-laden cloud.
7.016.013a The venerable Nandin, an alternative form of Śaṅkara, became enraged;
7.016.013c there he spoke to the Rākṣasa Daśagrīva who stood before him:
7.016.014a "O evil-minded Rākṣasa, since you, upon seeing me in the form of a monkey..."
Out of folly you despise me and you utter derisive laughter; therefore, monkeys endowed with my form and equal in prowess and splendor to my own shall be born for the sake of destroying your lineage.
"O night-stalker, what can I possibly do for you now, since you are not to be killed? For you have already been slain by your own past deeds.
Disregarding those words of Nandi, the night-stalker then—
Having reached that mountain, he spoke these words:
"O Lord of Mountains, because of you my movement as I travel has been cut off;
therefore, I shall uproot this mountain from its very foundation."
"By what power does Bhava sport there like a king? You do not recognize that which must be known; a place of terror has arrived.
Having spoken thus, O King, he then threw his arms upon the mountain.
He lifted that mountain, together with its deer, serpents,
and trees. Then, O Rāma, Mahādeva, seeing what he had done, laughed and playfully pressed down that mountain with his big toe.
Then those arms of his, being thus tormented, sank down beneath the mountain;
and there the ministers of that *rākṣasa* were struck with amazement by that *rākṣasa*,
due both to his wrath and the crushing of their arms.
A truly great roar was released, by which the three worlds were filled. Terrified by the sound, human beings thought the destruction of the world had come;
even the deities were agitated and faltered in their respective duties.
7.016.025a Then Mahādeva, standing upon the mountain peak, was pleased;
7.016.025c releasing his arms, O King, he spoke these words to the ten-faced one:
7.016.026a "O night-stalker, I am pleased with your heroism and your prowess."
From that most dreadful sound of his crying out, released from pain,
these three worlds were made to shriek and were struck with fear;
therefore, you shall be known by the name Rāvaṇa.
"Devas, humans, yakṣas,
and whoever else exists upon the surface of the earth will thus address you as Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out.
Go, O descendant of Pulastya, with confidence by whichever path you desire."
"O Lord of the Rākṣasas, you have been granted permission by me; you may go.
Having thus been given his name by Maheśvara himself, he who was named Rāvaṇa paid homage to Mahādeva and ascended that celestial chariot.

7.016.031a Then, O Rāma, Rāvaṇa roamed across the surface of the earth, 7.016.031c harassing Kṣatriyas of great prowess here and there. 7.017.001a Then, O King, that mighty-armed one, wandering over the surface of the earth—

Having reached the forest of the Himalayas, Rāvaṇa wandered about. There he saw a maiden wearing a bark-garment and matted hair, engaged in the practice of the sages, performing austerities like a goddess.
Having seen that maiden, endowed with beauty and firm in her great vow,
his soul overwhelmed by the delusion of lust, he asked as if laughing:
"What is this that you are doing, O blessed lady, which is so contrary to your youth?"
"Indeed, this treatment is not fitting for such beauty as yours.
O blessed one, whose daughter are you? And who is your husband, O sinless lady?
Tell me quickly as I ask: what is the motive for your accumulation of ascetic merit?"
Thus addressed by that ignoble Rākṣasa, the maiden,
whose wealth was her asceticism, performed the rites of hospitality for him according to tradition and replied:
"My father is the righteous Brahmarṣi named Kuśadhvaja."

The illustrious son of Bṛhaspati was equal to Bṛhaspati himself in intelligence. As that high-souled one was constantly engaged in the study of the Vedas, a daughter born of his speech was produced; she is known by the name Vedavatī.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas,
and Pannagas, went to my father and requested him for my hand;
yet, O Lord of Rākṣasas, that father did not give me to them.
I shall tell you the reason for this; listen, O mighty-armed one!
It is said that Viṣṇu, the supreme lord of the gods, is the son-in-law of my father;
since he is the desired lord of the three worlds, no other man can be my father-in-law.

Hearing that the righteous-souled one wished to give [the kingdom], King Śambhu, who was arrogant in his strength, became enraged at the Daityas. By that wicked man, my father was slain while he was fast asleep at night.
Then my mother, distressed and highly fortunate, embraced that body of my father and entered the fire along with it. Thereafter,
the desire of my father regarding Nārāyaṇa was fulfilled.

"The desire 'I shall do it' is firmly established in my heart; even for my father who has gone to the realm of the departed, I shall fulfill his longing. Having made this vow, I am practicing extensive austerity.
7.017.016a All this has been told to you by me, O bull among Rākṣasas; 7.017.016c know that I have taken refuge in Dharma through the will of Nārāyaṇa, my husband.
7.017.017a For you are known to me, O King; go now, O delighter of the Paulastyas.

"By means of my ascetic power, I know everything that exists within the three worlds. Then Rāvaṇa, afflicted by the arrows of Kandarpa, descended from the top of his celestial chariot and spoke there to that maiden of great vows.
"You are deluded, O fair-hipped one, you whose mind is such as this;
for you, O fawn-eyed one, the accumulation of dharma shines brightly among the elders. Endowed with every virtue, you ought not to do such a thing."

"O timid one, O most beautiful woman in the three worlds, you are in your youth; what manner of decrepitude do you see? And who is this person whom you address as Viṣṇu—[one who is superior] in heroism, ascetic power, enjoyment, and strength?"
"O blessed lady, O beautiful woman, he whom you desire is not my equal.
"Do not say such a thing," the maiden said to that night-stalker,
while the Rākṣasa seized her by the hair with the tips of his fingers.
Then Vedavatī, enraged, tore out her hair with her hand;
having prepared the fire, she spoke in haste, intent on death:
"O ignoble one, since I have been violated by you, my life is no longer worth living."
"Therefore, O Rākṣasa, while you look on, I shall enter the fire.
But because I, though innocent, have been insulted like one who is helpless,
I shall indeed be born again for the purpose of slaying you."
"O wicked one, it is not possible for a woman to destroy you, especially since you are such a person. Furthermore, if I were to cast a curse upon you, my ascetic merit would be exhausted.
However, if there is anything at all that I have done, given, or offered in sacrifice..."
"By this act, may I become a virtuous daughter born not from a womb to a righteous man.
Having spoken thus, she entered the blazing fire,
and a divine shower of flowers fell from the sky on all sides.
"Previously, that enemy who was slain by you was already struck down by anger;
relying upon your superhuman prowess which resembles a mountain, he was thus destroyed.
In this same way, this highly fortunate woman is born again among mortals."
When the field was being furrowed by the mouth of the plow, this [river], resembling a crest of fire upon the altar,
was formerly known as Vedavatī in the Kṛta Yuga;
but upon reaching the Tretā Yuga, she appeared for the sake of slaying that Rākṣasa.
7.017.031e Because she was born from cold, she is further called Śītā by humans. 7.018.001a But when Vedavatī had entered the fire, Rāvaṇa,
having mounted that Puṣpaka chariot, wandered over the earth.
Then, having reached Uśīrabīja, that Rākṣasa beheld King Marutta performing a sacrifice together with the gods;
there he saw the Brahman-sage named Saṃvarta, the actual brother of Bṛhaspati.
7.018.003c The knower of dharma, surrounded by all the hosts of Brahmins, performed the sacrifice.
7.018.004a But seeing that Rākṣasa invincible due to the granting of the boon, the gods,
fearing his assault, entered various wombs.
Indra became a peacock, while Dharmarāja became a crow; the Lord of Wealth became a chameleon, and Varuṇa indeed became a swan.
And having approached that king, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas—
"Give me battle," he said, "or say, 'I am defeated.
Then King Marutta asked him, "Who are you?
Thereupon, casting aside his mockery, the Rākṣasa spoke these words.
"O King, I am pleased with you because of your lack of curiosity,
since you do not recognize me as Rāvaṇa, the younger brother of the Giver of Wealth. Who exists in the three worlds who does not know my power?"
"By whom this brother was defeated and this celestial chariot was seized.
Then King Marutta spoke to that Rākṣasa:
"Truly, you are fortunate, for by you the elder brother was conquered in battle."

7.018.011a An act joined with unrighteousness is not praiseworthy, nor is one that is contrary to the world. 7.018.011c Having committed an act of wickedness, you boast of your victory over your brother. 7.018.012a What excellent boon did you obtain by practicing dharma alone in the past?
"For never before have I heard such words as you yourself have spoken.
Then, seizing his bow and arrows, that king set out for battle in a rage; Saṃvarta blocked his path.
That great seer spoke with affection to Marutta:
"If my words are worthy of being heard, you must refrain from this combat;
for if this sacrifice dedicated to Maheśvara is not completed, it will consume your lineage."
"How can there be war for one who is consecrated? How can there be cruelty in one who is consecrated? Furthermore, there is constant uncertainty in battle, and this Rākṣasa is difficult to conquer.
At these words of his preceptor, Marutta, the lord of the earth, desisted.
Having cast aside his bow and arrow, he became composed and turned toward the sacrifice. Then, considering him defeated, Śuka proclaimed, "Rāvaṇa has won! and let out a roar of joy.

Having devoured those great seers who had come to the sacrifice while they remained there, and being satiated with their blood, he returned once more to the earth. When Rāvaṇa had departed, the gods and the inhabitants of heaven, including Indra, [returned].
Then, having returned to their own source, those beings spoke;
at that time, Indra, out of joy, spoke to the peacock with the blue plumage:
"O knower of dharma, O bird, I am pleased with you because of your service."

"O lord of men, those thousand eyes of mine shall become your peacock feathers; when I pour down rain, you shall obtain joy as a sign of my favor. Indeed, O ruler of men, in ancient times the feathers of peacocks were blue."
7.018.022c Having obtained a boon from the Lord of the Suras, they all returned to their various forms.
7.018.023a O Rāma, Dharmarāja spoke to the crow standing in the sacrificial hall:
7.018.023c "O bird, I am well-pleased with you; listen to the words of one who is pleased."

"Just as other living beings are afflicted by various diseases, those [diseases] shall not prevail over me when I am pleased; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, O bird, you have no fear of death, for I grant you this boon."
"As long as men do not slay you, so long shall you remain. Furthermore,
those humans dwelling within my domain who are afflicted by hunger will become satisfied along with their kinsmen once you have eaten."
7.018.027a Varuṇa then spoke to the swan who roamed the waters of the Gaṅgā:
7.018.027c "O lord of birds, listen with a heart full of joy to these words:
7.018.028a 'Your color is enchanting and gentle, resembling the orb of the moon.'"
"Having entered my body, you shall become exalted, possessing a luster like white foam, and you will be eternally beautiful;
you shall attain incomparable joy— this is the sign of my affection."
"O Rāma, in former times the color of swans was not entirely white;
their wings were covered with blue tips, and their breasts were as pure as the tips of young grass.
Then Vaiśravaṇa spoke to the chameleon standing on the mountain.
"I bestow upon you this golden complexion, and I shall also grant you joy. Your head shall forever possess wealth and be inexhaustible;
by my favor, this golden hue shall belong to you."
7.018.033a Having thus granted those boons to them during that sacrificial festival, the gods,
7.018.033c when it had concluded, returned to their own abodes together with the king.
7.019.001a Then, having defeated Marutta, that lord of the Rākṣasas departed.
Desiring battle, the Ten-faced one approached the cities of the lords of men; having encountered those great kings who were like Mahendra and Varuṇa,
the lord of the Rākṣasas said, "Give me battle!"
"Say, 'We have been conquered,' for this is my firm resolve. For those who act otherwise, liberation from me will not be possible.
Then many wise kings, firm in their commitment to righteousness, [spoke].
"‘We have been conquered,’ they said, having recognized the superior strength of their enemy.
Duṣyanta, Suratha, Gādhi, King Gaya, and Purūravas—
all these monarchs, O dear one, declared, ‘We have been conquered.’"
Then, having reached Ayodhyā— which was well-guarded by Anaraṇya like Amarāvatī by Śakra— Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas,
approached the king and said, "Grant me battle."
"Or say, 'I am defeated'; this is my command here.
Then Anaraṇya, greatly incensed, spoke to the lord of the rākṣasas:
"O sovereign of the rākṣasas, a duel shall be granted to you by me."
Then, that very great army of the lord of men, which had previously been prepared with the purpose heard earlier, marched forth intent on the slaughter of the Rākṣasa;
it consisted of many thousands of elephants and likewise ten thousand horses.

Covering the earth, he emerged in an instant with his infantry and chariots. Upon encountering that army of Rāvaṇa, O King, the force of that lord of the earth perished then and there, like an oblation poured into the fire.
7.019.012a That lord of men beheld his great army perishing,
like the waters of the five rivers upon reaching the great ocean.
7.019.013a Then, stretching his bow himself, which resembled the rainbow of Śakra—
Overcome with rage, that lord of men struck Rāvaṇa;
then, the joy of the Ikṣvāku dynasty loosed eight hundred arrows upon the head of that king of the Rākṣasas.
As those arrows fell upon him, they did not cause a wound anywhere,
just as streams of water falling from clouds leave no mark on the summit of a mountain.
Then, by the enraged king of the Rākṣasas, the monarch was [struck] at that time.
Struck on the head by that palm, he fell down from his chariot.
That king, fallen upon the ground with trembling limbs and agitated,
was like a great *sāla* tree in the forest struck down by a thunderbolt.
Laughing, the Rākṣasa said to that Ikṣvāku lord of the earth:
"What fruit have you now obtained by fighting against me? O lord of men, there is no one in the three worlds who could withstand a duel with me."
"I suspect you are intoxicated by pleasures and do not hear my strength. To him who was speaking thus, the king, his life-breath failing, replied:
"What indeed can be done here, since time is insurmountable?"

"O Rākṣasa, I have not been defeated by you, who praise yourself; rather, I am ruined here by Time, and you have merely become the instrument for my destruction. But now that my life is at its end, what can possibly be done by me?"
"O Rākṣasa, because I have been favored by the Ikṣvākus, I shall speak these words: If I have given gifts, if I have offered oblations, if I have performed well-performed austerity,
and if my subjects have been properly protected— by all this, may my word come true."
"In this very lineage of the high-souled Ikṣvākus,
there shall arise a king of supreme splendor who will take away your life.
Then, like a formidable rain-cloud, the drum of the gods was struck.
When that curse had been uttered, a rain of flowers fell from the sky.
Then, O Indra among kings, that monarch departed for his station in Triviṣṭapa.
And when the king had ascended to heaven, O Rāma, that rākṣasa turned back.

Then, terrifying mortals upon the earth, the lord of the Rākṣasas encountered Nārada, the best of sages, in that dense thicket. But Nārada, the celestial seer of great splendor and immeasurable radiance—
Seated upon the back of a cloud, he spoke to Rāvaṇa, who was stationed in the Puṣpaka chariot:
"O gentle lord of the rākṣasas, son of Viśravas, stay!
O you endowed with noble lineage, I am pleased with your mighty exploits."
Viṣṇu has been greatly gratified by the slaying of the Daityas, by Tārkṣya’s subduing of the serpents, and by your own crushing of foes in battle; yet,
I shall say something to you, which you must listen to if you will hear it.
"O bull among Rākṣasas, immediately upon hearing this, you must act.
Why is this world being slaughtered by you, who cannot be slain even by the gods?
For this world is already as good as dead once it has fallen under the power of Death."
7.020.007a Behold, O mighty-armed one, the lord of the Rākṣasas who has become human;
7.020.007c this world of manifold purposes, whose course is not understood. 7.020.008a In some places, musical instruments and dances are enjoyed by joyful people.

Others, afflicted and with faces and eyes streaming with tears, weep; for this person, destroyed by delusion through affection for mother, father, and son, and through the charms of wife and kinsmen, does not perceive his own suffering.
"7.020.010a Why, then, having thus afflicted the world which is already overcome by delusion?
7.020.010c O gentle one, the mortal world has already been conquered by you; of this there is no doubt.
7.020.011a Thus addressed, the Lord of Laṅkā, blazing as it were with splendor,"
Having greeted Nārada there with a smile, he said to him:
"O great seer, who sports among gods and gandharvas and who delights in battle,
I am indeed prepared to go to the subterranean realm (rasātala) seeking victory."
"Then, having conquered the three worlds and brought the Nāgas and gods under my control,
I shall churn the ocean, the abode of fluids, for the sake of the nectar of immortality.
Then the venerable sage Nārada spoke to the Ten-necked One:
"Where indeed will you go now by this path?
This road leading toward the city of the King of the Ancestors is truly difficult to traverse; it is impassable, O subduer of enemies, for Yama."
But having let out a laugh that resembled an autumnal cloud, the Ten-faced one said,
"It is done," and spoke these words:
"Therefore, O Great Brahmin, he is intent on the slaying of Vaivasvata."
"I am going to the southern quarter where the king, the son of the Sun, resides.
For, O Blessed One, desiring battle, I made a vow out of anger:
'I shall conquer the four world-protectors,' O Lord."
"By that [deed], I have indeed set out toward the city of the King of the Ancestors;
I shall unite this perpetrator of suffering for living beings with Death.
Having spoken thus, the Ten-necked One paid homage to that sage.
He set out toward the southern direction together with his joyful ministers.
But Nārada, of great splendor, having remained in meditation for a moment,
that best of Brahmins reflected like a smokeless fire.
By whom the three worlds, including Indra, along with all things moving and stationary, are afflicted;
when his lifespan and merit are exhausted, how indeed can that Time be harmed?
He by whose constant fear the three worlds flee, tormented by dread.
How can that lord of the Rākṣasas approach him in person—
he who is both the ordainer and the sustainer according to one's good and evil deeds, and by whom the three worlds have been conquered? How indeed will he ever defeat him?
"What else could he have done that would result in such an arrangement? Driven by curiosity, I shall go to the abode of Yama.
Having reflected thus, the lord of brahmins, swift in his stride, departed.
To relate exactly what had occurred regarding Yama’s abode:
he saw Yama there, the god, preceded by Agni,
presiding over the ordinance according to the nature of each living being.

7.021.003a But Yama, seeing that the great seer Nārada had arrived there, 7.021.003c spoke to him as he sat comfortably after offering him the traditional guest-offering (arghya) according to dharma: 7.021.004a "Is all well, O divine seer? Does dharma not perish?"
"What is the purpose of your arrival, O you who are served by gods and gandharvas?
Then the venerable rishi Nārada spoke these words:
"Listen, I shall declare it; let the prescribed ritual be performed."
"O King of the Ancestors, this night-stalker named Daśagrīva approaches with the intent to bring you, who are so difficult to conquer, under his control by means of his prowess.
For this reason, O Lord, I have come here in haste."
"What indeed will your staff-weapon do today?
In that interval, from afar, there was seen approaching the divine celestial chariot of that Rākṣasa, shining like the risen sun.
Having made that entire region free from darkness by the radiance of that *puṣpaka*, the mighty one approached nearby. Then,
the ten-necked one of great arms looked here and there.
7.021.010c Living beings were experiencing the fruits of their good deeds as well as their evil deeds.
7.021.011a Then, as they were being tormented by their own evil karmas, the powerful Rāvaṇa, by means of his prowess, forcibly liberated them.
7.021.012 While the pretas were being released by the powerful Rākṣasa,
the guardians of the pretas, highly enraged, rushed toward the lord of the Rākṣasas.
7.021.013 They [assailed him] with spears, iron clubs, pikes, mallets, javelins, and lances.
7.021.013c The heroes showered Puṣpaka by the hundreds of thousands. 7.021.014a They quickly shattered its seats, palaces, altars, and carpets, like bees [devouring flowers].
7.021.015a That Puṣpaka chariot, which had become the very seat of the gods in battle,
7.021.015c remained likewise indestructible by the power of Brahmā’s splendor even as it was being shattered.
7.021.016a Then those ministers of Rāvaṇa, according to their desire and according to their strength, [acted].
Those of great prowess fought, as did that ten-faced king;
their limbs smeared with blood and struck by every kind of weapon,
the ministers of the lord of the Rākṣasas waged a great battle.
And those highly fortunate ones struck one another with weapons in battle—
the great army of Yama and the ministers of the Rākṣasa. Yet,
they abandoned those ministers of the mighty Rākṣasa.
They rushed toward that very Ten-faced one with showers of spears.
Then, his limbs smeared with blood and mangled by the blows,
that best of Rākṣasas shone in his celestial chariot like a blossoming Aśoka tree.
7.021.021a That powerful one, by the strength of his weapons, released spears, maces, darts, pikes, javelins, and arrows; 7.021.021c as well as clubs, stones, and trees.
But having warded off all those [missiles] and neutralized that weapon, [the opponent acted].
7.021.022c Those hundreds of thousands struck down that single, terrible Rākṣasa.
7.021.023a And they all surrounded him like masses of clouds surrounding a mountain;
7.021.023c with *bhindipāla* slings and spears, they rendered him breathless.
His armor shattered and enraged, drenched by streams of blood,
he abandoned the Puṣpaka chariot and stood upon the earth.
Then that lord of the Rākṣasas remained on the ground, equipped with his bow and arrows.
Regaining consciousness after a moment, he stood enraged like the God of Death.
Then, having fixed the divine Pāśupata weapon upon his bow, he cried out to them, "Stay! Stay! and drew that bow back.
That arrow, garlanded with flames and followed by flesh-eating spirits, having been released in battle,
rushed forward after reducing the thickets and trees to ashes.
Those soldiers of Vaivasvata were consumed by its fiery energy.
In that battle, they fell like trees consumed by a forest fire.
Then that Rākṣasa of terrifying prowess, together with his ministers,
let out a tremendous roar as if making the earth tremble.
7.022.001 Hearing that great roar of his, Yama, the son of Vivasvat,
considered his enemy victorious and his own army destroyed. 7.022.002 Thinking his warriors slain, his eyes became clouded with rage.
He quickly said to the charioteer, "Let the chariot be brought near.
Having presented a divine, loud-sounding chariot to him, the charioteer stood by,
and that one of great splendor ascended the great chariot.
And Death stood before him, holding a noose and a mallet in his hands—
he by whom the entire triple world, with all that is moving and unmoving, is brought to an end. And the Staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa) stood at his side, embodied and stationed upon the chariot.
That divine weapon of Yama, as if blazing with splendor,
[fell]. Then the three worlds were terrified and the inhabitants of heaven trembled,
seeing Kāla enraged and bringing fear to the three worlds.

But when the ministers of the lord of the Rākṣasas saw that deformed chariot, accompanied by Death and bringing terror to all the worlds, they were all overcome by fear; their courage failing them, they lost their senses and were tormented by dread.
"7.022.008c We are not capable of fighting here," they said, and fled away.
7.022.009a But seeing that chariot, which brought fear to the world, 7.022.009c the Rākṣasa was not agitated then, nor did any distress arise within him.
But having encountered Rāvaṇa and discharging spears and javelins,
the enraged Yama cut through the vital organs of the Rākṣasa.
Rāvaṇa, however, remaining composed and steady, released a shower of arrows.
Upon that chariot of Vaivasvata, he was like a cloud pouring down a rain of water.
Then, as hundreds of great spears were being hurled at his broad chest,
that Rākṣasa, tormented by the shafts, was unable to retaliate.

Thus, for seven nights, though he was struck with various weapons by Yama, the crusher of enemies, the army was neither broken nor defeated. Then, once again, a battle took place between Yama and the Rākṣasa.
Desirous of victory there and never retreating in battles,
the gods, along with the gandharvas, siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis,
placing Prajāpati at their head, beheld that field of battle.
As those two fought, it was like the dissolution of the worlds for the chief of the Rākṣasas and the lord of the Pretas.
Then the king of the Rākṣasas, enraged, drew his bow in the encounter.
Making the sky appear as if it were without any gaps, he released his arrows;
with four shafts he struck Death, with seven he afflicted the charioteer,
and with a thousand arrows he swiftly struck Yama in his vital organs.
Then, from the mouth of Yama as he suddenly became enraged, there issued forth a breath wreathed in flames, like the fire of his wrath. Then the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas beheld that marvel.
Seeing the blazing fire born of his wrath, desiring to consume the enemy's army, Death, being supremely enraged, then spoke to Vaivasvata:
"O Lord, release me quickly; I shall slay the enemy in battle."
Naraka, Śambara, Vṛtra, Śambhu, the powerful Kārtasvara,
Namuci, Virocana, and both Madhu and Kaiṭabha—
these and many other mighty and invincible beings [were slain].
"I have seen those fallen into misfortune; what anxiety can there be regarding this night-stalker?
Release me quickly, O knower of dharma, so that I may slay him. For I have never seen anyone who survives even for a moment [once attacked by him]."
"This is not my power; rather, this is a natural boundary. For it is certain that no one touched by me shall live.
Having heard these words, the majestic Dharmarāja [Yudhiṣṭhira]...
There he said to Death, "I shall slay this man.
Then the lord Vaivasvata, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
took up that infallible Staff of Time (*kāladaṇḍa*) in his hand and brandished it.
On his sides stand the seamless nooses of Time (Kālapāśa),
and a personified mallet, resembling the touch of fire, stands ready;
by the mere sight of it, he severs the life-breaths of living beings.
How much more so, then, when a living being is struck or even oppressed? That staff, surrounded by flames as if drinking up the night-stalker,
becomes exceedingly terrible and enraged when touched by the hand of a powerful man.
Then all the beings fled from that battlefield; and the gods were agitated upon seeing Yama with the staff of death raised.
As he was desirous of striking Rāvaṇa, having lifted up his staff—
7.022.032c The Grandfather, having shown himself directly to Yama, spoke these words:
7.022.033a "O Vaivasvata, O mighty-armed one of incomparable prowess, you must certainly not strike this night-stalker with this staff."
"O bull among the gods, a boon has indeed been granted by me to him;
therefore, you must not make false that word which was uttered by me.
For this [boon] is unfailing in the destruction of all creatures."
7.022.035c The Staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa) was created by me in the past, preceded by Death itself.
7.022.036a Therefore, O gentle one, this must certainly not be hurled by you at the head of the Rākṣasa; 7.022.036c for once it has fallen upon him, no one lives even for a moment.
For if this Rākṣasa were not to die when struck by this [weapon],
or if the Ten-necked one were to die [instead], in either case it would be a falsehood. Therefore,
O Lord of Rākṣasas, restrain today this one who is intent on killing him with punishment.
"Having considered the worlds, make this truth of mine come true.
Thus addressed, the righteous-souled Yama then replied:
"This rod of punishment has been turned back, for you are our sovereign lord."
7.022.040a But what can I possibly do now while standing on the battlefield?
7.022.040c Since this Rākṣasa, arrogant because of his boon, must not be slain by me;
7.022.041a therefore, I shall vanish from the sight of this Rākṣasa.
Having spoken thus, he vanished right there along with his chariot and horses.
But Daśagrīva, having conquered him and proclaimed his own name,
departed from the abode of Yama in great joy by means of the Puṣpaka chariot.
Then Vaivasvata, together with the gods led by Brahmā,
and the great sage Nārada, departed for the third heaven in high spirits.
Having thus conquered Yama, the bull among the thirty gods, the ten-necked one—
7.023.001 Rāvaṇa, boasting of his victory, beheld his own companions.
7.023.002 Having then congratulated Mārīca and the others on their victory, they all, consoled by Rāvaṇa, mounted the Puṣpaka chariot.
Then, delighted, he entered Rasātala, the oceanic abode,
which was inhabited by hosts of Daityas and Uragas and well-guarded by Varuṇa. Having reached the city of Bhogavatī, protected by Vāsuki, he—
Having brought the *nāgas* under his control, he proceeded to the city of Maṇimatī. There dwelt the Daityas known as the Nivātakavacas, who had obtained boons;
encountering them, the Rākṣasa challenged them to battle.
All those Daityas, exceedingly valiant and possessed of great strength,
fought there with various weapons, intoxicated by the frenzy of battle;
and as they were thus engaged in combat, more than a full year passed away.
And there was neither victory nor even destruction for either of the two sides. Then the Grandfather, the imperishable refuge of the three worlds,
arrived swiftly there, the god mounted upon his excellent celestial chariot.
Having halted that act of war against the Nivātakavacas,
the aged Grandfather, who understood the true state of affairs, spoke these words:
"Indeed, this Rāvaṇa cannot be conquered in battle even by the gods and the asuras."
"You cannot be brought to ruin even by the gods and asuras together with Indra.
Indeed, friendship with this Rākṣasa is pleasing to you;
for there is no doubt that all interests of friends are shared in common."

Then Rāvaṇa formed a friendship there with the Nivātakavacas, having them as witnesses by fire; he was filled with joy and dwelt happily among them for a year, being honored by them according to custom.
7.023.013c And Daśānana received worship no different from that given in his own city. 7.023.014a But having mastered ninety-nine illusions, that self-possessed one,
seeking the city of the Lord of Waters, wandered through the netherworld (rasātala).
Then, having conquered in a mere moment the city named Aśmanagara, which was protected by the Kālakeyas, he slew four hundred Daityas. After that,
[he encountered] a mountain resembling a white cloud, standing like Mount Kailāsa.
The lord of the rākṣasas beheld the divine abode of Varuṇa,
where stood the fragrant cow who constantly flows with milk;
from the outpouring of her milk, the ocean named Kṣīroda was formed.
From him the moon originates, cool-rayed and beneficial to all creatures;
having reached whom the supreme ṛṣis who subsist on froth live on,
and from whom nectar was produced, as well as the wine for those who consume it.
That cow which men in the world call by the name Surabhi—
having circumambulated that most wonderful being, Rāvaṇa entered the exceedingly formidable place, which was guarded by many kinds of forces.
Then he beheld the supreme palace of Varuṇa, which was strewn with hundreds of streams, resembled an autumnal cloud, and was ever-joyful; then,
having slain the commanders of the forces in battle, he was struck by them in turn.
He said, "Tell me quickly where your king has gone;
Rāvaṇa has arrived seeking battle—let battle be given to him.
Or else, with palms joined in reverence, say: 'I am defeated,' and you shall have no fear."
In the meantime, the sons and grandsons of the high-souled Varuṇa, namely Gau and Puṣkara, emerged in a state of anger.
Endowed with the qualities of heroism, they were surrounded by their own forces.
Having yoked chariots that moved at will and possessed the brilliance of the rising sun,
there then ensued a fierce battle that made the hair stand on end between the sons of the Lord of Waters and the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa.
But by the immensely powerful ministers of the ten-necked Rākṣasa,
that entire army of Varuṇa was struck down in an instant.
Then, having observed their own forces in the battle, the sons of Varuṇa—
Afflicted by the net of arrows, they desisted from their martial efforts;
having fallen to the surface of the earth, they saw Rāvaṇa in the Puṣpaka chariot and quickly entered the sky in their swift-moving vehicles.
7.023.029a Then, having attained that equal position, a great [battle] ensued for them; 7.023.029c a tumultuous battle in the sky, like that between the gods and the dānavas.
7.023.030a Then they [assailed] Rāvaṇa in battle with arrows resembling fire.
Turning their backs [on the enemy], they roared various cries with great joy.
Then Mahodara, seeing the king overwhelmed, became enraged;
casting aside the fear of death, the hero looked about, longing for battle.
By him, those horses of theirs— which could go wherever they desired and were like the wind—
were struck by Mahodara with his mace and fell to the earth.
Having slain those warriors and horses of the sons of Varuṇa, [he proceeded].
Seeing them standing there deprived of their chariots, he quickly let out a great roar. Their chariots, along with the horses and the excellent charioteers,
were struck down by Mahodara and fell to the surface of the earth.

But those sons of the high-souled Varuṇa, having abandoned their chariots, stood firm in the sky; being heroes, they were not shaken by their own power. Having strung their bows, they pierced Mahodara.
Enraged, they united and rushed together toward Rāvaṇa in battle.
Then the ten-necked one, filled with wrath and standing like the fire of cosmic destruction,
unleashed a shower of arrows of great velocity upon their vital organs.
Standing firm above them, that invincible hero then brought down various maces, hundreds of broad-headed arrows, as well as swords, spears, *śataghnīs*, and lances.
Then those pierced heroes, the foot-soldiers,
rushed forth; thereupon the Rākṣasa, letting out a great roar, struck down the Vāruṇas with various terrible weapons, like a cloud with its downpours of rain.
Then they all turned away and fell upon the surface of the earth;
quickly led by their own men from the battlefield, they were brought into their homes.
Then the Rākṣasa said to them, "Let them be reported to Varuṇa."
Then the minister named Prabhāsa, the son of Varuṇa, said to Rāvaṇa:
"The lord of the waters, possessed of great splendor, has indeed gone to the world of Brahmā to listen to Gāndharva music— he whom you challenge to battle."
"O hero, why do you exhaust yourself in vain now that the king has departed? Those heroes who were present—the princes—have been defeated.
Having heard this, the lord of the rākṣasas proclaimed his own name.
Releasing a roar out of joy, he indeed emerged from the abode of Varuṇa;
having arrived by the same path by which he had come,
that Rākṣasa turned back and traveled toward Laṅkā through the expanse of the sky.
7.024.001a Returning, that evil-minded Rāvaṇa was filled with joy; 7.024.001c on the road, he carried off the daughters of kings, sages, gods, and gandharvas.
7.024.002a For whichever maiden or woman the rākṣasa saw who was beautiful to behold, [he seized her].
Having slain her kinsmen, he settled her in his celestial chariot (vimāna).
There, Rāvaṇa took as wives the daughters of the Pannagas, Yakṣas, humans, Rākṣasas, Daityas, and Dānavas.
With long hair, beautiful limbs, and faces like the full moon,
all those young women, their breasts heaving, were overcome by grief;
there, the fire born of the fear of sorrow was equal to the flames of a physical fire.

Trembling and afflicted by grief, they shed tears born of sorrow. As they sighed, the sighs of those women caused the *puṣpaka*— its fires now extinguished— to blaze up as if it were an *agnihotra* sacrifice.
7.024.007a One woman, afflicted by extreme suffering, thought: "He might even kill me," 7.024.007c remembering her mothers, fathers, brothers, sons, and even her fathers-in-law.
7.024.007e Overwhelmed by pain and grief, all the women lamented together.
"How indeed will my son fare without me?
How shall I, his mother, and how shall his brother fare, submerged as we are in an ocean of grief?
Alas, how shall I manage without my husband, who was my very deity?"
"O Death, be gracious; I entreat you, lead me to the abode of Yama.
What evil deed was committed by me in a previous body?
Because of that, I have been overcome by this [suffering] and have fallen into an ocean of grief."

7.024.011a Indeed, I do not see an end to my own suffering here now. 7.024.011c Alas, shame on the worlds of men; there is surely no one more wretched! 7.024.012a For my weak kinsmen have been seized by the powerful Rāvaṇa.
Like stars destroyed by the risen sun, they have been eliminated.
Alas, this exceedingly powerful Rākṣasa delights in the means of slaughter!
Alas, he does not himself perceive his own wicked conduct.
In every respect, the prowess of this evil-minded one is indeed worthy;
however, this act of violating another's wife is unworthy.
For this fool takes pleasure in the wives of others.
"Therefore, indeed, the elephant shall meet his death because of a woman.
Thus cursed by women, he was then deprived of his splendor and rendered lusterless,
for he had been confronted by virtuous wives devoted to their husbands who stood firm upon the path of righteousness.
While they were thus lamenting, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
entered the city of Laṅkā, being honored by the night-stalkers. Then the sister of the king of the rākṣasas, being exceedingly distressed, [spoke].
Falling at his feet, she began to speak.
Then Rāvaṇa, raising his sister and consoling her, said:
"What is this, blessed lady? You ought to tell me quickly."
With her eyes choked with tears, that rākṣasī spoke these words:
"O King, I am destroyed; I have been rendered a widow by you, the powerful one.
O King, it is through your prowess that these Daityas have been slain in battle."
Known as the Kālakeyas, they possessed great strength and prowess. There my husband was slain— he who was dearer to me than life itself— by you, his brother, who was indeed equal to an enemy.
"O King, since I have been slain here by you yourself, my own kinsman,
I shall now endure the sorrow and the reputation of widowhood bestowed upon me by you.
Surely, even in battles, a son-in-law ought to be protected by you!"
"O King, having slain him yourself in battle, you feel no shame. Thus addressed by his sister as she cried out, the Rākṣasa consoled her and spoke these words with conciliatory intent.
"Enough, child! Desist from despair, and do not fear in any way.
I shall constantly gratify you with special honors and gifts.
[For] in battle, one who is heedless, distracted, and desirous of victory hurls his arrows [in vain]."
"O auspicious lady, in battles I do not distinguish between my own people and the enemy;
therefore, O sister, that husband of yours was slain by me in the fray.
But at this time, I shall do whatever is appropriate and beneficial for you."
"Be by the side of your brother Khara, who is established in sovereignty;
you shall be the leader of fourteen thousand highly powerful Rākṣasas in matters of marching forth and bestowing gifts."
"There, your brother Khara, the son of your maternal aunt, shall be your lord;
he will always do whatever you yourself say.
Let this hero go quickly to protect the Daṇḍaka forest."
7.024.031c Dūṣaṇa, who possesses great strength, shall be his commander-in-chief.
7.024.032a For that forest region was cursed long ago by the enraged Uśanas:
"Without a doubt, this shall become the dwelling place of Rākṣasas."
Having spoken thus, the Ten-necked one commanded his army—
fourteen thousand Rākṣasas capable of changing their form at will.
Surrounded by all those Rākṣasas of terrible appearance, he set forth.
Khara departed swiftly for Daṇḍaka, free from fear from any quarter;
there he ruled a kingdom from which all thorns had been removed,
while Śūrpaṇakhā, filled with joy, dwelt in the Daṇḍaka forest.
Having bestowed that formidable forest upon Khara and having consoled his sister, the ten-necked one became joyful and more at ease. Then there was a great grove of Laṅkā named Nikumbhilā.

The high-souled lord of the Rākṣasas entered there with his followers. There he beheld the sacrifice, crowded with hundreds of sacrificial posts and adorned with beautiful shrines, standing resplendent as if ablaze with glory.
Then he beheld his son Meghanāda, the subduer of enemies, there wearing a black antelope skin, with a water-pot and a tuft of hair as his banner;
the lord of the Rākṣasas approached him and embraced him with his arms.
"What is this that is happening here, my child? Tell me that.
To him, Uśanas—the preceptor of great ascetic power and the best of the twice-born—spoke there for the sake of the success of the sacrifice regarding Rāvaṇa, the foremost of the Rākṣasas.
7.025.007a "I shall tell you, O King; let all of it be heard. 7.025.007c Seven sacrifices of great extent were performed by your son.
7.025.008a The Agniṣṭoma, the Aśvamedha, and the Bahusuvarṇaka sacrifice."
The Rājasūya sacrifice, as well as the Gomedha and the Vaiṣṇava sacrifices—
when the Māheśvara sacrifice, so difficult for men to attain,
was performed, your son obtained boons here directly from Paśupati himself.
A divine chariot that moves at will, travels through the air, and is steadfast;
and a power of illusion called Tāmasī, by which darkness is produced.
Indeed, O Lord of the Rākṣasas, with this very illusion in battle—
Indeed, the course of one engaged in combat cannot be known even by the gods and asuras.
O gentle one, his two quivers are inexhaustible, his bow is most difficult to conquer,
and his weapon is powerful, destroying enemies in battle.
"O Ten-faced One, having obtained all these boons, this son of yours—
on the completion of the sacrifice today, I stand here waiting for you.
Then the Ten-necked One said, "This which has been done is not well."
7.025.014c Since the enemies, led by Indra, have been honored with riches, 7.025.015a come now; for that which has been done cannot be undone.
7.025.015c Come, gentle one, let us go toward our own abode.
Then Daśagrīva, having gone there with his sons and Vibhīṣaṇa,
caused all those women— who were overwhelmed with tears,
worthy of respect, and the jewels among the wives of gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas— to disembark.
Adorned with various ornaments and blazing with their own splendor,
Vibhīṣaṇa, seeing those women overwhelmed with grief and perceiving his intention,
that righteous-souled one spoke these words:

By such conduct as this, which destroys reputation, wealth, and family, you act according to your own will, inflicting violence upon living beings. Having indeed oppressed your kinsmen, these beautiful women have been brought here by you.
"O King, having bypassed you, Kumbhīnasī was carried off by Madhu.
Rāvaṇa, however, spoke these words: "I do not understand what this is;
who is this person named 'Madhu' whom you have mentioned?"
7.025.022a But Vibhīṣaṇa, filled with rage, spoke these words to his brother:
7.025.022c "Listen to the fruit that has arrived for this sinful deed.
7.025.023a He who was our maternal grandfather’s eldest brother, Sumālin—"

7.025.023c There was a night-stalker renowned as Mālyavān, aged and wise. 7.025.024a He was the elder brother of our father and mother, and thus he became our grandfather (āryaka). 7.025.024c His daughter’s daughter was named Kumbhīnasī.
"Moreover, that maiden born from fire was the daughter of our maternal aunt;
according to dharma, she is indeed the sister of us brothers.
O King, she has been carried off by the powerful Rākṣasa Madhu."
"O King, while your son was engaged in sacrifice and while I remained submerged within the water,
those foremost among the Rākṣasas killed your esteemed ministers, overpowered me,
and carried me away, even though I was protected within your inner apartments."
7.025.028a Having heard this, O Great King, he was indeed killed by forgiveness;
7.025.028c for daughters must necessarily be given to a husband by their givers.
7.025.028e This has come to pass even in this world; let it be known to you.
Then the ten-necked one, enraged and with bloodshot eyes, said:
"Let my chariot be prepared quickly, and let the heroes ready themselves! Let my brother Kumbhakarṇa and those who are the chief night-stalkers also prepare."
"Let them mount their vehicles, equipped with various weapons and missiles.
Today, having slain that Madhu— who brings no fear to Rāvaṇa— in battle,
I, longing for combat and surrounded by my friends, shall go to the world of Indra."
"Then, having conquered the third heaven and brought Purandara under my control,
I shall dwell in contentment, adorned with the sovereignty over the three worlds. Four thousand fierce akṣauhiṇīs of rākṣasas [shall be my army]."
Various weapons quickly issued forth from those eager for battle. Indrajit led the army at the front, encompassing the soldiers;
the heroic Rāvaṇa was in the middle, and Kumbhakarṇa was at the rear.

But the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa continued to practice dharma in Laṅkā. All those illustrious ones, however, set out toward Madhupura on chariots, elephants, mules, camels, horses, and radiant great serpents.
All the Rākṣasas set forth, filling the sky without interval;
and hundreds of Daityas there, who had long-standing enmity with the gods,
seeing Rāvaṇa departing, followed behind him.
Having gone to Madhupura and entered it, the ten-faced one did not see Madhu there, but he saw his sister there. She,
bowing low with palms joined in reverence, fell at his feet with her head.
Kumbhīnasī, the sister of that king of the rākṣasas, was terrified; Rāvaṇa, the best of the rākṣasas, raised her up, saying, "Do not fear; what can I do for you?"

She said, "O King, O one of great strength, if you are pleased with me, you ought not to kill my husband here today, O giver of honor. Be true to your word, O Indra among kings; look upon me as I entreat you."
"O mighty-armed one, you yourself indeed said, 'You must not fear.
But Rāvaṇa, being arrogant, spoke there to his sister who stood nearby:
'Where is that husband of yours? Let him be reported to me immediately.'"
"I shall go with him to the world of the gods for victory;
out of compassion and friendship for you, I have desisted from the slaughter of Madhu.
Having spoken thus, she roused that sleeping night-stalker.
7.025.045c The Rākṣasī, as if greatly delighted, spoke to the highly wise one:
7.025.046a "This ten-necked night-stalker, my brother, has arrived; 7.025.046c Desiring to conquer the world of the gods, he chooses you for assistance."
"Therefore, O Rākṣasa, go with your kinsmen to assist him;
it is right to provide aid for one who is affectionate and devoted.
Having heard those words of hers, Madhu replied, "So be it."
Having approached the best of the Rākṣasas in the prescribed manner,
he honored Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, according to dharma. Having received such honors in the honey-chamber, the heroic ten-necked one remained there.
Having stayed there for one night, he prepared to depart.
Then, having reached Mount Kailāsa, the abode of Vaiśravaṇa,
the lord of the Rākṣasas, who resembled Mahendra, encamped his army.
But there, the valiant Ten-necked one, together with his army,
decided upon a place to stay when the sun had set;
and when the stainless moon, possessing a luster like a mountain, had risen.
There he beheld various excellences adorned by the rays of the moon:
divine groves of *karṇikāra* trees, thickets of *kadamba*,
lotus ponds in full bloom, and the waters of the Mandākinī.
A sweet-sounding resonance like the chiming of bells was heard from the throngs of Apsarases singing in the abode of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Trees, shaken by the wind, released showers of flowers.
7.026.005c As if perfuming that mountain, winds fragrant with honey and springtime scents [blew].
7.026.006a Carrying an abundant fragrance mixed with the pollen of honey-flowers, a pleasant breeze blew, increasing the passion of Rāvaṇa.
Due to the singing, the abundance of flowers, the qualities of the mountain breeze’s coolness,
the onset of night, and the rising of the moon,
Rāvaṇa, possessed of great heroism, fell under the power of the arrows of love.

Sighing again and again, he gazed intently at the moon. In that interval, Rambhā— the foremost of all the Apsarases, adorned with celestial flowers and possessing a face like the full moon— appeared there.
Adorned with fresh decorative marks and celebrating the festival of flowers of all six seasons,
she was veiled in a blue garment resembling a water-laden cloud;
her face was like the moon, and her auspicious eyebrows were like bows.
With thighs like the trunks of elephants and hands as tender as young shoots,
she was noticed by Rāvaṇa as she was walking through the midst of the army. Afflicted by the power of the arrows of love, the Lord of the Rakṣasas rose up toward her.
Taking her by the hand as she was walking away, he spoke to her with a smile:
"Where are you going, O lady of beautiful hips? What perfection do you seek for yourself? For whom has this time of prosperity arrived, that he shall enjoy you?"
"Who today shall attain satiety from the nectar of your mouth, which possesses the fragrance of lotuses and water-lilies, like the essence of celestial ambrosia?
O timid one, your two breasts are plump, auspicious, closely set, and resemble golden jars."
Whose chest will these two breasts of yours touch? Who today shall ascend your broad hips, which resemble golden wheels and are adorned with golden girdles, as you take your place in heaven?
"O Śakra, Viṣṇu, or the two Aśvins—what other man is superior to me? O timid one, it is not fitting that you should pass me by.
Rest here upon this auspicious stone surface, O lady of broad hips."
"In the three worlds, there is no one who is my equal, for I am both the lord and the master of the triple world;
therefore, this ten-faced one, bowing with palms joined in reverence, entreats you:
accept me."
Thus addressed, Rambhā, trembling and with palms joined in reverence, said:
"Be gracious; you ought not to speak such words, for you are my superior.
Even from others, I must be protected by you should I fall into disgrace."
"By the very nature of things, I am your daughter-in-law; I tell you this as the truth.
To her, who stood with her face cast down toward her feet, the Ten-necked One replied:
"If you are the wife of my son, then you shall become my daughter-in-law."
"So be it," Rambhā replied to Rāvaṇa in response.
"O bull among Rākṣasas, according to dharma, I am the wife of your son;
indeed, your son is dearer to him than his own life."
He who is renowned throughout the three worlds as Nalakūbara—he who, by his righteousness, would be a Brahmin; by his heroism, a Kṣatriya;
who is like fire in his wrath, yet equal to the earth in his forbearance.
I have indeed made a secret appointment with that son of a world-guardian;
it was with him in mind that all these ornaments were prepared for me. For the heart of no one else at all is set upon me.
"By that truth, O King, subduer of enemies, you ought to release me. For that righteous-souled one is currently staying there, longing for me;
therefore, you should not create an obstacle for your son here—release me."
"O bull among Rākṣasas, follow the path practiced by the virtuous.
For you are to be honored by me, and likewise, I am to be cherished by you.
To Rambhā, who was speaking these words consistent with dharma and artha, [he replied:]
7.026.030c Having rebuked her out of delusion, the powerful Rākṣasa seized her by force; 7.026.030e overcome by the delusion of lust, he proceeded to engage in sexual union.
7.026.031a Then Rambhā was released, her garlands and ornaments fallen away.
Like a river agitated and churned by a lordly elephant,
she— trembling, ashamed, and terrified— with her hands joined in *añjali*,
approached Nalakūbara and fell at his feet.
Seeing her in that state, the high-souled Nalakūbara said, "What is this, blessed lady? Why have you fallen at my feet?
She, however, sighing and trembling, with her hands joined in reverence, [spoke].
7.026.034c He began to relate everything to him exactly as it had happened.
7.026.035a "O Lord, this Ten-necked one has arrived, intending to go to the third heaven.
7.026.035c With his army as his companion, he is passing the night here."
"O subduer of enemies, I was seen by him as I was coming to your presence. That *rākṣasa* seized me and asked, 'To whom do you belong? And I reported everything to him exactly as it is."

My soul overwhelmed by lust and delusion, O Lord, I did not heed those words of mine as I entreated you, saying, "O God, I am your daughter-in-law. Setting all that aside, I was violated by him by force.
"O giver of honor, you ought to forgive this offense of mine;
for indeed, O gentle one, the strength of a woman and that of a man are not equal.
Having heard this, the son of Vaiśravaṇa then became enraged.
Having heard of that supreme insult, he entered into deep meditation. Then, perceiving his action, the son of Vaiśravaṇa,
his eyes copper-red with rage, seized water in his hand in an instant.
Having taken up divine water and sipped it according to the prescribed rite,
he then uttered a terrible curse upon the lord of the Rākṣasas:
"O blessed lady, since you were forcibly violated by him against your will..."
Therefore, he will not approach another young woman who is unwilling.
But when, driven by lust, he violates a woman against her will,
his head shall then shatter into seven pieces.
When that curse, radiant like a blazing fire, had been uttered,
the drums of the gods resounded and a rain of flowers fell from the sky.
And all the gods, headed by Prajāpati, were filled with great joy.
Having understood the entire course of the world and the death of that Rākṣasa,
and having heard that hair-raising curse,
the ten-necked one no longer took pleasure in sexual union with women who were unwilling.

Then, having leaped over Kailāsa, the ten-necked one, that night-stalker of great splendor, together with his rākṣasas, reached the world of Indra. As that army of rākṣasas was approaching from all sides, [the earth shook].
The sound, resembling the crashing of the ocean, reached the world of the gods.
Hearing that Rāvaṇa had arrived, Indra’s throne trembled,
and he spoke there to all the assembled gods.
"O Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, Sādhyas, and hosts of Maruts,
prepare yourselves for battle against the evil-minded Rāvaṇa!
Thus addressed by Śakra, the gods, who were his equals in combat, [prepared accordingly].
7.027.005c Those great beings, filled with a desire for battle, put on their armor.
7.027.006a But Mahendra, dejected and terrified of Rāvaṇa,
approached Viṣṇu and spoke these words.
"O Viṣṇu, of great heroism and prowess, how shall we act? For that powerful Rākṣasa advances for the sake of battle;
he is strong because of the granting of a boon, and certainly not for any other reason."
"O Lord Prajāpati, that word must indeed be made true. Therefore,
act in such a way that Namuci, Vṛtra, Bali, Naraka, and Śambara are utterly consumed, having been overwhelmed by your resolve."
7.027.010a For indeed, O God, among the gods, there is no other of such great strength in times of distress, 7.027.010c nor is there any other refuge or ultimate resort except you, O Supreme Person.
7.027.011a For you are the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the lotus-navelled one, the eternal.
7.027.011c "And by you I have been established in this eternal sovereignty over the gods.
7.027.012a "Therefore, O God of gods, tell me yourself according to the truth:
7.027.012c how it is that you, with only a sword and a discus as your companions, fight the enemy in battle."
Thus addressed by Śakra, the lordly god Nārāyaṇa said:
"You need not fear; listen to me.
This wicked one cannot yet be overcome even by the gods and the Dānavas."
Having encountered him in battle, he is difficult to conquer due to the granting of the boon;
yet, being fierce in his strength, he will perform great deeds in every way. It is evident by his very nature that this Rākṣasa, aided by his son, will do so.
"O Śakra, as for what you say to me— that you will fight in battle—
I shall certainly not fight against that Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas. For Viṣṇu does not turn back without having slain his enemy."
"And this desire is difficult to attain today, having obtained a boon from a Rākṣasa.
"I solemnly declare in your presence, O Lord of the Gods, O Śatakratu:
I myself shall be the cause of this Rākṣasa's death."
"I shall slay this Rāvaṇa along with his sons in battle;
having recognized that the time has arrived, I shall gratify the gods. In the interval between these thoughts, at the end of the night, a roar was heard.
As that army of Rāvaṇa fought on all sides,
a battle then ensued between the gods and the rākṣasas—
terrible, with a tumultuous roar, and featuring various weapons and missiles.
In the meantime, by the command of Rāvaṇa, heroic Rākṣasas of fearsome appearance— his ministers,
including Mārīca, Prahasta, Mahāpārśva, and Mahodara— rushed forward for the sake of battle.
Akampana, Nikumbha, Śuka, and Sāraṇa; Saṃhrādi, Dhūmaketu, Mahādaṃṣṭra, and Mahāmukha;
Jambumālī, Mahāmālī, and the Rākṣasa Virūpākṣa.

Surrounded by all these highly valiant ones, Sumāli, the bull among Rākṣasas and the grandfather of Rāvaṇa, entered the army. For he [was capable of] [assailing] all the hosts of gods with various sharp weapons.
Enraged, he destroyed [the enemy] along with those night-stalkers. In the meantime, the heroic eighth of the Vasus,
renowned as Sāvitra, entered the great battle.
Then a battle took place between the gods and the rākṣasas—
those enraged rākṣasas who never retreat in combat and whose fame is established in battles.
Then those heroic rākṣasas [attacked] the gods standing in the fray.

With various terrible weapons, they struck them by the hundreds of thousands. But the gods, by their own splendor, sent those fierce and immensely powerful Rākṣasas to the abode of Yama in battle with various missiles.
In the meantime, a heroic Rākṣasa named Sumālī,
enraged, rushed toward the battle with various weapons. With his sharp, diverse weapons, he assailed that entire army of the gods.
Enraged, he destroyed them like the wind dispersing the clouds. Oppressed by his showers of great arrows, spears, and terrible javelins,
all the gods could not stand their ground, though they remained composed.
Then, while the gods were being put to flight by Sumālin,
the eighth deity of the Vasus, Sāvitra, stood his ground,
surrounded by his own troops as he struck at the night-stalker.
With great prowess, that one of mighty splendor warded him off in the encounter.
Between those two, who were both highly intoxicated and never retreating in battles— the Sumālin and the Vāsava— there occurred a most terrible combat in the world.

Then, by means of his great arrows, the high-souled Vasu instantly brought down that great chariot of the serpent-demon. Having destroyed his chariot in the encounter with hundreds of sharp shafts, [he struck him].

Vasu took up a mace in his hand for the purpose of slaying him. Grasping that blazing, auspicious weapon, which resembled the staff of Death, the son of Savitṛ swiftly brought it down upon the head of Sumālin.
Then, a meteor-like object fell upon his head and blazed forth,
like a great thunderbolt released by the thousand-eyed Indra falling upon a mountain.
At that moment, neither his bones, nor his body, nor his flesh could be seen.
Reduced to ashes by the mace, he was struck down in that battle. Seeing him slain in the fray, all those rākṣasas fled together from every side, crying out with a great roar.
Having seen Sumālī slain and reduced to ashes by Vasu,
and observing his own army fleeing while being tormented by arrows,
the powerful son of Rāvaṇa then became enraged in battle.
Having turned back all the rākṣasas, Meghanāda took his stand;
that great car-warrior, on a fire-colored chariot that moved at will,
rushed toward that army like a blazing fire through the forests.
Then, as he entered bearing various weapons,
all the gods fled in every direction at the mere sight of him;
not a single one remained there in the battle as he sought to fight.
Seeing them all agitated and terrified, Śakra addressed them:
"Do not fear; do not flee; turn back toward the battle! Here comes my son, unconquered, for the sake of combat."
Then the god who was the son of Śakra, renowned as Jayanta,
advanced toward the battle in a chariot of wondrous design.
Thereupon, all those thirty gods surrounded the son of Śacī.
Having encountered the son of Rāvaṇa in battle, they stood their ground.
A great battle took place between them, worthy of gods and rākṣasas,
for the sake of Mahendra’s son and the son of the lord of rākṣasas.
Then, against Mātali’s son Gomukha,
the charioteer, the son of the Rākṣasa discharged arrows adorned with gold.
Jayanta, the son of Śacī, likewise [discharged arrows] at his charioteer.
And in that arena of battle, the enraged [Hanumān] struck back at that son of Rāvaṇa.
Then, the highly energetic Rākṣasa, his eyes wide with fury,
the son of Rāvaṇa, overwhelmed the son of Śakra with a rain of arrows.
Then, seizing powerful and massive weapons—
*śataghnīs*, *tomaras*, spears, maces, swords, and axes—
the son of Rāvaṇa hurled down enormous mountain peaks.
Then the worlds were greatly distressed, and a vast darkness arose as that son of Rāvaṇa was then slaughtering his enemies. Then that host of gods [surrounded] that son of Śacī on all sides.
In many ways distressed, it ran hither and thither;
at that time, they could not recognize one another, nor whether they were enemies or deities,
as they fled in every direction, utterly bewildered.
In the meantime, a powerful Daitya named Puloman, a hero,
seized Śacī’s son and carried him away.
Having taken his grandson, he entered the great ocean.
His maternal grandfather was Aryaka, by whom that Śacī, the daughter of Puloman,
was won. But when the gods beheld the most terrible destruction of Jayanta,
they became distressed and joyless, and fled in every direction.
Then the son of Rāvaṇa, greatly rejoiced and surrounded by his own forces,
rushed toward those gods and let out a mighty roar,
seeing the destruction of his son and the prowess of Rāvaṇa.
The lord of the gods said to Mātali: "Let the chariot be brought near.
That divine, great, and formidable chariot was already ready;
it stood before him, driven by Mātali, swift as thought.
Then, clouds accompanied by lightning and great thunder, flickering with the wind, moved ahead of that chariot and roared; meanwhile,
various musical instruments were played and composed hymns of praise were intoned.
And as Vāsava set out for battle, throngs of Apsarases danced;
surrounded by the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts,
the lord of the thirty gods went forth, equipped with various weapons.
As Śakra was departing, a harsh wind blew;
the sun became lusterless, and great meteors fell.
In that interval, the heroic and majestic Daśagrīva appeared.
He ascended a divine chariot fashioned by Viśvakarman,
which was encircled by serpents of immense body that caused one's hair to stand on end; by the wind of their hissing breath, the battle appeared as if set ablaze.
Surrounded by brave Daityas and night-stalkers, that divine chariot turned toward Mahendra, facing the battle. Having restrained his son, he himself took up his position there.
Having emerged from the battle, that son of Rāvaṇa also sat down.
Then the battle between the gods and the Rākṣasas commenced,
a terrible rain of weapons like that of clouds in the conflict.
But the evil-minded Kumbhakarṇa, with various weapons raised,
could not be distinguished at that time in the battle as to whom he was fighting;
[he fought] with his tusks, his two arms, his feet, and with spears, javelins, and arrows.
Enraged by whatever means possible, he indeed struck the gods.
Then the night-stalker fought with the highly fortunate Rudras and Ādityas,
and was incessantly mangled by their weapons in that battle.
Then that entire Rākṣasa army was routed in battle by the gods together with the hosts of Maruts using various sharp weapons;
some, struck down by the arms, writhed upon the surface of the earth.
Others remained stationed in the battle, still mounted upon their vehicles;
[they were] chariots, elephants, donkeys, camels,
serpents, and likewise horses, porpoises, boars, and those with the faces of *piśācas*.
Embracing them with their arms, some remained firm while others stood tall; pierced by the weapons of the gods, the night-stalkers perished.
That tumultuous clash among them appeared like a work of painting.
Upon the surface of the earth, where the heedless rākṣasas had been slain,
there flowed at the front of the battle a river with blood for its water, teeming with herons and vultures,
and possessing weapons for its crocodiles.
In that interval, the powerful Ten-necked one, enraged upon seeing that entire army struck down by the gods,
quickly plunged into that surging ocean of troops.
Slaying the gods of the thirty-three in battle, he advanced directly toward Śakra.
Then Śakra, having drawn his great bow which produced a tremendous sound—
by the roar of whose string the ten directions resounded— [attacked him].
Drawing back that great bow, Indra discharged arrows possessing the brilliance of fire and the sun upon Rāvaṇa’s head;
yet the ten-necked one, mighty-armed as he was, remained firm in his position just as before.
He covered Śakra with showers of arrows released from his bow.
Then, as the two of them fought, with showers of arrows falling on all sides,
nothing at all could be discerned, for everything was shrouded in darkness.

Then, when darkness had set in, the Rākṣasas, intoxicated by their own strength, fought with the deities, slaughtering one another. Thereupon, the great army of the Rākṣasas was [assailed] by the celestial host.
In that battle, one-tenth remained standing, while the rest were led to the abode of Yama.
When everything was shrouded in darkness, all those gods and rākṣasas,
fighting one another, could no longer recognize each other.
Indra, Rāvaṇa himself, and the mighty son of Rāvaṇa—
these three did not fall into delusion while that [place] was shrouded by the net of darkness.
But Rāvaṇa, seeing his entire army slain in battle, [was overcome].

He was seized by a fierce rage and let out a great roar. Out of anger, the invincible one spoke to his charioteer, who stood upon the chariot: "Lead me through the very midst of the enemy army to its end."
Today, with my own prowess in battle, I shall destroy all these gods from the vault of heaven using various weapons of great power.
I myself shall slay Indra, Varuṇa, Kubera, and Yama.
"Having swiftly struck down the gods of the thirty-three, I myself shall then stand above them. You must not feel despondent; drive my chariot quickly.
Indeed, I tell you this twice today: lead me to the very end."
"This is that region of Nandana where we now dwell; lead me today to that place where Mount Udaya stands.
Having heard those words of his, he [yoked] the horses swift as thought.

Then the charioteer commanded [the horses] to pass right through the midst of the enemies. Having understood his resolve, Śakra, the lord of the gods, standing upon his chariot, then spoke these words to the gods stationed on the battlefield:
7.029.013a O gods, listen to my words, which seem best to me:
7.029.013c Let the ten-necked Rākṣasa be captured while he is still alive.
7.029.014a For he is exceedingly powerful in the army, [mounted] on a chariot with the speed of the wind.
He will advance like the ocean with its waves swelling at the change of the moon;
for he cannot be slain today, being rendered utterly fearless by the granting of a boon. Therefore, we shall capture the rākṣasa; remain vigilant in this battle.
"Just as I enjoy these three worlds by having subdued Bali,
so too does the subjugation of this wicked one please me.
Then Śakra, abandoning Rāvaṇa, took up residence in another region.
The one of great splendor fought on, destroying the rākṣasas in battle;
meanwhile, the Ten-necked one entered from the north without turning back,
while Śatakratu entered from the southern side.
Then that lord of the Rākṣasas, having entered a hundred yojanas deep,
overwhelmed the entire host of the gods with showers of arrows.
Then Śakra, seeing that he had entered his own army, [reflected].
Unperturbed, he turned back and surrounded the ten-faced Rāvaṇa. In the meantime, a cry was let out by the Dānavas and Rākṣasas:
"Alas! We are destroyed! upon seeing Rāvaṇa seized by Śakra.
Then, mounting his chariot, the son of Rāvaṇa, overwhelmed with rage and exceedingly incensed,
entered that most dreadful army.
Having entered, he [encountered] that illusion which had been granted by Gopati in the past.
Invisible to all beings, he overwhelmed that army.
Then, abandoning the gods, he rushed swiftly toward Śakra alone;
yet Mahendra, possessed of great splendor, could not see the son of his enemy.
Having struck Mātali and the horses with his finest arrows, he,
being swift-handed, covered Mahendra with a rain of shafts.
Then Śakra, abandoning the chariot and dismissing Mātali, [fled].
Having mounted Airāvata, he pursued the son of Rāvaṇa;
yet that Rākṣasa, by the power of his *māyā*, could not be seen in the battle as he showered a flood of arrows upon Mahendra of immeasurable prowess.
When the son of Rāvaṇa perceived that Indra was exhausted,
he then bound him with his illusory power (māyā) and led him away toward his own army.
Then, seeing him forcibly carried off from the battlefield by means of that illusion, [he was overcome with grief].
All the immortals cried out to Mahendra, "What indeed is this?
for the learned one was not to be seen, as he was being carried away by means of illusion. In that interval, all the hosts of gods then—
Highly incensed, they rushed at Rāvaṇa with showers of weapons.
But Rāvaṇa, having encountered the hosts of Vasus, Ādityas, and Maruts,
was unable to stand his ground in battle nor to fight, being tormented by their weapons.
Seeing his father exhausted in battle, his skin mangled by blows, the son of Rāvaṇa, remaining invisible, spoke these words:
"Come, father, let us go; that work of war is finished."

"Victory is yours; let it be known to you, O Lord! Be at ease and free from feverish distress. For this Śakra, who is the lord of the celestial army and of the three worlds, has been captured by me, and the gods have been rendered humbled in spirit."
"Enjoy the three worlds as you wish, having subdued your enemy by your own prowess.
Why undergo this fruitless exertion? For your battle is indeed without result.
Thus addressed, he desisted from the act of war due to the power of the gods.
Having heard those words of Rāvaṇa’s son, the ten-faced lord, his mind composed and free from the fever of battle,
attained victory as the sovereign of the night-stalkers.
Then, filled with joy upon obtaining his own son, he went toward his palace and spoke these words:
"By means of those feats of prowess equal to the exceedingly powerful [gods]..."
O you whose prowess is equal to that of the immortals, you have increased the glory of my lineage by conquering the lord of the thirty gods and the thirty gods themselves.
"Bring Vāsava here quickly;
depart from here for the city surrounded by your army. I too shall follow you swiftly as you go."
Accompanied by his ministers, he followed behind him. Then the son of Rāvaṇa, surrounded by his forces and with his mount, took hold of the Lord of the Thirty-three.
Having returned to his own abode, the Rākṣasa,
with a joyful mind, dismissed the Rākṣasas,
for Mahendra had been conquered by the exceedingly powerful son of Rāvaṇa.
Then, placing Prajāpati at their head, the gods went to Laṅkā.
Having approached Rāvaṇa, who was surrounded by his sons and brothers,
Prajāpati, standing in the sky, spoke to him with words of conciliation.
"O child Rāvaṇa, I am pleased with you, my son, in this battle!
Oh, what valor and magnanimity he possesses—whether equal to you or even superior!
For by your own splendor, you have indeed conquered the entire three worlds."
The vow you made has been fulfilled; I am truly pleased with my own son. And this son of yours, Rāvaṇa, who possesses exceeding strength, shall become renowned in the world as Indrajit.

"O King, this Rākṣasa shall become powerful and a conqueror of enemies; relying upon him, you have brought the thirty gods under your control. Therefore, O mighty-armed one, let Mahendra, the subduer of Pāka, be released."
"And what do the dwellers of heaven offer for the sake of his release?
Then the highly energetic Indrajit, victorious in assembly, replied:
"O Lord, I choose immortality here for the sake of his release."
Then the lotus-born god spoke to the son of Rāvaṇa:
"Indeed, there is no such thing as immortality for any living beings on earth.
Thereupon, Indrajit spoke to the lotus-born one who was standing there.

"Listen to what the success would have been had there been a release of Śatakratu. O God, it was my constant desire to worship the Purifier (Agni) with oblations before descending into battle, longing for victory over the enemies."
"O Lord, if I were to engage in battle while the recitation and the fire-oblation for Vibhāvasu were still incomplete, then my destruction would surely occur;
for every man indeed seeks immortality through ascetic penance."
"By my prowess, however, this immortality has been brought forth by me.
"So be it," the god Prajāpati said to him.
Then Śakra was released by Indrajit, and the gods departed for the third heaven.
7.030.015 In the meantime, Śakra, dejected, his garments and garlands fallen away, O Rāma, his soul overwhelmed by anxiety, fell into a state of deep meditation.
7.030.016 Seeing him in such a condition, the divine Lord of Creatures spoke to him.
"O Śakra, O Creator, why do you feel such longing? Remember your past misdeed!
O Lord of the Immortals, O Master, in the past many creatures were created by me, all of one caste, speaking the same language, and identical in form in every respect."
"There was indeed no distinction among them, whether in appearance or in their characteristics.
Therefore, with a one-pointed mind, I reflected upon those creatures.
To provide for their differentiation, I fashioned a single woman."
Whatever limb was most excellent among living beings, that very part was extracted [from them].
From those, I fashioned the woman Ahalyā with exquisite forms and qualities;
and "Ahalyā" indeed was the name I bestowed upon her.
"O Indra, Lord of the Gods, O bull among the Suras, when that woman had been created, the thought occurred to me: 'Whose will she be?
Then, O Śakra, O Lord, you recognized that woman with your mind."
"O Purandara, because of her superior status, she was my wife;
however, she was placed with me as a trust by the high-souled Gautama,
and after many years, she has now been returned by him."
Then, having recognized the steadfastness of that great sage and knowing his perfection in asceticism, I offered myself to him as a wife. That righteous-souled great sage took delight with her.
The gods had become despondent because of that gift bestowed upon Gautama;
yet you, O sage, being angry and driven by desire, went to the hermitage of that ascetic and beheld that woman, who was like a blazing flame of fire.
"O Śakra, she was violated by you while you were afflicted by lust and filled with fury.
And at that time, you were seen by that supreme ṛṣi in his hermitage.
Then, by him who possessed supreme splendor, you were cursed in his wrath."
"O Indra of the gods, you have gone to that state which is the reverse of the ten stages of life.
O Vāsava, because my wife was fearlessly violated by you,
therefore, O King, you shall fall into the hands of the enemy in battle."
But this state of affairs, O evil-minded one, which has been set in motion by you here,
will undoubtedly prevail among all human beings as well. In that regard, a great and exceedingly powerful unrighteousness shall arise.
"Of that [sin], half shall fall upon him who committed it, and the other half shall fall upon you; moreover, O Purandara, there shall be no stable station for you,
