because of this practice of unrighteousness which was initiated here by you."
"Whosoever shall be the lord of the gods, he shall not remain permanent"—
this was the curse released by me, which he then spoke to you.
Having thus rebuked his wife, that man of great asceticism said:
"O ill-behaved woman, perish from the vicinity of my hermitage! Since you, though endowed with beauty and youth, are unstable, therefore you shall not be the only beautiful woman in the world."
And all creatures shall attain that form which is so difficult to obtain— that very form by relying upon which this confusion has now come upon you.
From that time forward, creatures will for the most part be endowed with beauty.
"For all this has come upon you because of the release of that sage's curse.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, remember the evil deed which was committed by you,
by which you have fallen into the grasp of the enemy and not for any other reason, O Vāsava."
"Perform quickly the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice with a well-composed mind;
purified by that sacrifice, you shall thereafter go to the third heaven.
And your son, O Indra of the gods, has not perished in the great battle."
He was led and brought close by Aryaka into the great ocean.
Having heard this, Mahendra, after performing the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice,
ascended again to the third heaven and gave instructions to the deities.
"O Rāma, this is the power of Indrajit that I have described to you;
by him even the Lord of the Gods was conquered, let alone other living beings.
Then the highly effulgent Rāma, out of wonder, spoke once more.
Bowing down, he spoke these words to Agastya, the best of sages:
"O Blessed One, O best of the twice-born, why were the worlds empty at that time,
such that Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, did not encounter any resistance?"
"Or were those rulers of the earth deficient in prowess? Were many kings excluded from the contest of excellent weapons and utterly defeated?
Having heard these words of Rāghava, the venerable sage Agastya [replied].
7.031.004c He spoke to Rāma, laughing like the Grandfather [Brahmā] to Īśvara. 7.031.005a Thus harassing the kings, O bull among kings,
7.031.005c Rāvaṇa roamed the earth, O Rāma, lord of the earth.
Then he arrived at the city named Māhiṣmatī, which possessed the splendor of the city of heaven,
where the presence of Vasuretas was supreme;
in majesty, that king was equal to Vasuretas himself.
On that very day, the powerful lord Arjuna, the ruler of the Haihayas— whose fire always lay within his quiver of arrows—
went with his women to sport upon the Narmadā.
Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, questioned his ministers: "Where is that King Arjuna today? You ought to tell me quickly.
I am Rāvaṇa, arrived here desiring battle with that best of men."
"Let my arrival be announced by you without distraction.
Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, those highly wise ministers spoke to the lord of the Rākṣasas regarding the absence of the king.
7.031.012 Having heard that Arjuna had gone to the citizens, the son of Viśravas departed and went to Mount Vindhya, which resembled the Himavat mountain.
7.031.013 It was as if the sky had descended there, or as if the earth had been overturned.
Rāvaṇa beheld the Vindhya mountain, which seemed to scrape the sky;
it was endowed with a thousand peaks and its caves were inhabited by lions. With cold waters falling from its precipices, it appeared as if it were laughing aloud.
With gods, dānavas, gandharvas, along with hosts of apsarases and kinnaras,
sporting together with their women, that lofty place became like heaven;
its waters flowed through rivers in a manner beyond compare.

Beholding Mount Vindhya, which stood as if vomiting forth [fire] with its blazing, flickering tongues of flame, a mountain possessed of firebrands and caverns resembling the Himavat, Rāvaṇa then proceeded to the Narmadā.
The holy river, with its waters flowing and surging toward the western ocean,
had its pools of water agitated by buffaloes, *sṛmara* deer, lions, tigers, bears, and noble elephants— all parched by the heat and tormented by thirst.
It was surrounded by *cakravāka* birds, *kāraṇḍava* ducks, *haṃsa* swans, water-fowls,
cranes, and ever-intoxicated *dāmatta* birds, all warbling melodiously; it was adorned with blossoming trees as its head-ornaments and possessed pairs of *cakravāka* birds for breasts.
She whose hips were broad riverbanks, girdled by rows of swans;
her limbs were anointed with the pollen of flowers, and she wore the pure white raiment of water-foam;
she was cool to the touch from her immersion in the water, and her beautiful eyes were blossoming blue lotuses.
Quickly descending from the Puṣpaka chariot onto Narmadā, the best of rivers,
Daśānana plunged into her as if into a beloved and excellent woman;
he then went to her delightful bank, adorned with various flowers.
Seated together with his ministers, that bull among Rākṣasas,
the lord of the Rākṣasas, attained a joy born from the sight of the Narmadā. Then Rāvaṇa, the sovereign of the Rākṣasas, laughed sportively.
There he spoke to his ministers, Mārīca, Śuka, and Sāraṇa:
"This sun, having made the world as if of gold with its thousand rays,
stands in the midst of the sky, inflicting a piercing heat."

7.031.025e Knowing that I am seated here, the Moon and the Sun approach. 7.031.026a This wind, cool with the waters of the Narmadā, fragrant, and a quencher of fatigue, blows most steadily out of fear of me.
And this most excellent of rivers, the Narmadā, who increases joy,
stands like a frightened woman with her fish, birds, and waves hidden away;
for you have been wounded by weapons in battle with kings equal to Indra.
"Sprinkled with blood as if with the juice of sandalwood,
you all should plunge into the Narmadā, which bestows happiness upon men,
like intoxicated great elephants entering the Gaṅgā with their faces like great lotuses."
"Having bathed in this great river, you shall be liberated from sin.
I too, upon this sandy bank which possesses the luster of the autumnal moon,
will slowly perform an offering of flowers to the Lord of Umā."
Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, Mārīca, Śuka, and Sāraṇa,
together with Mahodara and Dhūmrākṣa, plunged into the Narmadā river.
By those elephants of the lord of the Rākṣasas, the river Narmadā was agitated.
Like the Gaṅgā with its great elephants, Vāmana, Añjana, Padma, and others,
those Rākṣasas then bathed in the excellent waters of the Narmadā;
having emerged, they gathered flowers for the purpose of an offering to Rāvaṇa.
On the delightful bank of the Narmadā, possessing a luster like that of a white cloud,
the lords of the Rākṣasas in a mere moment fashioned a mountain made of flowers. As soon as the flowers had been brought, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, [proceeded].
He descended into the river to bathe, like a great elephant entering the Gaṅgā;
having bathed there according to the prescribed rites and recited the unsurpassed prayers,
Rāvaṇa emerged from those waters of the Narmadā.
Seven Rākṣasas followed Rāvaṇa as he went with palms joined in reverence;
wherever that Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, went,
there a golden *liṅga* was carried.
Having placed that *liṅga* in the middle of an altar of sand, Rāvaṇa worshipped it with perfumes and flowers possessing the fragrance of nectar.
Then he [worshipped] Hara, the supreme remover of the distress of the virtuous.
Having worshipped the granter of boons who is adorned with moonbeams, that night-stalker spoke;
stretching out his long arms, he danced.
7.032.001 On the banks of the Narmadā, not far from the place where Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, offers floral oblations,
7.032.002 stands Arjuna, the best among victors, the sovereign lord of Māhiṣmatī.
While sporting with the women, having resorted to the waters of the Narmadā,
King Arjuna then shone in their midst like an elephant standing in the middle of a thousand female elephants.
Desiring to test the supreme strength of his thousand arms,
Arjuna then blocked the current of the Narmadā with those very arms;
and having reached that dam formed by the arms of Kārtavīrya, the water became perfectly clear.
Carrying away the banks and rushing against the current,
that torrent of the Narmadā’s waters— filled with fish, crocodiles, and sharks, and strewn with flowers and *kuśa* grass— shone like the onset of the rainy season.
Like a surge of water sent forth by Kārtavīrya,
that [wind] carried away all of Rāvaṇa’s floral offerings.
Then Rāvaṇa, having abandoned his religious observance while it was only half-finished, [departed].
He beheld the lovely Narmadā as if she were an unfaithful beloved;
then, seeing from the west that surge resembling the swelling of the ocean,
he entered the eastern quarter as the force of the waters increased.

Then Rāvaṇa beheld the river, where the birds were no longer agitated and which remained in its supreme natural state; it appeared as if its very form were free from emotion. And with the finger of his right hand, the ten-faced one made a sound.
7.032.011c He dispatched Śuka and Sāraṇa to search for the source of that speed.
7.032.012a Those two heroic brothers, Śuka and Sāraṇa, commanded by Rāvaṇa, 7.032.012c traveling through the midst of the sky, set out facing toward the west.
Having traveled a distance of half a yojana, those two night-rangers beheld a man sporting with a woman in the water;
he resembled a great *sāla* tree, his hair disheveled by the water.
With eyes reddened at the corners by intoxication, possessing a splendor like the form of the God of Love,
that crusher of enemies blocked the river with his thousand arms,
as if obstructing the earth itself with a thousand feet.
Surrounded by a thousand young and excellent women,
like an elephant amidst a thousand rutting female elephants,
Śuka and Sāraṇa beheld that most wonderful being.
Having returned, they approached Rāvaṇa and said to him:
"O Lord of the Rākṣasas, there is someone resembling a great *sāla* tree who,
having blocked the Narmadā like a dam, is making the women sport."
With those thousand arms, he has blocked the river whose waters were flowing;
it repeatedly emits surges resembling the billowing of the ocean.
Having heard Śuka and Sāraṇa speaking thus, [Rāvaṇa said:]
Having said, "I am Rāvaṇa, Arjuna," he rose up, eager for battle.
As that lord of the rākṣasas set out toward Arjuna,
the clouds emitted a blood-red roar all at once.
Surrounded by Mahodara, Mahāpārśva, Dhūmrākṣa, Śuka, and Sāraṇa,
the lord of the rākṣasas went to that place where Arjuna was; after no very long time, that powerful rākṣasa arrived there.

He, shining with the luster of collyrium, arrived at that formidable lake on the Narmadā. There, the king of the Rākṣasas beheld Arjuna, the lord of men, surrounded by women like an elephant by female elephants.
With eyes red with rage and arrogant in his strength, that lord of the Rākṣasas spoke thus to Arjuna’s ministers in a deep voice:
"O ministers, quickly inform King Haihaya!"

7.032.026c One named Rāvaṇa has arrived for the purpose of battle. 7.032.027a Having heard the words of Rāvaṇa, those ministers of Arjuna 7.032.027c rose up with their weapons and spoke these words to Rāvaṇa.
"The time for battle has been recognized; well done, O noble Rāvaṇa!
Well done indeed, you who wish to fight our king while he is intoxicated and surrounded by women—like a tiger attacking an elephant in rut in the midst of its females."
"Forgive me today, O Ten-necked One; let the night be spent by you here.
But if there is a desire for battle, my dear, then tomorrow in the encounter you shall face Arjuna.
Or, if you are in haste, being overwhelmed by a thirst for combat—"
"Having slain us, you will then engage in battle with Arjuna.
Then those ministers of the king were slaughtered by Rāvaṇa’s ministers in the battle and devoured by those who were hungry.
Then a tumultuous roar arose along the banks of the Narmadā from the followers of Arjuna and the ministers of Rāvaṇa;
[they fought] with arrows, javelins, and spears that were like thunderbolts and equipped with hooks.
Rushing forward from all sides and crushing the chariots,
the onset of the Haihaya warriors was most terrible,
like the roar of an ocean teeming with crabs, fish, and sea-monsters.
Then those ministers of Rāvaṇa— Prahasta, Śuka, and Sāraṇa—
possessing the brilliance of fire, became enraged and began to consume the army of Kārtavīrya.
They reported that deed of Rāvaṇa and his ministers to Arjuna.
While he was thus playing, it was told to him by the men guarding the gate;
having said to the women, "Do not be afraid," Arjuna then emerged from those waters like Añjana from the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Then, O Arjuna, that fire, its eyes defiled by anger,
blazed forth most terribly like the conflagration at the end of an eon.
Taking up his mace, which was adorned with excellent gold bands, he moved with even greater speed.
Like the sun driving away the darkness, he rushed toward the Rākṣasas;
raising his great mace with a sweeping motion of his arms,
Arjuna descended with the speed of Garuḍa.
Blocking his path like Mount Vindhya obstructing the sun,
Prahasta stood there with his club as weapon, as immovable as the Vindhya mountain itself.
Then, arrogant with pride, he raised his terrible iron-bound club against him.
7.032.042c Enraged, Prahasta dispatched [the messenger] and roared like a rain-cloud.
7.032.043a At the tip of that mace was a fire resembling a cluster of *aśoka* flowers;
7.032.043c Released from Prahasta’s hand, it seemed as though it were burning everything in its path.

Then Arjuna Kārtavīrya, possessing the prowess of an elephant and armed with a mace, skillfully evaded the club as it was being hurled at him. Thereupon, the lord of the Haihayas rushed toward Prahasta.
Brandishing his heavy mace, which rose five hundred cubits high,
he struck Prahasta with great force; thus smitten by the mace,
Prahasta fell down like a mountain standing firm when struck by the thunderbolt of Indra.

Seeing Prahasta fallen, Mārīca, Śuka, and Sāraṇa, along with Mahodara and Dhumrakṣa, retreated from the field of battle. When the ministers had withdrawn and Prahasta was struck down, [the situation became clear].
Rāvaṇa swiftly rushed toward Arjuna, the best of kings. That battle between the thousand-armed one and the twenty-armed one, between the king and the Rākṣasa, was fierce and hair-raising.
They were like two agitated oceans, like two mountains whose foundations have shifted,
like two suns endowed with brilliance, or like two fires consuming everything;
they were like two elephants intoxicated by strength, or like two bulls for the sake of a mate.
Roaring like clouds and fierce in their strength like lions, those two—
the Rākṣasa and Arjuna— were as enraged as Rudra and Kāla;
thus they struck each other violently with their maces.
Just as mountains endure terrible blows from thunderbolts without wavering, so did those two—
the man and the rākṣasa— endure the blows of their clubs. And just as an echo arises from the sounds of a thunderbolt, so it was with them.
Likewise, by the blows of their maces, echoes resounded in all directions. As Arjuna’s mace was brought down upon his enemy’s chest,
it made the sky appear like gold, just as a flash of lightning illuminates the heavens.
In that very manner, as it was struck again and again by Rāvaṇa,
the mace shone upon Arjuna’s chest like a meteor upon a great mountain;
neither did Arjuna feel exhaustion, nor did the lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas.
The battle between those two was equal, like that of old between Bali and Indra;
like two great bulls with their horns or two elephants with the tips of their tusks,
those two best of men and rākṣasas struck one another down.
Then, by the enraged Arjuna, that mace was released with all his might at the chest of Rāvaṇa in the great battle; yet,
because of the protection afforded by the granting of the boon, that mace struck Rāvaṇa’s breast.
Like a weak army broken in two, it fell to the earth. Struck by the blow of the mace released by Arjuna, Rāvaṇa recoiled a distance of a bow’s length and sank down, groaning aloud.
Seeing Daśagrīva thus overwhelmed, Arjuna then suddenly seized him, as Garuḍa seizes a serpent. Grasping that ten-faced one by force with his thousand arms, he—
The powerful king bound him as Nārāyaṇa bound Bali. While the ten-necked one was being bound, the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and gods,
crying out "Excellent!", showered flowers upon the head of Arjuna.
Like a tiger seizing a deer, or a lion-king a tusker,
King Haihaya roared repeatedly in joy like a thundercloud.
But Prahasta, having recovered his composure, saw that the Ten-faced one was bound.
Enraged, he rushed toward the king along with those *rākṣasas*.
The speed of those night-stalkers as they charged forward shone forth like the wondrous surge of the oceans when the heat of the sun has subsided.
Crying out repeatedly, "Release him! Release him! and "Stay!
Stay!", they then hurled clubs and spears at Arjuna; but Arjuna, remaining unperturbed, quickly struck them down before they could reach him.
The slayer of enemies seized the weapons of the foes of the immortals;
then, with those very formidable and excellent weapons,
he pierced and put the *rākṣasas* to flight, just as the wind scatters the clouds.
Having terrified the Rākṣasas, Kārtavīryārjuna then seized Rāvaṇa and entered his city surrounded by his friends. He was showered with heaps of flowers and parched grain.
Then Arjuna, resembling Indra, entered that city accompanied by the twice-born and the citizens,
just as the thousand-eyed god enters after having subdued Bali.

The seer Pulastya heard that capture of Rāvaṇa, which was like the seizing of Vāyu, as it was being recounted by the gods in heaven. Then, though possessed of great fortitude, he trembled out of affection for his grandson.

The great Ṛṣi came to see the lord of Māhiṣmatī. Taking to the path of the wind, that twice-born one, whose speed was equal to the wind and whose prowess was like the intensity of thought, reached the city of Māhiṣmatī.
He entered that city, which resembled Amarāvatī and was filled with joyful and well-fed people, just as Brahmā enters Indra’s Amarāvatī;
he was like the sun on foot, difficult to behold as he emerged.
Then, having recognized him, they announced him to Arjuna.
Hearing those words, "It is Pulastya," the lord of the Haihayas raised his joined palms to his head and went out to meet that best of the twice-born.
7.033.007a His domestic priest, taking the guest-offering (arghya) as well as the honey-mixture (madhuparka), 7.033.007c went before the king, just as Bṛhaspati goes before Indra.
7.033.008a Then, seeing that ṛṣi approaching like the rising sun,
Seeing that Pulastya had arrived, Arjuna paid homage to him as Indra pays homage to the Lord.
Causing the offering of *madhuparka*, water for the feet, and the guest-offering (*arghya*) to be presented to him,
the king of kings spoke to Pulastya in a voice faltering with joy.
7.033.010a Today this Māhiṣmatī has been made equal to Amarāvatī;
7.033.010c today, O best of the lords of the twice-born, because I behold that which is difficult to see.
7.033.011a Today I have attained well-being, O Lord; today my lineage has been uplifted.
7.033.011c I worship these two feet of yours, which are worthy of being saluted by the hosts of gods.
7.033.012a This kingdom, these sons, these wives, and we ourselves— 7.033.012c O Brahmin, what shall we do? What task must be performed? May your lordship command us.
Having then inquired after the welfare of that king regarding his religious duties, his sacred fires, and his dependents,
Pulastya spoke to Arjuna, the king of the Haihayas—
O lord of kings, whose face resembles a stainless lotus and the full moon.

"Your strength is incomparable, by which you have conquered the Ten-necked one; before whose fear the ocean and the wind stand motionless. That very grandson of mine, who was exceedingly difficult to defeat, has today been bound by you."
"O son, you have caused your vast fame to resound;
therefore, at my word, being entreated today, release the Ten-faced one, my child. Then Arjuna, accepting the command of Pulastya, [heeded] the words of the One Possessing Nothing.
The lord of the kings of the earth, filled with joy, released the lord of the rākṣasas. Having released that enemy of the gods, Arjuna honored him with divine ornaments, garlands, and garments.
Having entered into friendship with Ahiṃsaka and his sacrificial fires,
and having paid homage to the son of Brahmā, he went home.
Then the powerful lord of the Rākṣasas also met with Pulastya.
Having offered him hospitality with an embrace, the Grandfather’s son, Pulastya, that best of sages, dismissed him while feeling some bashfulness;
having thus released the Ten-necked one, he departed for the world of Brahmā.
Thus Rāvaṇa was overcome by Kārtavīrya due to his insolence,
yet he obtained release once again through the word of Pulastya.
In this way, O delighter of the Raghus, there are those who are stronger than the strong.
"One who desires his own welfare should not show contempt toward others.
Then that king, having gained the friendship of the flesh-eaters from the thousand-armed one;
7.033.023c He again wrought slaughter among men;
and out of pride, he roamed over the entire earth.
7.034.001a But Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, having been released by Arjuna, [departed].

Thus treated, he wandered the entire earth without despondency. Whenever Rāvaṇa heard of any being, whether a Rākṣasa or a human, who was superior in strength, the arrogant one would approach him and challenge him to battle.
Then, on one occasion, having gone to the city of Kiṣkindhā ruled by Vālin,
he challenged Vālin, who wore a golden garland, to battle.
Thereupon, Tāra, the lordly minister of the monkeys and father of Tārā, [spoke].
He spoke these words to Rāvaṇa, who had arrived desiring battle:
"O Lord of Rākṣasas, Vālī has gone, he who would be a match for you;
no other monkey is capable of standing before you."
"O Rāvaṇa, having performed his twilight devotions at all four oceans, Vālī will arrive in this very moment; wait for a short while!
Behold these heaps of bones, white as conch shells."
"O King, these [demons] were seeking battle through the splendor of the lord of monkeys. O Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa, since you drank the nectar of immortality,
your life shall likewise come to an end upon encountering Vālin."
"Or rather, if you are in a hurry to die, go to the southern ocean;
there you shall see Vālin like the sun resting upon the earth.
Then Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, having rebuked Tāra, [departed].
Having ascended that Puṣpaka chariot, he set out for the southern ocean.
There, Rāvaṇa beheld Vālin— who resembled a mountain of gold and whose face was like the rising sun— intent upon his twilight devotions.
Then Rāvaṇa, resembling a heap of collyrium, descended from the Puṣpaka chariot and rushed forward with silent steps to seize Vālin quickly; meanwhile,
Rāvaṇa was spotted by Vālin, who happened to open his eyes.
Though he perceived Rāvaṇa’s evil intent, Vālī felt no agitation;
like a lion sighting a hare or Garuḍa a serpent,
he did not think twice about that Rāvaṇa of wicked resolve.
Today, having made this evil-minded Rāvaṇa hang from my armpit as I wish to seize him, I shall go to the great ocean;
they shall see my enemy seated upon my lap, with his thighs, hands, and garments hanging down.
"Daśagrīva is hanging there like a serpent from Garuḍa"—
having formed this resolve, Vālī leaned against his ear and,
reciting the Vedic mantras, stood firm like the king of mountains.
Desiring to seize one another, those two— the monkey and the king of the rākṣasas—
endeavored with great effort and, emboldened by their strength, exerted themselves in that task.
Thinking that Rāvaṇa was within reach of his grasp by the sound of his footsteps, [Hanumān acted].
Even with his back turned, Vālin seized him as a bird seizes a snake. Grasping that lord of the rākṣasas who desired to seize him,
the monkey leapt into the sky with speed, holding him tucked under his arm.
7.034.021a While Rāvaṇa was thus being tormented and repeatedly clawed by him, Vālī seized him as the wind seizes a cloud.
7.034.022a Then, while the Ten-faced one was being carried away, those ministers of the Rākṣasa—
Desiring to set him free, those terrible ones rushed forward, roaring;
pursued by them, Vālin shone as he moved through the midst of the sky,
like the sun situated in the heavens being followed by masses of clouds.

Unable to withstand Vālin when he arrived, those foremost of Rākṣasas fell down, exhausted by the force of his arms and thighs; indeed, as he moved along the path of Vālin, the lords of mountains were cast aside.
Free from the flight of flocks of birds, the lord of monkeys, possessed of great speed,
gradually paid homage at the time of twilight to all the oceans. While being honored by the beings moving in the sky, the monkey, himself a traveler of the skies, proceeded on his way.
Vālin, together with Rāvaṇa, arrived at the western ocean.
Having performed his twilight devotions there, bathed, and recited prayers,
the monkey set out for the northern ocean, carrying the ten-faced one.
Having performed the twilight rites at the northern ocean, Vālī, carrying the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, went toward the eastern great ocean;
there too, that lord of monkeys, the son of Indra, performed the twilight rites.
Taking Rāvaṇa with him, he returned toward Kiṣkindhā. Having performed his twilight devotions at all four oceans, the monkey,
exhausted from carrying Rāvaṇa, alighted in the grove of Kiṣkindhā.
Then the best of monkeys released Rāvaṇa from his armpit and,
laughing at Rāvaṇa, said, "Where have you come from?
Having fallen into great amazement, he looked about for a place to rest.
The Lord of the Rākṣasas spoke these words to that Lord of the Monkeys:
"O King of Monkeys, who resembles Mahendra, I am Rāvaṇa, the Lord of the Rākṣasas.
Desiring battle, I have arrived, and today I have been encountered by you."
"Oh, what strength! Oh, what heroism! Oh, what profundity you possess, by which I have been seized like a beast and whirled around the four oceans!
Thus it is, O hero, O monkey, that you act so tirelessly and with such speed."
"And while I am carrying you, what other hero could possibly proceed?
O monkey, this capacity for movement belongs only to three beings:
the mind, the wind, and Suparṇa—or to you; of this there is no doubt."
"O bull among monkeys, having now seen your strength, I desire a long-lasting and very affectionate friendship with you in the presence of the sacred fire.
My wives, sons, city, kingdom, enjoyments, clothing, and food [are yours]."
"O Lord of Monkeys, everything shall indeed be shared between us without division.
Then, having kindled the fire, both the monkey and the Rākṣasa,
having entered into brotherhood, embraced one another.
Then, with their arms entwined around one another, those two— the monkey and the Rākṣasa—
entered Kiṣkindhā joyfully, like two lions entering a mountain cave. There,
Rāvaṇa dwelt for a month, just as Sugrīva had done.

7.034.042c When the ministers arrived, the base one [Rāvaṇa] sought the destruction of the three worlds. 7.034.043a O Lord, this is how it happened in the past: Rāvaṇa was humiliated by Vālin and made his brother in the presence of the Fire-god.
"O Rāma, Vālin possessed supreme and incomparable strength;
yet he too was utterly consumed by her, like a moth by fire.
Thereupon, Rāma questioned the sage who dwelt in the southern quarter.
With palms joined in reverence and full of humility, he spoke these meaningful words:
"The strength of both Vālin and Rāvaṇa was incomparable;
yet it is my conviction that neither of them was equal to the prowess of Hanumān."
Valor, skill, strength, fortitude, wisdom, the means of policy,
prowess, and majesty— all these have made their home in Hanumān. Then, seeing the ocean, that army of monkeys began to despair.
Having comforted the monkeys once more, he leaped across a hundred yojanas;
having overpowered the city of Laṅkā as well as Rāvaṇa’s inner apartments,
he beheld Sītā, spoke with her, and likewise inspired her with confidence.
The army leaders, the sons of the ministers, the servants, and the son of Rāvaṇa—
all these were struck down there by Hanumān alone,
after he had been released from his bonds and had spoken with the Ten-faced One.

7.035.007c Laṅkā was reduced to ashes by him, as the earth is by fire. 7.035.008a Neither of Kāla, nor of Śakra, nor of Viṣṇu, nor of the Lord of Wealth (Vittapa) are deeds such as those heard of, which were performed by Hanumān in battle.
"By the strength of his arms, O Lakṣmaṇa, Laṅkā, Sītā,
victory, my kingdom, friends, and kinsmen were all obtained by me;
for had Hanumān, the friend of the lord of monkeys, not been mine," so he said.
Who would have been capable of knowing even that which had transpired regarding Jānakī?
For what reason was Vālin not consumed like a blade of grass when that enmity arose, even though he desired to do what was pleasing to Sugrīva?
7.035.012a "I do not think that Hanumān truly knew his own strength, 7.035.012c since he saw the lord of monkeys, who cherished life, suffering.
7.035.013a "O Blessed One, O great sage, [please explain] all of this regarding Hanumān."
"O one honored by the immortals, let us relate it in detail according to the truth.
Having heard these words of Rāghava, which were full of reason, the Ṛṣi then spoke these words to him in the presence of Hanumān.
"O best of the Raghus, what you say regarding Hanumān is true:
there is no one equal to him in strength, nor superior in speed, nor in intellect. Yet, in the past, a curse was placed upon him by the sages, whose curses are never in vain."

7.035.016c No one knows the strength by which you, being powerful, crush your enemies. 7.035.017a O mighty Rāma, even the deed performed by him in childhood cannot be described to you because of his extreme youth.
"Or if you have the intention to hear it, O Rāghava, then,
O Rāma, having composed your mind, listen as I speak.
There is a mountain named Sumeru, with golden peaks bestowed by the Sun."
In that place where his father, named Keśarī, ruled the kingdom, he had a beloved wife well-known as Añjanā. Upon her, Vāyu begot an excellent son.
Then Añjanā gave birth to him, who shone like the awn of a rice stalk;
she had gone out into the dense forest desiring to gather fruits. And he was severely afflicted by both separation from his mother and by hunger.
The infant cried out excessively, like a young lion; then,
seeing the rising sun resembling a cluster of hibiscus flowers,
he flew toward the sun out of a desire for its fruit.
Facing the morning sun, the boy was like the morning sun incarnate;
desiring to seize the morning sun, he leaped into the midst of the sky. While Hanumān was thus leaping in his state of childhood,
A very great wonder arose among the gods, dānavas, and siddhas. Neither the wind, nor Garuḍa, nor even the mind possesses such speed as this son of Vāyu, who traverses the highest heavens.
"If this child already possesses such speed and prowess,
what will his velocity be like when he attains youth and strength?
The wind follows after his own son as he leaps."
Out of fear of being scorched by the sun, the Rākṣasa, cooled by masses of frost,
traverses the sky for many thousands of yojanas; yet,
due to his father's power and his own childhood, he has come into the vicinity of the sun.
Thinking, "This one is but a child and ignorant of faults," and considering that the task at hand depended upon him, the Sun did not burn him.
For on the very day he leaped up to seize the Sun, [he was protected].
On that very day, Rāhu sought to seize the sun. O Rāma, when he was seized by him, Rāhu— the crusher of the moon and sun— became terrified and fled from the chariot of the sun.
Having gone to Indra’s abode, the son of Siṃhikā, filled with rage,
knit his brows and spoke to the god who was surrounded by the hosts of gods:
"O Vāsava, having granted me the moon and the sun as a means to appease my hunger..."
"O slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, what is this that you have given to another?
Today, at the time of the lunar node, I came desiring to seize the sun; yet another Rāhu, having approached, has suddenly seized the sun."
Having heard Rāhu’s words, Vāsava, filled with agitation,
rose up from his seat, casting off his golden garland.
Then [he mounted] the four-tusked elephant, which resembled a peak of Kailāsa and was flowing with rut.
Mounting his lordly elephant— tall, adorned with golden bells that seemed to laugh aloud, and capable of inspiring passion—
Indra set forth with Rāhu as his vanguard toward where the sun was located, accompanied by this Hanumān.
Then Rāhu, having abandoned Vāsava, arrived with great impetuosity;
he was seen by him as he rushed forward like a mountain peak. Then, letting go of the Sun and beholding Rāhu in this manner, [he acted].
7.035.040c He leapt up again into the sky to seize the son of Siṃhikā.
7.035.041a O Rāma, seeing this monkey rushing toward him after letting go of the sun, Rāhu turned back; with only his head remaining, he fled with his face averted.
Hoping for Indra as his protector, the son of Siṃhikā cried out "Indra! Indra! again and again out of terror;
yet even as Rāhu was crying out, his voice had already been perceived before he could be seen.
Hearing this, Indra said to me, "Do not fear; here, I shall slay him.
Then, seeing Airāvata and thinking, "This is truly great," the son of the Wind-god rushed toward that king of elephants as if toward a fruit.
Then, as he rushed forward with the desire to seize Airāvata,
his form for a moment became terrible, yet radiant like that of Indra and Agni.
But the Lord of Śacī was not excessively enraged as he thus charged toward him.
With the tip of his hand, he struck him with a thunderbolt that had been released; then, struck by Indra’s vajra, he fell upon the mountain,
and as he was falling, his left jaw was shattered.
When that boy had fallen, overwhelmed by the blow of the thunderbolt,
Vāyu became enraged at Indra and at all that was inauspicious for living beings;
the powerful one entered within creatures, obstructing their receptacles of feces and urine.
He obstructed all beings, just as Indra [obstructs] with rain during the monsoon.
Due to the agitation of the wind, all beings everywhere became breathless;
their joints breaking apart, they became like pieces of wood.
Devoid of the *svadhā* call, devoid of the *vaṣaṭ* call, inactive, and bereft of dharma,
the three worlds, due to the agitation of Vāyu, appeared as if situated in hell.
Then the subjects— including Gandharvas, gods, Asuras, and humans— [were likewise affected].
Afflicted by unhappiness and seeking comfort, they approached Prajāpati;
with palms joined in reverence, the gods, whose bellies were sunken like those of emaciated people, said:
"O Blessed One, O Lord of Creatures, we fourfold classes of beings have been created by you."
"O Wind, this lord of our life was given to us by you. Having become the master of our breaths, O best of beings, why does he now obstruct us today,
producing such grief as women feel within the inner apartments?"
"Therefore, O Lord, we have come to you for refuge, afflicted by the wind. O slayer of enemies, dispel this suffering of ours born from the obstruction of the vital breath.
Having heard this from his subjects, the Lord of Creatures, Prajāpati, [spoke].
Having said to them, "It was for a specific reason," he spoke again to the subjects:
"O subjects, listen to all that reason for which Vāyu became angry with you and obstructed you; it is something you ought to hear and find within yourselves."
Today his son has been struck down by Indra, the lord of the immortals;
having heeded the words of Rāhu, the King has provoked you, O Anila.
The bodiless Vāyu moves within bodies, protecting them.
For the body, indeed, when separated from the wind, becomes level with the dust.
The wind is the vital breaths, the wind is happiness; the wind is this entire world.
Deprived of the wind, the world finds no happiness.
This very day the world has been abandoned by Vāyu in its life-force;
this very day these [beings] stand breathless, like wood or a wall. Therefore, let us go to where Māruta dwells, for he is the one who inflicts pain upon you.
"Let us not go to destruction without propitiating the son of Aditi.
Then Prajāpati, together with his subjects, along with the gods, Gandharvas, Bhujaṅgas, and Guhyakas, [approached him].
He went there where the wind blows,
taking up the son who had been struck down by the lord of the gods; then [he beheld him] possessing the radiance of the sun, Vaiśvānara, and gold.
Then, seeing Suta always seated upon his lap during his movements, the Four-faced One felt compassion for him,
as did the gods, Siddhas, Ṛṣis, Bhujaṃgas, and Rākṣasas.
Then, seeing the Grandfather, Vāyu, afflicted by the slaughter of his son,
took up that infant and stood before the Creator. He was adorned with trembling earrings, a crown, garlands, and ornaments of refined gold.

Vāyu fell at the feet of the Creator and remained there for three days. Then the foremost knower of the Vedas, having raised Vāyu with his hand— which was adorned with hanging ornaments— caressed that child.
Then, as soon as he was touched playfully by the Lotus-born One,
he regained his life, like a crop sprinkled with water. Seeing him restored to life, the Wind, the bearer of fragrance, rejoiced.
He moved among all beings as he had done before, remaining fully composed within them.
Freed from the disease of the wind, the subjects indeed became joyful,
like lotus ponds with their blossoms when released from cold winds.

Then Brahmā— the one who exists in three pairs, the three-peaked, the one with three abodes, and the one worshipped by the thirty gods— spoke to the deities out of a desire to do what was pleasing to the Maruts:
"O Mahendra, Agni, Varuṇa, Dhaneśvara, and Maheśvara!"
"Even though you already know all this, I shall speak what is beneficial; listen.
This child will have work to do for you; therefore, all of you grant him boons to give satisfaction to this son of the Wind."
Then the thousand-eyed one, his face auspicious and his heart colored with affection,
cast down a garland made of *kuśa* grass and spoke these words:
"Since his jaw has been wounded by the thunderbolt released from my hand,"
"By this name, this tiger among monkeys shall be known as Hanumān.
I myself shall grant him the most excellent and supreme boon:
from this day forward, he shall be invulnerable to my thunderbolt."
Then the blessed Mārtaṇḍa, the dispeller of darkness, said there:
"I shall grant him a hundredth part of this, my own splendor,
when he becomes capable of studying the scriptures."
"Then I shall give him this scripture by which he will become eloquent;
and Varuṇa has granted him a boon that death shall not come to him even after a hundred thousand years, nor from my noose, nor even from water."
Yama too, being pleased, grants him the boon of immunity from punishment, perpetual freedom from disease, and lack of despondency in battle;
yet this mace of mine shall not slay him in combat.
Thus did the bestower of boons, whose single eye is tawny, speak at that time:
"He shall not be slain by me, nor by my weapons of intoxication.
In this way, Śaṃkara also granted him this supreme boon.
"He shall be invulnerable to all the Brahma-staffs;
he shall be long-lived and high-souled"—thus spoke Brahmā.
But Viśvakarman, seeing that infant who resembled the rising sun, [said:]
The high-minded preeminent artisan spoke this boon for him:
"Whatever weapons of the gods have been fashioned here,
he shall be invulnerable by them at the time of battle."
Then, seeing him thus gratified by the boons of the gods,
the four-faced Teacher of the World spoke with a pleased countenance to Vāyu:
"He shall be a source of fear to his enemies and a giver of fearlessness to his friends."
"Your son here, born of the Maruts and the daughter of the Maruts, shall be invincible.
He will perform deeds in battle that cause the hair to stand on end— deeds intended for the destruction of Rāvaṇa and for the delight of Rāma."

Having spoken thus and taken leave of that Wind-god, they all, led by the Grandfather (Brahmā), departed with the immortals as they had come. He too, the Bearer of Fragrance (Vāyu), took his son and brought him home.
Having announced the boon granted to Añjanā,
he departed; O Rāma, having obtained these boons, he was filled with the power inherent in those gifts, like the overflowing ocean.
"For this bull among monkeys,
being filled with insolence, commits offenses fearlessly against the hermitages of the great seers;
he destroys the sacrificial ladles, the vessels for the *agnihotra*, and the stores of bark garments."

He renders all those who are broken, severed, and destroyed utterly peaceful; for he has been made unslayable by Brahmā against all forms of the Brahmin’s curse. Knowing this, the sages indeed always forgive him.
When this monkey, even though forbidden by Keśarin, Vāyu, and Sāñjana, continued to transgress the bounds of propriety,
the great seers born of the lineages of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras became enraged.
7.036.032c O best of the Raghus, they cursed him, though not excessively enraged or filled with great wrath.
7.036.033a "O monkey, since you oppress us by relying upon your strength,
7.036.033c you shall experience that for a long time, deluded as you are by our curse."
Then, his vigor and strength having been taken away by the power of the great seer’s word,
he moved about in a state of mildness, no longer resorting to exertion.
Now, there was one named Ṛkṣarajas, the father of Vālin and Sugrīva.
He was the king of all the monkeys, like the sun in his splendor.
Having ruled the kingdom of the monkeys for a long time, that lord of the monkeys,
named Arkṣarajas, then met his end through the law of time.
When he had passed away, Vālī was succeeded on his father’s throne as king in Vālī’s place by Sugrīva, with the assistance of ministers skilled in counsel;
and his alliance with Sugrīva was undivided and free from any flaw.

Their friendship became as unbreakable as that between the wind and the fire. It was solely due to the power of a curse that he did not know his own strength when the enmity between Vālin and Sugrīva arose because of Rāma.
For even though he was being tormented by Vālin, this Sugrīva did not reveal it,
nor did Māruti perceive his own strength, [let alone that of the other],
through its prowess, energy, intelligence, and majesty.
In terms of good character, sweetness, policy, and its opposite, as well as depth, cleverness, great heroism, and fortitude,
there is no one in the world who surpasses Hanumān.
Long ago, when that lord of monkeys was about to learn grammar,
he went from the mountain of sunrise to the mountain of sunset with his back turned toward the sun.
Bearing a vast and immeasurable collection of scriptures, he was like the ocean wishing to overflow its bounds,
or like a fire wishing to consume the worlds.
In the destruction of worlds, as it were, who could stand before Hanumān, even as he faces the Ender? He,
and these other great lords of monkeys, [are here].
O Rāma, Sugrīva, Mainda, Dvivida, along with Nīla,
Tārā, Tāreya, Anala, and Sarambha—
these were indeed created by the gods for your sake.
All this that you have asked me has been told; I have related this deed of Hanumān from his childhood. You have been seen and spoken with, O Rāma; let us depart.
Having spoken thus, all those sages departed as they had come. Then,
after reflecting, Rāma embraced his friend Pratardana, the lord of Kāśī who was fearless from any quarter, and spoke these words:
"O King, you have shown your affection and displayed supreme friendship;
you and Bharata have both exerted yourselves.
Therefore, may you go today to the city of Kāśī, Vārāṇasī."
"Protected by you, it shall be delightful, with excellent ramparts and beautiful gateways.
Having said this much, the righteous-souled descendant of Kakutstha rose from his supreme seat and embraced him closely against his chest.
Having dismissed that companion and welcomed the lords of the earth,
Rāghava, smiling, spoke these sweet-syllabled words:
"Your pleasure is undisturbed, protected as it is by your own splendor."
Dharma is eternally constant for you, and truth always abides with you. By the power and splendor of you great-souled ones,
the evil-minded and wicked Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, has been slain.
I was merely the instrument there, slain by the power of your splendors; Rāvaṇa, along with his hosts, his sons, and his kinsmen, has been destroyed in battle.
And you have all been brought here by the high-souled Bharata.
Having heard that King Janaka’s daughter had been abducted in the forest,
and that a very long time has passed while all those high-souled kings have been prepared for her recovery, let your minds be inclined toward setting out.
Filled with great joy, the kings replied to him:
"By good fortune, O Rāma, you are victorious and the kingdom is firmly established;
by good fortune, Sītā has been recovered, and by good fortune, the enemy has been defeated."
"This is our supreme desire, this is our highest glory, O Rāma: that we behold you victorious, with your enemies slain. And it is fitting, O descendant of Kakutstha, that you should praise us."
For those worthy of praise know how to speak such praise as this:
"We take our leave and shall depart; may you ever remain in our hearts. And may you, O Great King, always feel affection for us."

7.038.001 Those high-souled kings set out in every direction, those heroes causing the earth to tremble as they joyfully departed for their own cities. 7.038.002 They assembled there in great numbers, by the thousands of *akṣauhiṇīs*.
7.038.002c All those who had gathered for the sake of Rāghava returned delighted; 7.038.003a and the kings, filled with pride in their strength, said:
"We truly do not see Rāvaṇa standing before us in battle."
7.038.004a We were brought back later by Bharata for no purpose;
7.038.004c for the rākṣasas there would undoubtedly have been slain by the kings themselves.
7.038.005a [We were spared] because we were protected by the strength of Rāma’s arms and that of Lakṣmaṇa.
"May we fight happily on the far shore of the ocean, free from all anxiety. Speaking these and thousands of other such words, those great car-warriors entered their own kingdoms.
Having gone to their respective cities as before, the kings gave various jewels and offerings to Rāma out of a desire to please him:
horses, gems, garments, and elephants fierce with rut.
Taking divine sandalwood and celestial ornaments,
Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, and the great chariot-warrior Śatrughna returned to Ayodhyā with those jewels.
And having arrived at the beautiful city of Ayodhyā, those bulls among men presented all their jewels to the high-souled descendant of Raghu.
And Rāghava, filled with joy, accepted all of that.
He bestowed all of them upon the high-souled Sugrīva,
and he gave them to Vibhīṣaṇa and to the other bears and monkeys—
the heroes headed by Hanumān and the mighty Rākṣasas.
Then, all those mighty ones, with joyful minds, bore upon their heads and arms those gifts bestowed by Rāma;
and they drank various kinds of fragrant honey.
They ate well-prepared meats and tasted various fruits.
As they lived in this manner, more than a month passed;
yet, through their devotion to Rāma, they perceived all that time as being like a mere moment.
Rāma sported together with those monkeys who could assume any form at will,
as well as with the kings of great heroism and the Rākṣasas of great strength.
In this manner, their second month of the cool season passed happily.
7.038.017c Among the monkeys who were greatly rejoicing and among the Rākṣasas on all sides,
7.039.001a as those bears, monkeys, and Rākṣasas were thus dwelling,
7.039.001c Rāghava, possessed of great splendor, spoke this to Sugrīva:
"Go, gentle one, to Kiṣkindhā, which is unassailable even by gods and asuras;
rule the kingdom, free of all thorns, together with your ministers. And [entrust it] to Aṅgada, O mighty-armed one, filled with the highest affection."
Behold Hanumān and Nala, who possess great strength; Suṣeṇa, your heroic father-in-law; Tāra, the best among the powerful;
and the invincible Kumuda and the exceedingly mighty Nīla.
Vīra and Śatabali, as well as Mainda and Dvivida; Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, and the mighty Śarabha;
and the invincible King of Bears, Jāmbavān, possessed of great strength.
"Behold Gandhamādana as well, filled with joy;
and behold those other great-souled ones who have sacrificed their lives for my sake. Look upon them with affection and do nothing that would displease them."
Having spoken thus and having praised Sugrīva again and again,
Rāma then addressed Vibhīṣaṇa with sweet words:
"O King, rule Taṅkā according to dharma, for you are esteemed by me."
Of the city, of the Rākṣasas, and of your brother Vaiśravaṇa;
O King, you must never, under any circumstances, set your mind upon unrighteousness,
for wise kings certainly enjoy the earth.

"And I, O King, together with Sugrīva, must always be remembered by you with the highest affection; go now, free from all distress. Having heard the words spoken by Rāma, the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas—
"Excellent! Excellent! they said, praising the descendant of Kakutstha again and again:
"O mighty-armed one, your intellect and your prowess are truly marvelous;
O Rāma, your supreme sweetness is constant, like that of the Self-born One himself."
While those monkeys and rakshasas were speaking thus,
Hanumān, bowing down, addressed these words to Rāghava:
"O King, my supreme affection is ever firmly established in you."

"O hero, my devotion is constant; my heart shall go nowhere else. O hero, as long as I hear the story of Rāma upon this earth, so long shall my vital breaths remain within my body—of this there is no doubt."
To Hanumān who was speaking thus, the lord of kings rose from his seat, embraced him, and spoke these words:
"It shall be so, O best of monkeys; there is no doubt in this matter."

"For as long as the worlds shall endure, so long shall my story remain; indeed, this story of mine shall circulate throughout the worlds for that long. For as long as it does, your vital breaths shall dwell within your body—of this there is no doubt."
Then, having removed from his own neck that necklace shining like the moon and studded with shimmering cat's-eye gems, Rāghava affectionately fastened it upon Hanumān.
With that necklace bound upon his chest, that great monkey—
The lord of golden mountains shone with its peak occupied by the moon.
Having heard this from Rāghava, those mighty monkeys rose again and again,
and bowing their heads at his feet, they departed.
The mighty-armed Sugrīva was embraced by Rāma,
and the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa was held closely against his chest;
and they were all choked with tears, their eyes filled with weeping, and distraught.
As if bewildered by grief, they then abandoned Rāghava. Having dismissed the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas, the mighty-armed Rāma, together with his brothers, rejoiced happily in his happiness.
Then, at the time of afternoon, Rāghava, together with his brothers,
heard a sweet voice being uttered from the sky:
"O gentle Rāma, look upon me with your gentle face."
"Know me, O Lord, as Puṣkara, who has come from the peak of Kailāsa. Having received your command, I went to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) to attend upon him, O best of men; and he replied to me."
"You have been conquered by the high-souled Raghava, the lord of men,
who, having slain the invincible Ravana, the sovereign of the rakshasas, in battle—
when that evil-minded one was killed, my own supreme joy was realized."
O gentle one, since Rāvaṇa has been defeated by Rāma— the Supreme Soul— along with his hosts, sons, ministers, and kinsmen, you too have been conquered in Laṅkā; therefore,
O gentle one, carry him out, for I command you so.

"This is my supreme desire: that you should carry the joy of the Raghus, so that you may go forth free from feverish anxiety on this journey for the world. Having understood that command of the high-souled Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), [he departed].

"Having returned to your presence once again, please accept me in this way. "Very well," said the descendant of Kakutstha, and he honored the Puṣpaka with parched grain, unbroken rice, flowers, and highly fragrant perfumes.
"Go as you please, and come whenever I remember you.
"So be it," said Rāma, and having been dismissed by him, the Puṣpaka,
adorned with flowers, departed once more toward its desired direction.
When that Puṣpaka chariot, which possessed various forms, had thus vanished,
Bharata, with palms joined in reverence, addressed these words to the joy of the Raghus:
"Most wonderful things are seen while you are ruling the kingdom."
The cries of non-human beings are heard repeatedly;
yet a full month has passed since the mortals were freed from illness,
and even for those beings who are aged, death does not come, O Raghava.
Women give birth to sons, and men become handsome; O King, the joy of the city-dwellers is exceedingly great,
and Vāsava sends down rain at the proper time, like nectar.
"Even the winds blow with pleasant touch, bestowing happiness.
'O Lord of Men, may such a king as this be ours for a long time!'—
thus do the citizens speak in the city and the people in the countryside."
Having heard these very sweet words uttered by Bharata, Rāma was filled with joy; being happy himself, he rejoiced in happiness.
Then, having dismissed the gold-adorned Puṣpaka chariot, Rāma departed.
Then the mighty-armed one entered the Aśoka grove,
which was adorned on all sides with sandalwood, agallochum, mango trees, tall kāleyaka trees, and forests of devadāru.
It was covered with *priyaṅgu*, *kadamba*, and *kurabaka* trees, as well as with *jambū*, *pāṭalī*, and *kovidāra* trees,
which were always beautiful with lovely flowers and delightful with their fruit.
Adorned with hundreds of variegated mango trees— rich with beautiful sprouts and blossoms, swarming with intoxicated bees,
and graced by cuckoos, *bhṛṅgarāja* birds, and birds of many colors—
it was made radiant by these wonderful floral ornaments.
Some trees there shone like gold, some were like the crests of fire, and others resembled blue collyrium.
There were also oblong ponds of various shapes, filled with the most excellent water.
With crystal floors beneath stairways of highly precious jewels,
they possess groves of blooming lotuses and water-lilies adorned by ruddy geese;
they are further beautified by walls of various forms and surfaces of stone.
In various forest regions there, they were endowed with the most excellent meadows resembling lapis lazuli gems and filled with flowering trees,
just like Indra’s Nandana grove or Brahmā’s Caitraratha garden.
For such was that forest established for Rāma;
having entered the flourishing Aśoka grove, which was filled with many seats and houses and surrounded by bowers of creepers, the joy of the Raghus took up his residence there.
On a seat of auspicious form, adorned with clusters of flowers and covered with a woolen rug, Rāma sat down;
embracing Sītā with his arms, he [offered her] the finest honey-wine and maireya.
Kākutstha made her drink it, just as Indra makes Śacī drink the nectar of immortality. And the servants quickly brought various kinds of meats and diverse fruits for Rāma’s meal.

7.041.015a Those skilled in dance and song performed for the king; 7.041.015c so too did young women of beautiful form who had succumbed to the influence of drink. 7.041.016a Thus Rāma, filled with joy, [beheld] Sītā of the most radiant countenance.
Day after day, like a god, he delighted Vaidehī. While the high-souled Rāghava, that lord of men, was thus enjoying himself, the auspicious winter season passed away.

Having performed his civic duties in accordance with dharma during the forenoon, the knower of dharma spent the remaining half of the day’s portion within the inner apartments. And Sītā, having likewise performed her morning religious rites, [remained there].
Standing with palms joined in reverence before all her mothers-in-law without distinction,
she, adorned with many wonderful ornaments, then approached Rāma,
just as Śacī approaches the thousand-eyed Indra seated in Triviṣṭapa.
But seeing his wife endowed with auspiciousness, Rāghava experienced incomparable joy and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! "O Vaidehī, this attainment of offspring has come to me."
"Tell me, what do you desire? What wish of yours shall be fulfilled?
Vaidehī, smiling, then spoke these words to Rāma:
"O Rāghava, I wish to see the sacred groves of the ascetics."
O hero, it is my supreme desire that I may dwell at the feet of those sages of meritorious deeds who subsist on fruits and roots and are settled along the banks of the Gaṅgā.
"O descendant of Kakutstha, may I dwell for even a single night among those who possess merit.
Rāma, whose actions are effortless, replied, "So be it.
"Be confident, O Vaidehī; tomorrow you shall depart without a doubt."
Having spoken thus to Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha,
departed for the middle enclosure surrounded by his friends.
There, the wise ministers were attending upon the seated king.
7.042.001c There were storytellers of various tales who provided laughter on all sides.
7.042.002a Vijaya, Madhumatta, Kāśyapa, Piṅgala, Kuśa, 7.042.002c Surāji, Kāliya, Bhadra, Dantavakra, and Samāgadha.
7.042.003a These various kinds of stories, filled with jests,
7.042.003c they recounted with great joy to the high-souled Rāghava.
7.042.004a Then, in the course of a certain story, Rāghava spoke.
"O auspicious one, what conversations are taking place in the city and in the provinces? What do the people of the towns and the countryside say regarding me?
And what do they say concerning Sītā, Bharata, and Lakṣmaṇa?"
"Relying on Śatrughna and my mother Kaikeyī, what indeed must the kings say regarding the blame in this new kingdom?
When Rāma had spoken thus, Bhadra replied with palms joined in reverence:

7.042.007c O King, auspicious stories remain current among the city-dwellers. 7.042.008a But this account, O gentle one, concerning the slaying of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa, 7.042.008c is most frequently told by the citizens in their own city, O bull among men.
Thus addressed by Bhadra, Rāghava spoke these words:
"Tell me everything exactly as it is, without omission—
whatever auspicious or inauspicious words the city-dwellers have spoken."
"Having heard this now, I shall perform what is auspicious and avoid what is inauspicious. Speak with confidence, fearlessly and free from anxiety,
just as the citizens and the people in the countryside speak."
Thus addressed by Rāghava with these most excellent words, Bhadra,
with palms joined in reverence and mind well-composed, replied to the mighty-armed one:
"Listen, O King, to what the citizens say regarding both the auspicious and the inauspicious."
In the squares, marketplaces, and streets, as well as in the forests and groves,
Rāma has performed a difficult feat: the construction of a bridge across the ocean,
which had never been accomplished before by any of the ancient gods or even the Dānavas.
The invincible Rāvaṇa has been slain along with his army and vehicles;
the monkeys, bears, and rākṣasas have been brought under control.
And having killed Rāvaṇa in battle, Rāghava has recovered Sītā.
Casting aside his indignation, he brought her back to his own home once more. What kind of pleasure, born of union with Sītā, was in his heart—
having previously placed upon his lap her who had been forcibly seized by Rāvaṇa?
"How is it that Rāma does not reproach her for having been led back to Laṅkā, for having gone to the Aśoka grove, and for having fallen under the power of the Rākṣasas?
This same [conduct] will also have to be tolerated among our own wives."
"For as the king acts, so do his subjects follow"—
thus did the city-dwellers speak in many ways,
O King, throughout all the cities and the provinces.
Having heard these words of his, Rāghava, as if deeply afflicted,
said to all his friends, "How can this be explained?
Then they all, having saluted him and bowed their heads to the ground, spoke.
They replied to the dejected Rāghava, "It is even so, there is no doubt.
Having heard the words uttered by them all, Kākutstha,
the scorcher of his enemies, then dismissed them all.
Having dismissed his circle of friends and reached a firm decision through his intellect, Rāghava spoke these words to the doorkeeper sitting nearby:
"Quickly bring Saumitri Lakṣmaṇa, who is endowed with auspicious marks."
Having heard Rāma’s words regarding the mighty-armed Bharata and the unconquered Śatrughna, the gatekeeper placed his joined palms upon his head and,
having gone to Lakṣmaṇa’s house, entered unimpeded.
And then, raising his joined palms in reverence, he spoke these words:
"The king desires to see you; go there without delay.
Hearing Rāghava’s command, the son of Sumitrā replied, "So be it."

Mounting the chariot, he rushed to the residence of Raghava. Seeing Lakshmana departing, the gatekeeper approached Bharata and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words: "The King wishes to see you."
7.043.007a But Bharata, having heard the words spoken by Rāma from the gatekeeper,
7.043.007c sprang up quickly from his seat and then departed on foot.
7.043.008a Seeing Bharata departing in haste, [the gatekeeper] stood with palms joined in reverence.
Having gone to the palace of Śatrughna, he then spoke these words: "Come, come, O best of the Raghus; the king wishes to see you.
For Lakṣmaṇa has already gone, as has the highly illustrious Bharata."

Having heard those words, which were the command of Rāma, Śatrughna bowed his head to the earth and departed for where the descendant of Raghu was. Hearing that the princes had arrived, [Rāma’s] senses became agitated with anxiety.
With his head hanging down and his mind dejected, he spoke these words to the doorkeeper:
"Bring the princes into my presence with all haste;
upon them depends my life, for they are my very breath moving outside my body."
Commanded by the lord of men, the princes, dressed in white garments,
entered with focused minds, bowing low with palms joined in reverence.
Having seen his face, they beheld it like the moon eclipsed by Rāhu.
Seeing the eyes of the wise Rāma filled with tears, like the sun at twilight shorn of its radiance,
and beholding his face with its splendor destroyed like a lotus, they [were overcome].
Then, having quickly saluted the feet of Rāma with their heads, they all stood there composed; and Rāma shed tears. Embracing them with his arms and lifting them up, the mighty-armed one—
Having said, "Be seated," he then spoke these words:
"Gentlemen, you are my everything; you are my very life. O lords of men, it is by your grace that I protect this kingdom."
"O lords of men, you have mastered the meaning of the scriptures and are firmly established in wisdom; therefore, acting together, this matter of mine must be investigated.
As they were all seated there with dejected hearts, [he spoke].
7.044.001 With a parched mouth, the descendant of Kakutstha spoke these words:
7.044.002 "Listen all, may it be well with you; do not set your minds on any other course.
Such is the talk that circulates among the citizens concerning Sītā and me."
7.044.003a A very great public censure, both from the city and the countryside, is directed at me; that loathsome report cuts into my vital organs.
7.044.004a It is said that I was born into the family of the high-souled Ikṣvākus.
"How can I bring back Sītā, whose conduct is wicked,
to the city? For you know well, O gentle one, how Sītā was abducted by Rāvaṇa in the lonely Daṇḍaka forest, and how he was destroyed by me."
"O Saumitri, it was before your very eyes that the bearer of oblations to the gods [Agni],
and Vāyu who ranges through the sky, declared Maithilī to be sinless;
and long ago, the Moon and the Sun likewise proclaimed her so in the presence of the gods."

And by all the ṛṣis as well, the sinless daughter of Janaka was [declared pure]. Thus, she of pure conduct was placed into my hands by Mahendra on the island of Laṅkā in the presence of the gods and gandharvas.
"My inner self knows that the illustrious Sītā is pure;
therefore, having taken Vaidehī with me, I have come to Ayodhyā. Yet this great reproach and grief dwell within my heart."
There is great public censure from both the city and the countryside;
for whoever— be they anyone at all— has their ill-repute sung in the world,
they fall indeed to the lowest worlds as long as that report is proclaimed.
Disrepute is censured by the gods, while fame is honored among the gods.
Indeed, every undertaking of great-souled men is for the sake of fame.
O bulls among men, I would even give up my life or you all [for the sake of fame].
Terrified by the fear of scandal, how much more so would they be regarding the daughter of Janaka?
Therefore, let your honors behold her fallen into an ocean of grief;
for I do not see any further suffering greater than this.
"O Saumitri, tomorrow at dawn, having mounted the chariot driven by Sumantra and having helped Sītā ascend it, leave her at the border of the kingdom,
on the far bank of the Gaṅgā, at the hermitage of the great-souled Vālmīki."
7.044.016c There is a hermitage, appearing divine, situated on the bank of the Tamasā river.
7.044.017a Having left her there in that secluded thicket, O descendant of Raghu,
7.044.017c return quickly, O son of Sumitrā, and do as I say.
I must not be contradicted in any way regarding Sītā;
for if she were turned away, it would cause me the greatest displeasure. I adjure you all by my two arms and by my very life.
7.044.019c If anyone should speak to me in the midst of our conversation in order to conciliate me in any way, 7.044.020a let them honor me only if they abide by my command:
7.044.020c "Let Sītā be taken away from here this very day; do as I say."

"Previously, she told me that she wished to see the great hermitages on the bank of the Gaṅgā; let this desire of hers be fulfilled. Having spoken thus, the descendant of Kakutstha had his eyes clouded with tears.
7.044.022c That righteous-souled one entered, surrounded by his brothers.
7.045.001a Then, when the night had dawned, Lakṣmaṇa, with a dejected mind,
spoke these words to Sumantra with a parched face:
"O charioteer, quickly yoke the horses to the excellent chariot. Bring from the royal palace a well-spread seat for Sītā that is auspicious.
For Sītā must go from the royal palace to the hermitage of those who perform meritorious deeds."

"Let the chariot, which is the leader of the great seers, be brought quickly by me. Sumantra, having replied "So be it," [prepared] the chariot of brilliant appearance, yoked with excellent horses and well-spread with a comfortable seat.
Taking [the chariot], he said to the son of Sumitrā, who increases the joy of his friends: "This chariot has arrived; O Lord, let that which must be done be performed.
Thus addressed by Sumantra, Lakṣmaṇa went to the royal palace.
Having entered and approached Sītā, that bull among men spoke:
"O Queen, you must go quickly from this auspicious hermitage of the sages on the banks of the Gaṅgā and return at our king's command."
Thus addressed by the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa, Vaidehī attained incomparable joy and approved of the departure. She [prepared] costly garments and various kinds of jewels.
Having taken those ornaments, Vaidehī prepared to depart. "I shall give these ornaments to the wives of the sages," she said. Then Saumitri, saying "So be it," helped Maithilī onto the chariot.
7.045.010e He departed on his swift horse, mindful of Rāma’s command.
7.045.011a And then Sītā spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of prosperity: 7.045.011c “O delight of the Raghus, today I see many inauspicious omens.”
"O Saumitri, my eye is twitching today and a trembling arises in my limbs; moreover, I perceive my heart to be as if unwell. I am filled with the utmost anxiety and my fortitude has utterly failed."
O large-eyed one, I see the earth as if it were empty. O hero, may it be well with that brother of yours along with his brothers, and likewise with all my mothers-in-law without exception.
"May there be well-being for the people in the city and in the countryside as well"—
thus Sītā, with palms joined in reverence, prayed to the deities.
But Lakṣmaṇa, having heard that request, paid homage to Maithilī by bowing his head.
"May it be auspicious," he said, emboldened despite his parched heart.
Then, having arrived at a dwelling in a hermitage on the bank of the Gomatī,
the son of Sumitrā rose again at dawn and spoke to the charioteer.
"Yoke the chariot quickly today at the waters of the Bhāgīrathī;
I shall bear it upon my head, just as Tryambaka bears the mountain. Having swiftly groomed the horses and yoked them to the chariot, which were as swift as thought, [he prepared for the journey].
"Mount," the charioteer said to Vaidehī with palms joined in reverence;
at the charioteer's word, Sītā ascended that excellent chariot together with the son of Sumitrā and the wise Sumitra.
Then, having traveled for half a day, Lakṣmaṇa beheld a body of water on the Bhāgīrathī;
looking upon it, he wept aloud in deep distress. But Sītā, seeing Lakṣmaṇa so afflicted, became utterly despondent.
7.045.022c He spoke these words: "O knower of dharma, why is this being wept by you?
7.045.023a Having reached the bank of the Jāhnavī, which has been my long-cherished desire, 7.045.023c for what reason do you cause me grief, O Lakṣmaṇa, at a time that should be one of joy?"
"O bull among men, you have always remained at Rāma's feet; I trust that when separated from him for two nights, you did not fall into grief?
O Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma is as dear to me as my own life."
"I do not grieve in this way; do not be so foolish.
Help me cross the Gaṅgā and show me the ascetics.
Then I shall give you wealth, garments, and ornaments."
"Then, having offered salutations to the great seers as was appropriate,
and having stayed there for one night, we shall go back to that city again.
Having heard those words of his, she wiped her beautiful eyes.

Desiring to cross the auspicious Gaṅgā, Lakṣmaṇa brought forward a boat. Then the younger brother of Rāghava ascended the spacious boat provided by the Niṣādas, after first having the princess of Mithilā board it.
"Stay with Sumantra and the chariot," Lakṣmaṇa said, tormented by grief; and to the boatman, he said, "Depart.
Then, having reached the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, that Lakṣmaṇa—
With palms joined in reverence and his voice faltering with tears, he spoke these words to the princess of Mithilā:
"O noble Vaidehī, there is a great dart lodged in my heart, for on this account I have been made an object of public reproach by my wise elder brother."

"Indeed, death today would be better for me, or whatever may come after death, than to be employed in such a task as this, which is censured by the world. Be gracious; you ought not to show anger toward me, O lady of virtuous vows."
Having spoken thus, Lakṣmaṇa fell prostrate upon the ground with his hands joined in reverence.
Seeing him weeping with palms joined, longing for his own death,
Maithilī, deeply distressed, addressed these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
"7.046.008a What is this? I do not understand; tell me the truth, Lakṣmaṇa.
7.046.008c I see you, yet I do not see the king himself, nor even his well-being.
7.046.009a You are bound by oath by the lord of men, that you shall reveal your own distress."
"You should say that in my presence: 'I command you.
Thus urged by Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa, his heart distressed, with downcast face and voice choked with tears, spoke these words."
7.046.011a Having heard this most dreadful slander in the midst of the assembly, 7.046.011c as well as in the city and the countryside, on account of you, O daughter of Janaka,
7.046.012a those words, O Queen, need not be spoken by me in your presence.
"Those things which were placed in the king's heart, his indignation has been cast behind him.
Abandoned by the monarch, though innocent, you now abide in my presence. O Queen, he acted out of fear of public scandal; it must not be understood otherwise."
"And at the edge of the hermitages, you shall be abandoned by me, having understood the king's command regarding your pregnancy-longing. "Therefore,
this is the penance grove of the Brahman-sages on the bank of the Ganges."
"It is meritorious and delightful; do not despair, O auspicious lady.
This bull among sages, the highly illustrious brahmin Vālmīki, is the supreme friend of my father, King Daśaratha."
"O daughter of Janaka, having come into the shadow of the feet of this great-souled one, dwell there happily, devoted to fasting and single-minded,
abiding in the vow of a faithful wife and always keeping Rāma in your heart."
"O Goddess, by acting thus, your supreme welfare will be secured.
Having heard these harsh words of Lakṣmaṇa, Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka,
fell down, overcome by extreme despondency.
For a moment, her consciousness clouded and her eyes agitated by tears,
the daughter of Janaka spoke to Lakṣmaṇa in a piteous voice:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, surely this body of mine was created for nothing but suffering."
7.047.003c By the Creator, she has likewise been made to appear today as an embodiment of misery for me.
7.047.004a What sin was committed in the past, or who was separated from his wife, 7.047.004c that I, though pure in conduct and virtuous, have been abandoned by the king?
"O Saumitri, formerly I lived in the hermitage following at the feet of Rāma,
even while enduring the revolving cycle of suffering;
how then, O gentle one, shall I dwell in the hermitage now that it has been made desolate?"
To whom shall I, devoted to sorrow, recount my grief?
And what shall I say to the sages? What wrong have I done to the king, or for what reason have I been abandoned by the high-souled Rāghava?

"O Saumitri, it is certainly not this very day that I shall give up my life in the waters of the Jahnavi; rather, the lineage of my husband would be lost. O Saumitri, do as you have been commanded: abandon me, who am a partaker of sorrow."
"Abide by the command of the king, and hear these words of mine:
with palms joined in reverence and with humility, bowing your head to the feet of your mothers-in-law without distinction, inquire after the welfare of the monarch."

7.047.011 Just as you would behave toward your brothers, so should you always behave toward the citizens; for this would be the supreme dharma and this the unsurpassed glory. 7.047.012 O King, that you should win over the people of the city through righteousness.
"But I do not grieve for my own body, O bull among men, nor for the ancient calumny against me, O delight of the Raghus," Sītā said. While she was speaking thus, Lakṣmaṇa’s heart became despondent.
Having fallen to the ground with his head, he was indeed unable to speak. Having performed a circumambulation while weeping with a great sound,
he climbed back onto the boat and urged the boatman forward.
Having reached the northern bank, burdened by a weight of grief and as if bewildered by his sorrow, he quickly mounted the chariot;
turning back again and again, he gazed upon Sītā like one who is helpless.
Then Lakṣmaṇa proceeded toward Sītā as she stood on the opposite bank,
writhing in distress. Seeing the chariot at a distance and looking repeatedly at Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā became anxious, and grief took possession of her.
Bowed down by the burden of sorrow,
that ascetic Yaśodharā, finding no protector, wept in the forest resounding with the cries of peacocks.
Seeing Sītā weeping with a great cry, overcome by sorrow, those young sons of sages who were there ran to where the venerable Vālmīki, of foremost intellect, was staying.
Having saluted the feet of the sage, all the sons of the sage reported to the great seer the sound of her weeping:
"O Blessed One, she has never been seen before; to which great-souled man does she belong?"
"Like the goddess Śrī herself, our wife cries out with a distorted voice out of sheer delusion.
O Blessed One, please look upon her who has fallen from the sky like a deity;
for we do not know her to be human—let proper hospitality be extended to her."
Having heard those words of theirs and having determined the matter with his intellect, the knower of dharma,
who had obtained the power of vision through asceticism, rushed toward where Maithilī was. Having reached that region on foot for some distance, the great sage—
Taking the beautiful water-offering (arghya) and reaching the bank of the Jahnavi,
he beheld Sita, the beloved wife of Raghava, like one who was unprotected. Valmiki, the bull among sages, saw her, white-complexioned and afflicted by a heavy burden of grief.
He spoke these sweet words, as if gladdening her with his splendor:
"You are the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha, the virtuous queen of Rāma; you are the daughter of King Janaka. Welcome to you, O devoted wife!"
"By means of my concentration on the Dharma, I have indeed recognized you as you approach;
I have perceived the entire cause within my heart.
O Sītā, through the vision obtained by ascetic power, I know you to be sinless."
"O Vaidehī, you now dwell within me with a pure heart. Not far from my hermitage, there are female ascetics established in penance;
they will protect you constantly, my child, as if you were their own offspring."
"Accept this water of honor (*arghya*), confident and free from distress;
having entered as if into your own home, do not give way to despondency.
Having heard these most wonderful words spoken by the sage, Sītā—
Having bowed his head at her feet, he replied, "So be it," with palms joined in reverence.
As the sage departed, Sītā followed behind him with palms joined, until she reached the place where the female ascetics, ever devoted to dharma and composed in mind, were staying.
Seeing the sage approaching, followed by Vaidehī, they then drew near filled with joy and spoke these words:
"Welcome to you, O best of sages; it has been a long time since your arrival, O Lord."
"We all salute you; tell us, what shall we do?
Having heard those words of theirs, Vālmīki spoke this:
"This is Sītā, the wife of the wise Rāma, who has arrived here."
"This daughter-in-law of Daśaratha, the virtuous daughter of Janaka, though sinless, has been abandoned by her husband; she must always be protected by me.
Let you all look upon her with the highest affection."
Out of respect for my words, she should be especially honored by you.
Having repeatedly consoled Vaidehī,
the highly illustrious one of great asceticism returned to his own hermitage, surrounded by his disciples.
Having seen Sītā, the princess of Mithilā, confined within the hermitage,
Lakṣmaṇa, his heart distressed, was overcome by terrible anguish.
And the one of great splendor spoke to Sumantra, the counselor and charioteer:

Behold the sorrow born of Sītā’s suffering that afflicts the wise Rāma. What indeed could be more painful for the descendant of Raghu than this— having abandoned his wife, the daughter of Janaka, who is pure in her conduct?
