"O charioteer, I clearly believe that by fate Vaidehī has come to separation from Rāghava; for fate is indeed difficult to overcome. For he [Rāma] is one who [could defeat] the gods along with the Gandharvas, the Asuras together with the Rākṣasas."

If Rāghava were to strike him in his anger, he would merely be following destiny. Previously, by the words of my father, he dwelt for nine and five years in the desolate forest of Daṇḍaka, that most dreadful place.
7.049.007a Furthermore, the exile of Sītā is even more painful than that.

7.049.007c Having heard the words of the citizens, this appears to me as a cruel act. 7.049.008a O charioteer, what basis in righteousness could there be for such an action, which destroys one's reputation?
7.049.008c He arrived before Maithilī, accompanied by the citizens who spoke words of lamentation. 7.049.009a Having heard these various words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa,
Sumantra joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words:
"O Saumitri, you should not feel distress regarding Maithilī;
this was foreseen long ago by the brahmins in the presence of your father, O Lakṣmaṇa:
that Rāma will surely endure much suffering and possess little happiness."
In the course of great time, that great and righteous-souled one will likewise abandon you, as well as Maithilī, Śatrughna,
and Bharata. However, O Saumitri, this must not be spoken of to you, nor even to Bharata.
7.049.012c The words that Durvāsas spoke to you were indeed spoken by the king;
7.049.013a and in the presence of the great king and myself as well, O bull among men,
7.049.013c those words were uttered by the Ṛṣi in the vicinity of Vasiṣṭha.
Having heard the words of the ṛṣi, that bull among men said to me:
"O Sūta, you must never speak in this manner in the presence of people. With a deeply concentrated mind, I [accepted] those words of that world-protector.
"O gentle one, it is my conviction that I shall never speak an untruth.
In every way, O gentle one, there is nothing that should not be told by me in your presence.
If you have faith in hearing it, listen, O delight of the Raghus."
"Even though I was previously informed of this secret by the lord of men, I shall nevertheless relate it; for destiny is indeed difficult to overcome.
Having heard those words of his, which were profound in meaning and significant in their phrasing, [he spoke].
"Speak the truth," Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, then said to the charioteer. Thus urged by the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa,
the charioteer began to relate those words spoken by the seer.
Formerly, the great sage Durvāsas, the son of Atri,
dwelt during the rainy season in the holy hermitage of Vasiṣṭha. Your father, who was possessed of great splendor and immense fame, [went] to that hermitage.
Desiring to see the high-souled family priest, he went there in person. He beheld that great sage, who resembled the sun and was as if blazing with splendor, seated on the left side of Vasiṣṭha.
7.050.004e The humble [king] paid homage to those two sages, the best of ascetics.
7.050.005a Honored by them with a welcome and a seat, as well as with water for the feet and fruits and roots, the king sat down together with the sages.
7.050.006 While those supreme ṛṣis were seated there, various very sweet conversations took place as the sun reached the meridian. 7.050.007 Then,
during one such conversation, King Pragraha, with palms joined in reverence, [spoke].
He spoke to that high-souled son of Atri, whose wealth was asceticism:
"O Blessed One, what will be the extent of my lineage?
What will be the lifespan of my Rāma, and what will be the lifespans of my other sons?"
"And as for those who may be the sons of Rāma, what shall be their lifespan?
O Blessed One, by your grace, tell me the future course of this lineage.
Having heard these words spoken by King Daśaratha, [Vasiṣṭha replied:]
7.050.010c Durvāsas, possessed of great splendor, began to speak:
7.050.011a "Rāma shall be the lord of Ayodhyā for a long time; 7.050.011c and his younger brothers shall be happy and prosperous."
"In the course of some undertaking, that righteous-souled one will indeed abandon both you and the illustrious Maithilī after a long time—
ten thousand and ten hundred years."
7.050.013c Having served the kingdom, Rāma will go to the world of Brahmā.
7.050.014a Having performed many prosperous horse-sacrifices, that conqueror of enemy cities,
the descendant of Kakutstha, will establish many royal lineages.
Having related the entire history of the rise and fall of this royal lineage without exception,
that one of great majesty and immense splendor remained silent. When the sage had become silent, King Daśaratha then—
Having saluted the two high-souled ones, he returned once more to that best of cities.
These words were formerly spoken there by the sage; they have been heard by me and committed to my heart, and they shall not be otherwise.
"Since things have come to this pass, O Rāghava, you ought not to give way to grief.
Be firm for the sake of Sītā or for the sake of Rāghava, O best of men.
Having heard those most wonderful words spoken by the charioteer, [Rāma...]
He experienced incomparable joy and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
While Sūta and Lakṣmaṇa were thus conversing on the road, the sun set, and they spent the night there by the Gomatī river.
Having stayed there for that night by the Gomatī, the joy of the Raghus rose again at dawn and then set forth;
then, when midday had arrived, the great chariot-warrior entered [the city].

[He beheld] Ayodhyā, filled with jewels and crowded with happy and well-fed people. But the highly intelligent son of Sumitrā fell into a state of extreme dejection; having approached Rāma’s feet, he thought, "What shall I say now that I have come?"
While he was thus reflecting, the most magnificent palace of the king, resembling the moon, appeared before him. Then that best of men, having dismounted, stood at the gate of the king's palace.
With his face cast down and his mind dejected, he entered unopposed. Seeing Rāghava seated on the supreme throne,
he beheld his elder brother before him with eyes filled with tears.
Lakṣmaṇa, his heart distressed, grasped his feet;
with palms joined in reverence and deeply composed, he spoke in a piteous voice:
"Honoring the command of my noble brother, I have sent away the daughter of Janaka."

"O hero, I have returned once more to serve at your feet at the auspicious hermitage of Vālmīki on the banks of the Gaṅgā, just as it was pointed out. Do not grieve, O tiger among men; such is the course of time."
7.051.009c For those like you, who are courageous and wise, do not grieve.
7.051.010a All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall. 7.051.010c Unions end in separation, and life ends in death.
"O Kakutstha, you are indeed capable of conquering yourself by means of your own mind; how much more so all the worlds? What then of such suffering as this?
Bulls among men like you do not become bewildered in such circumstances."
"O King, for the sake of which Maithilī was abandoned out of fear of public censure—
you, O tiger among men, being well-composed through fortitude,
should cast off this weak-mindedness and do not give way to grief."
Thus addressed by the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa,
the descendant of Kakutstha spoke with supreme affection to the son of Sumitrā, who was so devoted to his friend:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, best among men, it is exactly as you say."

"O hero, I am thoroughly satisfied with your instruction regarding my duty; O gentle one, peace has been established and my distress dispelled. I have been consoled by your most sweet words, O Lakṣmaṇa."
Then Sumantra, having approached, spoke these words to Rāghava:
"O King, these ascetics stand at the gate, having been turned away;
they are great seers who have placed the descendant of Bhṛgu named Cyavana at their head."

"O Great King, the inhabitants of the banks of the Yamunā, those tigers among men, are eager and full of joy as they urge you to grant them an audience. Having heard those words of his, Rāma, the knower of dharma, spoke.
"Let the high-souled twice-born ones, headed by Bhārgava, be ushered in. Then, honoring the king's command, the gatekeeper, with palms joined above his head, ushered in many highly esteemed ascetics.
More than a hundred [ascetics], blazing with their own splendor,
entered the royal palace— those high-souled ascetics who were twice-born brahmins carrying full jars consecrated with water from all the sacred fords.
Having gathered many fruits and roots, they brought them to Rāma.
Accepting all of that with great affection, Rāma received all the waters from the sacred fords and the various kinds of fruits.
And the mighty-armed one said to all the great sages:
"Please sit upon these excellent seats as is appropriate.
Having heard Rāma's words, all the great seers [did so].
They sat down upon beautiful golden seats called *bṛsī*.
Seeing the sages seated there, Rāghava, the conqueror of enemy cities, became composed and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words.
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, what is the purpose of your arrival? What may I do for you?
I am at the command of the great seers, ready to fulfill every desire with ease.
This entire kingdom and even my very life reside within my heart."
7.052.012c "All this is for the sake of the twice-born; I tell you this as the truth.
7.052.013a Upon hearing those words of his, a great cry of "Well said!
arose 7.052.013c from the sages of fierce austerity who dwell upon the banks of the Yamunā.
And those high-souled ones, filled with great joy, said:
"O best of men, this is worthy of you alone on earth, and not of anyone else.
O King, many mighty monarchs have passed away."
7.052.015c Without hearing the gravity of the task, they did not approve of the promise.
7.052.016a But you, O Brahmin, out of respect for me, made this promise without considering the underlying reason.
"Perform it, for you are the doer; there is no doubt in this.
You ought to protect the sages from this great danger.
When the sages had spoken thus, the descendant of Kakutstha addressed these words to them.
"Tell me what must be done; I shall destroy your fear. When the descendant of Kakutstha spoke thus, Bhārgava addressed these words to him:
"O lord of men, hear from us the root cause of our fear regarding this land."
7.053.003a O Rāma, formerly in the Kṛta age, there was a Daitya of great strength;
7.053.003c the eldest son of Lola was a great Asura named Madhu.
7.053.004a He was devoted to Brahmanas, a protector of those seeking refuge, and firmly established in wisdom.

And by the most noble gods, he experienced incomparable joy. He was sweet-natured, endowed with heroism, and perfectly established in dharma; and out of great respect, Rudra granted him a wonderful boon.
Having extracted from the stake that spear of great power and great luster,
the high-souled one, being well-pleased, gave it [to him] and spoke these words:
"By you, through my grace, this incomparable and auspicious dharma has been performed."
Filled with supreme joy, I give you this most excellent weapon:
O great Asura, as long as you do not come into conflict with the gods or the Brahmins, so long shall this trident remain yours; otherwise, it shall meet its destruction.
"And whoever, free from anxiety, shall challenge you to battle,
that man you shall reduce to ashes with your trident and then return to your hand.
Having thus obtained this boon from Rudra, the great asura once again—
Having prostrated before Mahādeva, he spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, this is the supreme thorn in my lineage;
yet may it always be so, O God, for you are indeed the Lord of the gods."
To Madhu as he was speaking thus, the god Śiva, the lord of all beings, Mahādeva, replied: "This shall not come to pass;
let not your auspicious word, brought about by my grace, be rendered fruitless."
"However, this trident shall go to one son of yours. As long as this trident remains in the hand of your son,
he shall be invulnerable to all beings and shall carry the trident in his hand."

7.053.015 Having thus obtained from the god that most excellent and truly wonderful honey, the best of the Asuras caused a brilliantly shining palace to be built. 7.053.016 His wife was the highly fortunate and beloved Kumbhīnasī.
She was the offspring of Viśvāsā and Anālā, and she possessed great splendor. Her son was the fierce Lavaṇa, who was endowed with great heroism;
from his very childhood, he was evil-minded and practiced only sinful deeds.
Seeing his son so ill-behaved, Madhu was overcome with grief;
he fell into sorrow but said nothing to him. Having abandoned this world, he entered the abode of Varuṇa.
Having fixed his spear in the salt ocean, he offered it as a boon to him.
By the power of that spear and by his own wickedness,
he torments the three worlds, especially the ascetics.
"Lavaṇa possesses such power, and his trident is likewise formidable. Having heard this, O descendant of Kakutstha, you are indeed our supreme refuge.
In former times, O Rāma, many kings were [slain] by sages who were afflicted by fear."
"O hero, though we have sought safety from fear, we found no protector. Having heard that Rāvaṇa has been slain along with his army and vehicles,
O Rāma, we know no other lord of men on earth who can be our protector."
"Afflicted by fear of Lavana, we wish to protect it.
When they had spoken thus, Rāma replied to those sages with palms joined in reverence:
"What is Lavaṇa’s food, what is his conduct, and where does he dwell?"
Having heard the words of Rāghava, all those sages then reported how Lavaṇa had grown:
"His food consists of all living beings, and especially ascetics."
His conduct was always fierce, and he constantly dwelt in Madhuvana;
having slain ten thousand lions, tigers, deer, and elephants,
as well as human beings, he made them his daily meal.
Then that one of great strength devoured other beings as well,
like the Destroyer with his mouth wide open when the time of dissolution had arrived.
Having heard those words, Rāghava spoke to the great sages.
"I shall slay that Rākṣasa; let your fear depart. Having thus given his promise to those sages of fierce splendor, the joy of the Raghus spoke to all his brothers who were gathered together.
"O heroes, who shall be the slayer of Lavaṇa? To whom should his share be assigned—to the mighty-armed Bharata, or rather to Śatrughna?
When Rāghava had spoken thus, Bharata addressed these words:
"I shall slay him; let him be assigned as my share. Having heard these words of Bharata, which were endowed with heroism and valor, Lakṣmaṇa’s younger brother rose up, leaving his golden seat.
Then Śatrughna, the mighty-armed middle son of the Raghus who had accomplished his task, bowed down to the lord of men and spoke these words:
"Indeed, in former times, the noble one protected the city of Ayodhyā when it was empty."
"O King, maintaining a fever of anxiety in his heart regarding the arrival of the noble one, that high-souled man experienced many sufferings here while lying upon beds of misery in Nandigrāma."
"O King, having subsisted on fruits and roots and wearing matted hair and bark garments,
this delight of the Raghus has experienced such suffering;
now that I am present as his servant, he shall not undergo further distress."
When Śatrughna had spoken thus, Rāghava replied once more:
"O descendant of Kakutstha, let it be so; carry out my command.
I shall consecrate you in the auspicious city of Magadha as its king."
"O mighty-armed one, settle Bharata here if you have regard for him;
for you are a hero, learned, and capable of establishing [him in] the city inhabited by Madhu, as well as the auspicious provinces."
"For he who, having uprooted the lineage of a king at its very destruction,
does not appoint a ruler there, goes to hell. Therefore, you, having slain Lavaṇa, the son of Madhu, who is evil in his resolve— "

"Rule the kingdom with righteousness if you have regard for my words. O hero, you must not speak further in response to my speech; a younger brother must carry out the command of his elder—of this there is no doubt."
"O descendant of Kakutstha, accept from me this consecration,
prepared by the Brahmins headed by Vasiṣṭha and preceded by the prescribed rites and mantras.
Having been addressed thus by Rāma, he was overcome with great shame.

7.055.001c Śatrughna, endowed with heroism, spoke very softly: 7.055.002a "O bull among men, this command must certainly be carried out; 7.055.002c and your command, O highly fortunate one, is likewise impossible to transgress."
"O King, O bull among men, I am here at your service; I am yours to command.
When the great-souled and heroic Śatrughna had spoken thus, Rāma, filled with joy, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata as well.
"Bring the materials for the consecration with focused minds;
this very day I shall consecrate the invincible tiger among men.
[Bring] the two descendants of Kakutstha’s line, the family priest, the merchants, and likewise the officiating priests."
"By my command, bring all my ministers here.
Having received the king's decree, that great chariot-warrior acted accordingly,
placing the family priest at the head of the preparations for the consecration.

7.055.006e Having entered the royal palace, which resembled the abode of Purandara, 7.055.007a the consecration of the high-souled Śatrughna then proceeded; it was glorious, bringing great joy to Rāghava and to the city.
Then, having placed the consecrated Śatrughna upon his lap, Rāghava spoke these sweet words, filling him with splendor:
"This divine arrow of yours, O conqueror of enemy cities, is unfailing."
"By this, O gentle one, descendant of Raghu, you shall slay Lavana.
This arrow was fashioned, O Kākutstha, when the unconquered self-born god lay within the great ocean— a deity whom neither gods nor asuras had ever beheld."
"O hero, because it was invisible to all beings, this supreme arrow was indeed discharged by me,
overcome with wrath, for the destruction of those two wicked-souled ones,
Madhu and Kaiṭabha, as they were intent on their slaughter."

Desiring to create the three worlds, those two were slain by him in battle with this preeminent arrow; it was with this very arrow that he then fashioned the worlds. This arrow had not been used by me previously when I was seeking the death of Rāvaṇa.
"Let there be great terror for all beings, with Śatrughna as their leader.
And that great spear, the supreme weapon of Madhu, which had been given by the high-souled Tryambaka for the destruction of his enemies—
Having deposited it in his abode, where it is worshipped again and again,
and having gazed upon all the directions, he obtains food for himself. But when someone, desiring battle, should challenge him, he emerges from that place.

Then, having seized that trident, the Rākṣasa will turn that ash against him. Therefore, O tiger among men, you must stand at the gate with your weapon ready, before he has entered the city while being deprived of his weapon.

"O bull among men, O mighty-armed one, you should challenge him to battle while he has not yet entered his palace; then you shall slay the Rākṣasa. But if it is done otherwise, he will become invincible."
"O hero, if [the sacrifice] is performed in this manner, he will meet his destruction.
All this has been told to you regarding the trident and its reversal;
for the action of the illustrious Śitikaṇṭha is indeed difficult to overcome."
Having spoken thus to the descendant of Kakutstha and having praised him again and again,
the delighter of the Raghus spoke yet another speech:
"O bull among men, here are these four thousand horses."
Two thousand chariots and one hundred elephants,
as well as market streets adorned with various wares,
and likewise actors and dancers, should follow, O Śatrughna.
"O bull among men, O Śatrughna, take ten thousand pieces of gold and refined gold and go, provided with sufficient wealth and transport. And,
O hero, take an excellent army, well-maintained, cheerful, and robust."
"O best of men, delight them by means of conversation and gifts;
for neither wealth, nor wives, nor kinsmen remain there,
O Raghava, but where the circle of servants stands well-pleased."
Therefore, having dispatched that great army crowded with joyful men,
go alone as a wielder of the bow to the forest of Madhu,
so that he does not perceive you as you approach, longing for battle.
"Lavaṇa, however, is the son of Madhu; you should go there without hesitation.
O bull among men, he has no other death whatsoever;
for whoever comes within his sight must indeed be slain by Lavaṇa."
When summer has passed and the rainy season has arrived, O gentle one, you should slay Lavaṇa; for that is the time for this evil-minded one.
Let your soldiers set forth, placing the great seers at their head.
Just as one might cross the waters of the Ganges when only a remnant of summer remains, so you,
O one of swift prowess, having stationed the entire army on the riverbank with focused mind, should go ahead together with your bow.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Śatrughna summoned those mighty army commanders and spoke these words:
"These dwellings have been assigned for you, wherever you shall reside."
"One must abide without opposition so that no one is harmed.
Having thus instructed them and dispatched that great army,
he paid his respects to Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and Kaikeyī.
Having circumambulated Rāma and bowed his head in salutation,
Śatrughna, the scorcher of enemies, being permitted by Rāma,
prostrated himself with joined palms before Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata as well.
Then the self-restrained and mighty Śatrughna, having circumambulated the family priest Vasiṣṭha, departed. Having sent forth that entire army, he remained on the road for about a month.
Then Śatrughna, the hero and delighter of the Raghavas, proceeded swiftly and alone; having stayed for two nights along the way,
he reached the holy hermitage of Vālmīki, an excellent place of residence.
Having saluted the high-souled Vālmīki, the best of sages,
he then stood with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, having come here on business for my preceptor, I wish to dwell here."
"Tomorrow at dawn, I shall depart for the western quarter, the direction of Varuṇa.
Hearing Śatrughna’s words, the bull among sages laughed and replied to the high-souled one: "Welcome to you, O highly illustrious one!"
"O gentle one, this is my own hermitage belonging to the lineage of the Raghavas. Accept from me, without hesitation, a seat, water for the feet, and the guest-offering (arghya).
Having accepted that honor, as well as the fruit and root for food—"

The descendant of Kakutstha ate it and attained supreme satisfaction. Having eaten, the mighty-armed one said to that great seer: "To whom did this sacrificial abundance formerly belong near this hermitage?"
Having heard those words spoken by him, Vālmīki spoke these words:
"O Śatrughna, listen to whose sanctuary this was in former times—
the king who was the ancestor of you all, [the son] of the high-souled Sudāsa."
7.057.010c His son, named Mitrasaha, was heroic and exceedingly righteous.
7.057.011a While still a boy, that son of Sudāsa went out on a hunt. 7.057.011c Wandering about, that hero beheld two rākṣasas.
7.057.012 Those two terrible beings, in the form of tigers, were devouring many thousands of deer; insatiable, they did not reach a point of satisfaction.
7.057.013 But he, seeing those two Rākṣasas and the forest rendered devoid of deer, [reflected].
Overcome by great wrath, he struck one with a mighty arrow. Having felled that one, Saudāsa, that bull among men,
freed from fever and rid of his resentment, gazed upon the slain Rākṣasa.
Seeing him looking on, the companion of that Rākṣasa felt a terrible anguish and spoke thus to the son of Sudāsa:
"Since you have slain my companion who had committed no offense against you..."
"Therefore, O most sinful one, I shall give you retribution.
Having spoken thus to him, the *rākṣasa* vanished right there.
By the turn of time, King Mitrasaha came into being.
The king also performed a sacrifice near his hermitage—
the great horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*)— which Vasiṣṭha supervised.
There, that great sacrifice lasted for many tens of thousands of years.
Abounding in supreme splendor, it became equal to a sacrifice to the gods.
Then, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, remembering his former enmity,
the Rākṣasa, assuming the form of Vasiṣṭha, spoke thus to the king:

"Today, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, let a meal with meat be given to me immediately; there should be no hesitation in this matter. Having heard those words spoken by the Rākṣasa, who could assume any form at will, [he replied].
The lord of the earth, skilled in the preparation of food, said: "Prepare quickly such a meal— consisting of sacrificial offerings and meat, and delicious—
that our preceptor may be thoroughly satisfied."
At the command of the lord of kings, that cook, his mind agitated,
once again assumed the guise of a cook there;
he then presented human flesh to the king.
"O tiger among men, this delicious sacrificial food, along with meat and other provisions, has been brought here;
together with his wife Madayantī, he offered this meal to Vasiṣṭha—
food that had been seized by a Rākṣasa."
Then, having realized that this human food had been brought for his meal, the brahmin was overcome by great anger and began to speak:
"O King, since you wish to give me this food..."
"Therefore, this shall be your food; of this there is no doubt.
Then that king, together with his wife, having prostrated himself again and again, spoke once more to Vasiṣṭha regarding what had been said by him in the form of a Brahmin.
Having heard those words of the lord of kings and that act of the Rākṣasa,
Vasiṣṭha spoke again to the king, that bull among men:
"These words which were uttered by me while overcome with anger— "
"This cannot be made void, yet I shall grant you a boon.
The duration of this curse shall be twelve years;
and by my grace, O Indra among kings, you shall not remember what has passed."
7.057.033 Thus, having experienced that curse, that king, the crusher of enemies,
regained his kingdom and protected his subjects once more.
7.057.034 For that Kalmāṣapāda, there was a beautiful sacrificial ground.
"O Raghava, in this vicinity of the hermitage about which you ask—
having heard that most dreadful account of that lord of kings and having paid homage to the great seer— he entered the leaf-hut."
On the very night that Śatrughna entered the leaf-hut,
on that same night Sītā also gave birth to two sons.
Then, at the time of midnight, the young boys— those sons of the sages— [gathered].
They announced the auspicious birth of Sītā to Vālmīki, saying,
"O one of great splendor, perform for her a protection that destroys malevolent spirits.
Having heard those words of theirs, the sage was filled with joy.

And he performed for them a protection that slays malevolent spirits and destroys demons. Taking a handful of *kuśa* grass and a piece of *lava* wood, the twice-born Vālmīki bestowed upon them that protection which annihilates all beings.
7.058.005a He who was born as the elder of the two should be purified with *kuśa* grass consecrated by mantras; he shall be known by the name Kuśa.
7.058.006a And he who is the other of the two should be carefully settled by Lava.
"Lava shall be known by name as Nirmārjanīya, and Śaṅkha as Lava. Thus,
both those twin-born sons shall become famous by these names given by me."
With concentrated minds, they received that protective rite from the hand of the sage;
then, freed from all taint, they performed the protection for the two of them.
As that protection was being performed, [he spoke] their lineage and their names.
At midnight, Śatrughna heard the very great and pleasant news: the proclamation of Rāma’s name and the auspicious birth of Sītā’s two sons;
having gone to the leaf-hut at night, he exclaimed, "By good fortune! By good fortune!"
Thus, as that high-souled Śatrughna rejoiced, the rainy night of the month of Śrāvaṇa passed away with its swift course. Then at dawn, the one of great heroism performed his morning rites.
Having addressed the sage with palms joined in reverence, he turned back and departed facing westward.
Having traveled to the bank of the Yamunā and stayed there for seven nights on the road,
he arrived at the hermitage of sages of holy fame to take up residence.
7.058.014a There, the highly illustrious king, together with the sages headed by Bhārgava, 7.058.014c dwelt amidst various kinds of discourses.
7.059.001a Then, when night had set in, Śatrughna [addressed] the descendant of Bhṛgu.
He questioned the brahmin Cyavana regarding the strength and weakness of Lavaṇa,
as well as the power of the trident, O Brahmin, and who had previously been struck down by this spear-point when they entered into a duel with him.
Having heard those words spoken by the high-souled Śatrughna,
the immensely radiant Cyavana replied to the descendant of Raghu:
"O bull among men, the deeds performed by him are innumerable."
7.059.004c Listen to me as I relate what occurred concerning one born of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
7.059.005a Formerly, in Ayodhyā, there was a powerful king, the son of Yuvanāśva, 7.059.005c known as Māndhātṛ, who was renowned throughout the three worlds for his heroism.
Having brought the entire earth under his command, that lord of the earth,
the king, then made preparations to conquer the world of the gods.
Indra, however, felt intense fear, as did the high-souled deities.
When Māndhātṛ had exerted himself with the desire to conquer the world of the gods, the king—
being honored by the hosts of deities— undertook a vow to share half of Śakra’s throne and half of his kingdom.
Having understood his evil intention, Indra, the subduer of Pāka,
spoke these words with conciliation to the son of Yuvanāśva:
"O bull among men, you are not yet a king in the world of mortals."
7.059.010c Without having brought the earth under your control, you desire the sovereignty of the gods here.
7.059.011a O hero, if the entire earth in its completeness is under your power, then exercise the sovereignty of the gods here, together with your servants, forces, and vehicles.
To Indra, who was speaking thus, Māndhātṛ addressed these words:
"Where on the surface of the earth has my command been thwarted, O Śakra?
To him, the thousand-eyed one replied: "There is a Rākṣasa named Lavaṇa."
"O sinless one, the son of Madhu does not obey your command in the Madhuvana.
Having heard those unpleasant and terrible words spoken by the thousand-eyed Indra, the king was ashamed;
with his face cast down, he was unable to speak.
Having addressed the Thousand-Eyed One with his face somewhat cast down in shame,
the illustrious lord of men returned once more to this world. Having harbored indignation in his heart, he set out together with his servants, forces, and mounts.
The blameless one arrived, desiring to bring the son of Madhu under his control.
That bull among men, longing for a battle with Lavaṇa,
dispatched a messenger into the presence of Lavaṇa.
Having gone there, he spoke many unpleasant words to the son of Madhu;
as the messenger was speaking thus, the Rākṣasa devoured him.
When the messenger delayed for a long time, the king was filled with wrath.

He afflicted that Rākṣasa on all sides with a rain of arrows. Then, laughing, Lavaṇa seized a trident in his hand and released that supreme weapon for the destruction of [Rāma] along with his followers.

That flaming spear, having reduced the king along with his servants, army, and mounts to ashes, returned once more to the hand of Lavaṇa. Thus was that great king slain, together with his forces and vehicles.
O hero, the strength of Śūla is immeasurable and unsurpassed.
Tomorrow at dawn, you will slay Lavaṇa without a doubt;
for victory is certain for you, provided he has not yet taken up his weapon.
While they were telling stories and longing for the auspicious victory of the high-souled Śatrughna, the night quickly passed away. Then,
at that time when the morning was bright and clear, that Rākṣasa appeared.
Having departed from the city, the hero, impelled by the desire for food and drink,
[proceeded]. In the meantime, the valiant Śatrughna, having crossed the river Yamunā, stood at the gate of Madhupura with bow in hand.
Then, when midday had arrived, that Rākṣasa of cruel deeds came, bearing the burden of many thousands of living beings. There he beheld Śatrughna standing at the gate, weapon in hand.

Then the Rakshasa said to him: "O lowest of men, what will you do with this? Thousands of such as these, equipped with weapons, have been devoured by me in my wrath; why indeed do you wait for the appointed time?"
"O lowest of men, this food of mine is still incomplete; how is it that you have entered my mouth of your own accord, O evil-minded one? As he was speaking thus, he laughed again and again.
7.060.008c Śatrughna, endowed with heroism, shed tears out of rage. 7.060.009a From all his limbs, rays of fiery energy burst forth from that high-souled Śatrughna, who was overcome by wrath.
And, highly incensed, Śatrughna said to that night-stalker:
"O evil-minded one, I desire to fight a duel with you.
I am the son of Daśaratha and the brother of the wise Rāma."
"He who is named Śatrughna, the slayer of enemies, has come here desiring your death. Grant a duel to me, who am eager for battle;
you are the enemy of all living beings, and you shall not escape from me alive."
While he was speaking thus, the Rākṣasa, as if laughing, replied to that best of men: "By good fortune have you been found, O evil-minded one!
There is a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, who is the brother of my mother’s sister."
"O evil-minded one, O lowest of men, you were slain by Rāma for the sake of a woman.
And all that destruction of Rāvaṇa’s lineage was endured by me;
yet, having placed contempt before me, you especially [deserved my wrath]."
For all those who have been slain by me, and those who have been humiliated like blades of grass—
those of the past, those of the future, and you yourselves, O lowest of men—
I shall grant battle to you, O evil-minded one, for you desire war.
"I shall prepare whatever weapons you desire.
Then Śatrughna said to him: "Where will you go alive from me?
Even a weak enemy who has come before one must not be released by a self-controlled man."
"For he who, with a cowardly intellect, gave way to his enemy,
was slain because of his dull-wittedness, just like a base man.
Having heard those words of the high-souled Śatrughna, [he spoke].
He summoned a fierce rage and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Squeezing his hand against his hand and grinding his teeth, Lavaṇa repeatedly challenged that tiger among the Raghus.
To Lavaṇa, who was speaking those words and possessed of terrible prowess,
Śatrughna— the slayer of enemies— spoke these words:
"Śatrughna was not yet born at the time when others were being conquered by you."
Therefore, struck by my arrow today, go you to the abode of Yama.
O evil-souled one, let the seers, the learned brahmins, and the gods behold you slain by me in battle today, just as they beheld Rāvaṇa.
"O night-stalker, when you have fallen today, consumed by my arrows,
this city and its countryside shall become secure. Today, an arrow released from my arm, with a point like a thunderbolt— "
"It shall enter your heart like a ray of light born of the sun.
Thus addressed, Lavana, overwhelmed with rage, hurled a great tree at Śatrughna’s chest; the hero shattered it into a hundred pieces.
Seeing that his effort was fruitless, the powerful Rākṣasa once again seized many trees and hurled them at Śatrughna;
and the radiant Śatrughna [faced] those many trees as they fell upon him.
With three and four arrows each, whose joints were bent, he cut [them] down one by one.
Then the Rākṣasa unleashed a rain of arrows;
yet Śatrughna, endowed with prowess, was not distressed, nor was the Rākṣasa.
Then, laughing, Lavaṇa effortlessly uprooted a tree and struck the hero on the head; with his limbs collapsing, he indeed fell unconscious.
When that hero had fallen, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.

Even though he had gained the opportunity, the rākṣasa did not enter his own abode, disregarding Śatrughna— who was slain and fallen upon the earth— despite the presence of the hosts of ṛṣis, gods, gandharvas, and apsarases.

Nor did he take up his trident upon seeing him fallen on the ground; then, thinking "he is slain," he brought forth those foods. But after a moment, having regained consciousness, he stood up again, grasping his weapon.
7.061.016c Śatrughna, honored by the sages at the gate of the Rākṣasa,
7.061.017a then seized that supreme, divine, and unerring arrow,
7.061.017c which was blazing with terrible splendor and filling the ten directions.
With a vajra-like face and the speed of a vajra, possessing the massiveness of Mount Meru and Mandara,
he bows at all the joints and remains unconquered in all battles;
his limbs are smeared with blood like sandalwood paste, and he is a winged bird of beautiful feathers.
Seeing that fierce [weapon] of the lords of the Dānavas, the lords of the mountains, and the Asuras—
blazing like the fire of time when the end of the age has arrived—
all living beings were seized with terror.
7.061.021a The entire world— including the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, along with the sages and hosts of apsarases— being distressed, approached the Grandfather.
7.061.022a And they spoke to the Lord of the Gods, the Great-Grandfather, the bestower of boons:
"O Lord, has the destruction of the world arrived, or the end of the age?
O Great-Grandfather, never before have such things been seen or heard of, O Master—
the terror and delusion of the gods and the dissolution of the worlds."
Having heard those words of theirs, Brahmā,
the mind of the world-fathers and the granter of fearlessness to the gods, explained the cause of their fear:
"An arrow held by Śatrughna has been aimed at Lavaṇa for his slaughter in battle."

"By whose splendor all the best of the gods were utterly bewildered; for this, O children, was formerly the eternal arrow of the Creator of the World, composed of fiery energy, by which fear indeed came upon you."
7.061.027a This great arrow was indeed created by that Great-Souled One for the sake of Kaiṭabha and Madhu, 7.061.027c for the purpose of slaying those two Daityas.
7.061.028a Thus, you should know this arrow of Viṣṇu to be composed of his own splendor.
"And this was indeed the former body of that high-souled Viṣṇu.
As you go from here, behold the foremost of Rākṣasas, Lavaṇa, being slain by the heroic younger brother of Rāma, that great-souled one."
Having heard those sweet words of that God of gods,
they went to where both Śatrughna and Lavaṇa were fighting. [They saw] that arrow, resembling a celestial weapon, held in the hand of Śatrughna.
All living beings beheld him like the fire risen at the end of a Yuga. Having seen the sky covered by the gods, O descendant of Raghu,
he let out a lion’s roar again and again and looked once more at Lavaṇa.
Then, summoned by that high-souled Śatrughna,
Lavaṇa, filled with rage, stood ready for battle. Then, drawing that bow back to his ear, that best of archers—
He released a great arrow at Lavaṇa’s broad chest;
having quickly pierced his chest, it entered the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Having gone to the divine rasātala, that arrow, worshipped by the gods, [remained there].
Then, pierced by Śatrughna’s arrow, that night-stalker Lavaṇa quickly returned once more to the delighter of the Ikṣvāku clan;
he suddenly fell to the ground like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
And that great divine trident, while all beings were looking on, returned to the power of Rudra once the Rākṣasa Lavaṇa had been slain;
having destroyed fear with the discharge of a single arrow.
The hero of the Raghus appeared over these three worlds with his bow raised and arrows ready,
like the thousand-rayed sun dispelling the darkness.
When Lavaṇa had been slain, the gods, led by Indra and preceded by Agni, spoke these very sweet words to the scorcher of enemies, Śatrughna:
"By good fortune you have achieved victory, O child; by good fortune the Rākṣasa Lavaṇa has been destroyed."
"O tiger among men, O best of the Raghavas, choose a boon, for you have slain [the enemy].
O mighty-armed one, we have all assembled here as givers of boons;
desiring victory for you, our sight is indeed never in vain."
Having heard the speech of the gods, the mighty-armed Śatrughna, the hero of self-restraint, with palms joined over his head, replied:
"O Lord, this delightful city of Madhupurī was built by Madhu."
"May I quickly attain a dwelling; this is the boon I desire.
To him, the gods, with pleased minds, replied to the descendant of Raghu, "So be it!
There shall be a beautiful city called Śūrasenā, without a doubt."
Having spoken thus, those great-souled ones then ascended to heaven; Śatrughna, too, possessed of great splendor, led that army forward. Hearing Śatrughna’s command, that army advanced swiftly.

And by command, Śatrughna began the construction of the settlement. In the twelfth year, that auspicious city, resembling a celestial realm, was established as the domain of the Śūrasenas, free from fear from any quarter.

When Vāsava pours rain in due season, the fields are filled with crops; the people are free from disease and full of heroes, protected by the arms of the slayer of enemies. Resembling the crescent moon, the land is beautified by the banks of the Yamunā.
Adorned with excellent houses and beautified by crossroads and marketplaces,
the hero embellished that great void which had previously been created by Lavaṇa with an abundance of various wares for sale.

7.062.013 Having beheld that city in its full prosperity, Śatrughna, the younger brother of Bharata, whose own purposes were accomplished, was supremely pleased and attained the highest joy. 7.062.014 Once he had settled the city of Madhurā, the thought arose in his mind:
"In the auspicious twelfth year, I shall behold the feet of Rāma.
Then, in that twelfth year, Śatrughna, accompanied by a small retinue of servants and troops, desired to go to Ayodhyā, which was protected by Rāma.
Having dismissed his ministers, the army commanders,
and the family priest, he departed in a magnificent chariot yoked with excellent horses. Having traveled for seven or eight measured stages, that joy of the Raghus arrived.
7.063.003c He went swiftly to Ayodhyā, eager for a sight of Rāghava.
7.063.004a Having entered that beautiful city, the illustrious joy of the Ikṣvākus,
the mighty-armed one, entered where Rāma of great splendor was.
Having saluted that high-souled one who was as if blazing with splendor,
he spoke with palms joined in reverence to Rāma, whose prowess is truth:
"O Great King, I have performed everything exactly as commanded."
That wicked Lavaṇa has been slain and that city has been resettled.
Twelve years have passed without you, O delight of the Raghus;
deprived of you, O King, I cannot bear to live.
"O Kākutstha of immeasurable prowess, show me your favor;
like a calf deprived of its mother, I shall travel abroad without you.
To Śatrughna, who was speaking thus, he replied after embracing him:
"Do not despair, O hero; this is not the conduct of a kṣatriya.
Kings do not sink into despondency when living in exile, O Rāghava, for subjects must indeed be protected according to the duty of a kṣatriya, O Rāghava."
"O hero, O best of men, come from time to time to visit me in Ayodhyā, and you shall return to your own city;
for you are dear to me even as my own life, of this there is no doubt."

"The protection of the kingdom must certainly be carried out. Therefore, O descendant of Kakutstha, dwell with me for five nights; thereafter you shall go to Madhurā along with your servants, army, and vehicles."
Having heard these words of Rāma, which were consistent with righteousness and pleasing to the mind, Śatrughna replied with a sorrowful voice, "So be it. Then,
by the command of the descendant of Raghu, that scion of Kakutstha remained for five nights.
Having stayed there, that great archer prepared to depart.
Having taken leave of the high-souled Rāma, whose prowess is truth,
he mounted his great chariot along with Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa.
Followed for a long distance by the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa and by Bharata, Śatrughna then departed quickly for the city.
Having sent Śatrughna away along with his two brothers, that descendant of Raghu [departed].
7.064.001 He rejoiced, happy while protecting his kingdom according to dharma.
7.064.002 Then, after some days had passed, an elderly brahmin from the countryside arrived at the king’s gate, carrying the corpse of a child.
Weeping with various words filled with expressions of affection, he repeatedly uttered these words: "O son! O son!
"What evil deed have I committed in a previous life, in another body?"

7.064.004c Since I behold you, my only son, having met your end— 7.064.005a A mere child who had not yet reached youth, only five years of age— 7.064.005c Having met death at an untimely hour, O dear son, for my sorrow.
"In a few days I shall meet my end, there is no doubt;
both I and your mother, O son, [shall perish] through grief for you. Indeed, I do not recall ever speaking a falsehood, nor do I recall having committed any act of violence."
"By what evil deed has my son been led today to the abode of Vaivasvata while still a child, before he had even performed his duties toward his ancestors?
Never before have I seen or heard of such a terrifying sight."
"Death has come upon those who have not reached their time, as it did in the realm of Rāma.
There is no doubt that some great evil deed was committed by Rāma;
O King, bring this child back to life, for he has fallen under the power of death."
"O King, together with your brothers, may you attain a long life.
O one of great strength, we have lived happily in this kingdom of yours. Now, however, the realm of the high-souled Ikṣvākus is without a protector."
Having obtained Rāma, the king who brings an end to the young, as their protector here,
the subjects— when governed contrary to the law— perish through the faults of the king; indeed,
when the monarch is of evil conduct, the people die prematurely.
When people in cities and in the countryside commit improper acts and there is no protection, then that fear is caused by untimely factors.
It is evident that this will be a fault of the king; of this there is no doubt.
"Whether in the city or even in the countryside, this is indeed the slaughter of a child.
Thus, reproaching the king repeatedly with many such words, he, tormented by grief, embraced his son.
Thus Rāghava heard all that piteous lamentation of the twice-born man, filled as it was with pain and grief. Greatly tormented by sorrow, he summoned his ministers.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and his brothers along with the members of the assembly—
then those eight twice-born men were ushered in by Vasiṣṭha;
they then addressed the king, who resembled a god, saying, "May you prosper!"
Then Mārkaṇḍeya, Maudgalya, Vāmadeva, Kāśyapa,
Kātyāyana, Jābāli, Gautama, and likewise Nārada—
all these bulls among the twice-born— were seated upon the arrival of the guests.
The ministers and the merchants likewise addressed him with appropriate courtesy.
When all of them, radiant with splendor, were seated together,
the descendant of Raghu related everything concerning the reason why the twice-born man was weeping.
Having heard those words of the dejected king, Nārada replied with auspicious speech to the monarch in the presence of the sages:
"Listen, O King, to how this destruction of children has arrived at the appointed time."
"O hero, O delight of the Raghus, having heard what must be done, perform it!
Long ago in the Kṛta Yuga, O Rāma, only Brāhmaṇas were ascetics;
at that time, O King, no one who was not a Brāhmaṇa was an ascetic in any way whatsoever."
In that age, blazing and unobscured, having become Brahman,
all were then immortal and possessed far-sighted vision. Then came the age known as Tretā for the embodied descendants of Manu.
7.065.011c Where Kṣatriyas are born, endowed with former ascetic merit (tapas), 7.065.012a they are superior in both heroism and ascetic merit due to their previous birth;
7.065.012c those high-souled men [flourish] in that Tretā Yuga.
All that which belonged to the Brahmanas and the Kshatriyas, both in the former and the latter age, was endowed with equal power during those two yugas;
yet they all failed to perceive any further distinction between them.
7.065.014c They established the system of the four castes there in every respect. 7.065.015a But Adharma caused one foot to fall upon the surface of the earth;
7.065.015c for, being joined with that Adharma, the twice-born became dull-witted.

Then, at the beginning of the lifespan, when it was fully established, people practiced only auspicious deeds, being devoted to truth and righteousness. But in the Tretā Yuga, those who were Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas began to act otherwise.
7.065.017c All of them practiced austerities, while other people performed service. 7.065.018a That supreme duty of theirs then extended to the Vaiśyas and Śūdras;
7.065.018c and the Śūdras especially performed acts of worship for all the social orders.
Then he brought down a second foot of Adharma;
from that, the age known as Dvāpara arose. While that age called Dvāpara was prevailing at the end of the Yuga—
O bull among men, unrighteousness and falsehood indeed increased. During that period known as Dvāpara, asceticism entered the Vaiśyas;
O bull among men, the Śūdra did not obtain the opportunity to perform fierce austerities.
"O best of men, one of low caste performs very great asceticism;
for in the Kali age, the practice of austerity will indeed belong to those born of the Śūdra womb. O Rāma, in the Dvāpara age, the highest unrighteousness was maintained by the Śūdra."

"O King, that evil-minded Śūdra of great asceticism is indeed performing penance at the border of your territory; for this reason, this child has been killed. For whoever commits unrighteousness or an improper act within the domain of a king [is punished]."

O tiger among kings, if a man of evil mind acts [thus] within the city, he and the king himself will surely go quickly to hell; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, O tiger among men, search your own realm.
"Wherever you perceive wrongdoing, there you must apply effort.
In this way, O best of men, there will be an increase in your merit, an extension of the lifespan of men,
and the life of this child shall be preserved."
Having heard those words of Nārada, which were like nectar,
he experienced incomparable joy and spoke thus to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Go, gentle Lakṣmaṇa, and comfort that best of the twice-born."
"And place that body of the child in a vat of oil, O gentle one;
ensure it is treated with most excellent perfumes and highly fragrant oils so that the child does not decay."

"Act in such a way that there may be no misfortune or injury to the body of this youth, who is protected and whose deeds are untainted. Having thus instructed Lakṣmaṇa, who is endowed with auspicious marks, the descendant of Kakutstha [departed].
The highly illustrious one thought of the Puṣpaka chariot with his mind, saying,
"Come here. Perceiving that intention, the gold-adorned Puṣpaka arrived in an instant right before Rāghava.
Bowing down, he said: "O lord of men, here I am; O mighty-armed one, I have arrived as your submissive servant.
Having heard the charming speech of the Puṣpaka, the lord of men—
Having paid homage to those great seers, he ascended his celestial chariot;
taking up his bow, his two quivers, and his sword of radiant luster,
he left behind both the heroic sons of Sumitrā and Bharata in the city.
He set out toward the west, searching for the Maruts on all sides;
then the illustrious one went to the northern direction, which is covered by the Himalayas.
Even there, he did not see even the slightest trace of any misdeed.
Then the lord of men beheld the entire eastern quarter;
thereafter, that descendant of royal seers advanced toward the southern direction and,
on the northern side of Śaivala, beheld a very great lake.
In that lake, the illustrious Rāghava beheld an ascetic performing very great penance, hanging with his face turned downwards. Then,
approaching him as he was performing that supreme austerity, [he spoke].
Rāghava spoke these words: "O you of firm vows, you are blessed!
O you of steadfast prowess, in what womb were you born, that you abide in such increase of asceticism?
Out of curiosity I ask you this, for I am Rāma, the son of Daśaratha."
"O ascetic, what is the desired object of your wish—is it the attainment of heaven or the seeking of a boon? Relying upon which you have performed these austerities; I wish to hear this, O ascetic.
Are you a Brahmin—may you be blessed—or are you an invincible Kshatriya?"
"Whether he be a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, tell me this truth. Having heard those words of Rāma, whose deeds are effortless, he,
with his head bowed down, spoke these words.
"O Rāma, I was born from a Śūdra womb, yet I have undertaken fierce asceticism. O highly illustrious one, I pray for divinity in this very body.
O King, I do not speak falsely out of a desire to conquer the world of the gods."
"O descendant of Kakutstha, know me to be a Śūdra named Śambūka by name. As that Śūdra was speaking, Rāghava drew from its scabbard a stainless sword of brilliant luster and severed his head.
At that very moment, the boy was joined with life.
Then the lotus-eyed Rāma went to the hermitage of Agastya;
having approached and bowed to him with humility, he rejoiced in happiness.
Having saluted that high-souled one who was as if blazing with splendor,
and having received the highest hospitality, the lord of men sat down.
Then the pot-born Agastya, possessed of great energy and great asceticism, spoke to him.
"Welcome to you, O best of men; by good fortune you have arrived, O Rāghava.
You are highly esteemed by me, Rāma, on account of your many supreme virtues. As a guest worthy of worship, you dwell within my heart, O King."
"For the gods indeed tell me that you have come as the slayer of a Śūdra;
yet, by means of your dharma, you have restored the son of a Brāhmaṇa to life.
O Rāghava, stay here this night in my presence."
At dawn, you shall indeed depart for your own city by means of the Puṣpaka chariot.
And this ornament, O gentle one, was fashioned by Viśvakarman;
it is divine, possessing a celestial form, and blazing with its own splendor.
"Accept it, O descendant of Kakutstha; do what is pleasing to me, O Raghava.
For it is said that the gift of what has already been given yields a very great fruit.
Therefore, I shall bestow it according to the prescribed rites; accept it, O bull among men."
Rāma accepted from that high-souled sage that wonderful,
divine ornament, which was as radiant as the sun.
Having then received that supreme ornament, Rāma—
He then began to inquire about the origin of that divine [object]:
"O Brahmin, this most wonderful and supreme form endowed with such beauty—
how was it obtained by your lordship, from where did it come, or by whom was it brought?"
"O Brahmin of great renown, I ask you out of curiosity;
for you are the supreme treasury of many wonders.
When the descendant of Kakutstha had spoken thus, the sage then addressed these words:
7.067.018c Listen, O Rāma, to what occurred in the past when the Tretā Yuga had passed.
7.068.001a Long ago, in the Tretā Yuga, there was indeed a vast forest, 7.068.001c extending for a hundred yojanas in every direction, devoid of wild animals and shorn of birds.
"In that desolate forest, while he was performing supreme austerities,
O gentle one, I approached that forest with the intent to attack him.
Yet, I was unable to describe the appearance of that forest."
With trees of many forms that bore fruits and roots of pleasant taste,
in the midst of that forest was a lake a yojana in length,
filled with lotuses and water-lilies, and free from moss.
7.068.005 That place was like a supreme wonder, possessing an unsurpassed and exquisite flavor of bliss; it was free from dust, unshakeable, and filled with flocks of majestic birds.
7.068.006 Near that lake, however, stood a great and marvelous hermitage.
7.068.006c That ancient and exceedingly meritorious place was devoid of ascetics.
7.068.007a There, O bull among men, I dwelt for a night during the summer season. 7.068.007c Rising at dawn in the morning, I approached that lake.
Then, O King, I saw a corpse there— well-nourished and undecaying—
standing with supreme splendor in that body of water.
Reflecting upon the meaning of this for a moment, O Rāghava, I remained there.
"O Lord, standing on the bank of the lake, I wondered, 'What indeed could this be?
Then, in a mere moment, I beheld a divine and wonderful sight:
a most magnificent celestial chariot, yoked with swans and swift as thought."
O hero, descendant of Raghu, there in that celestial chariot, a thousand apsarases adorned with divine ornaments attend upon that exceedingly exalted inhabitant of heaven;
some sing beautiful songs while others play musical instruments.
"O Rāma, descendant of Raghu, while I was looking on, that celestial being descended from his celestial chariot and devoured that corpse. Then,
having eaten as much meat as he desired, both copiously and well— "
Having descended into the lake, that celestial being proceeded to touch its waters;
O bull among men, having performed the ritual ablution according to the rules, that celestial being prepared to ascend his most excellent and supreme celestial chariot.
7.068.015a Beholding him, who resembled a god, as he was ascending, O bull among men, I then spoke these words to that very person:
7.068.016a "Who are you, appearing like a god, and why this loathsome diet?"
"O gentle one, this [body] is being enjoyed by you; what is it that you ought to say?
Such a radiant state, esteemed by the gods, is truly marvelous.
O gentle one, your food is censurable; I wish to hear the truth of the matter."
"O Rāma, having heard my words spoken in auspicious syllables,
that celestial being, O descendant of Raghu, replied with palms joined in reverence:
'Listen, O Brahmin, to this account of my experiences as they truly occurred, both in happiness and in sorrow.'"
"O twice-born one, it is indeed difficult to overcome, just as you ask me.
Formerly, there was a king of Vidarbha, my father of great fame,
known as Sudeva, who was renowned throughout the three worlds for his prowess."
7.069.004a O Brahmin, he had two sons born of two wives.
7.069.004c I am known as Śveta, while the younger was Suratha. 7.069.005a Then, when my father had ascended to heaven, the citizens consecrated me.

7.069.005c There, I ruled the kingdom with righteousness, being well-composed. 7.069.006a Thus, O observer of noble vows, thousands of years passed by for me, O Brahmin, as I exercised sovereignty and protected my subjects according to dharma.
"O best of the twice-born, having discerned my lifespan through certain omens, I placed the law of time (death) in my heart and then departed for the forest. Thus,
I have come to this difficult forest, devoid of beasts and birds."
"O auspicious lady, having consecrated my brother Suratha as the lord of men upon the throne, I entered the vicinity of this lake to practice austerities;
having reached this lake, I have performed penance for a long time."
"O great sage, having performed extremely difficult austerities for three thousand years, I attained the unsurpassed world of Brahmā. Then,
O best of the twice-born, while I was established in heaven, hunger and thirst [assailed me]."
"O most noble one, they afflict me; therefore, with my senses distressed, I went to the Grandfather, the best in the three worlds, and said:
'O Blessed One, this world of Brahmā is free from hunger and thirst.'"
"By what karma have I come to this state, that I am now subject to hunger and thirst? O God, O Grandfather, tell me what my food shall be.
The Grandfather then said to me, "O son of Sudeva, your food shall be as follows:"

"O Śveta, eat those sweet pieces of your own flesh constantly; for while you were performing supreme austerity, you nourished your own body with them. O high-minded one, that which was never sown can never grow."
"7.069.016a Not even the slightest gift was given by you in the forest frequented by living beings;
7.069.016c therefore, my child, having gone to heaven, you are tormented by hunger and thirst.
7.069.017a You, whose own body was most excellent and well-nourished with food—"
"Consume the nectar of immortality; that shall be your satisfaction.
But when the great seer Agastya, who is invincible, enters that forest, O Śveta, then you shall be released from this distress."
"O gentle one, he is indeed capable of delivering even the hosts of gods;
how much more so you, O mighty-armed one, who have fallen under the power of hunger and thirst?
Having heard this resolve of the Blessed One, the God of gods, I—"
"O best of the twice-born, I consume this censurable food— my own body—
for many groups of years, O Brahmin;
yet it does not diminish, O Brahmarṣi, and my satisfaction remains supreme."
"Deliver me, who am in this state of distress, from this hardship.
For there is no other refuge here for others except for you, O twice-born one born from a jar.
O gentle one, O best of the twice-born, take these ornaments for the sake of my deliverance."
"Accept it, O Brahman-sage; you ought to show me favor.
Having heard those words of that deceased man, filled as they were with sorrow, I accepted that supreme ornament in order to deliver him.
When that auspicious ornament had been accepted by me,
the former human body of that royal sage indeed perished. When his body had vanished, that royal sage, with supreme joy, [attained his true state].

Satisfied and delighted, the king returned once more to the third heaven. O descendant of Kakutstha, it was for that reason that this divine ornament of wondrous appearance was given to me by him, who is equal to Śakra.
Having heard those most wonderful words of Agastya, Rāghava,
out of both reverence and amazement, proceeded to ask further:
"O Blessed One, that forest where he performs his austerities is formidable."
"How did King Śveta Vaidarbha enter that forest which was devoid of beasts and birds,
lacking in living beings, and empty, being abandoned by men? I wish to hear this in accordance with the truth as he entered there to practice asceticism."
Having heard Rāma’s speech, which was filled with curiosity,
the one of supreme splendor began to speak these words:
"In former times, O Rāma, during the Kṛta Yuga, Manu was the lord who wielded the rod of punishment."

He had a great son named Ikṣvāku, who increased his lineage. Having installed that son, who was invincible on earth, in the ancestral kingdom, he said to him: "Become the founder of royal dynasties upon the earth."
"‘So be it,’ O Rāghava, was the promise made by the son to his father.
Then Manu, exceedingly delighted, spoke once more:
‘I am pleased; you have performed a most noble deed, of this there is no doubt.’"
Protect your subjects with the rod of punishment, but do not inflict punishment without cause. Indeed, that punishment which is duly meted out against offenders among men leads the king to heaven.
"Therefore, O mighty-armed son, be diligent in the administration of punishment;
for as you perform it, dharma will become supreme for you in this world.
Having thus instructed his son extensively with focused concentration, Manu—

He went joyfully to the third heaven, to the unsurpassed world of Brahmā. When he had departed for the celestial realm, Ikṣvāku, of immeasurable splendor, became absorbed in thought: "How shall I procreate sons?"
Through various deeds of many kinds, that righteous son of Manu begot one hundred sons who resembled the sons of the gods.
O dear descendant of Raghu, he was the youngest of them all.
Foolish, lacking both proper form and learning, he did not wish to serve his elders;
therefore, his father gave that child of little luster the name Daṇḍa,
for punishment would inevitably fall upon his body.
Seeing that terrible fault of his son, O Rāghava,
that subduer of enemies bestowed the kingdom upon Vindhyaśaivala.
There, on the delightful mountain slope, Daṇḍa became king.
O Rāma, he established there an incomparable and unsurpassed city;
O Lord, he gave that city the name Madhumanta,
and he chose the highly virtuous Uśanas as its domestic priest.
Thus that king, together with his domestic priest, governed that kingdom,
which was crowded with joyful subjects, like the realm of the gods in heaven.
Having related this to Rāma, the great seer born from a jar—
In this very narrative, he further uttered these words:
"Then, O descendant of Kakutstha, that evil-minded Daṇḍa ruled there for many tens of thousands of years, his kingdom free from all thorns."
Then, at a certain time, during the delightful month of Caitra, the king went to the beautiful hermitage of Bhārgava. There he [beheld] the daughter of Bhārgava, whose beauty was peerless on earth.
While she was wandering in the forest region, Daṇḍa beheld that incomparable woman.
Seeing her, that evil-minded man, afflicted by the arrows of the bodiless god of love,
approached the maiden in great agitation and spoke these words.
"From where have you come, O fair-hipped one? Whose daughter are you, O auspicious lady? I am tormented by the god of love; therefore, O slender-waisted one, I ask you.
To him, as he spoke thus, deluded and maddened by lust—

7.071.007c The daughter of Bhṛgu replied with these conciliatory words to the king: 7.071.008a "Know me, O Indra among kings, to be the daughter of the god of effortless deeds, Bhārgava; 7.071.008c my name is Arajā, the eldest, living here in this hermitage."
"O Indra among kings, my father is my guru, and you are the disciple of that high-souled one.
If he were to become enraged, that man of great asceticism might inflict a very great calamity upon you.
Therefore, if there is anything to be done here by me according to the righteous path as seen through dharma,"
"O best of kings, choose my father of great splendor as your husband;
otherwise, a terrible consequence will befall you.
For in his wrath, this father of mine could consume even the three worlds."
To Arajā, who was speaking thus, Daṇḍa—afflicted by the arrows of desire and intoxicated with pride—replied, placing his joined palms to his head:
"Be gracious, O fair-hipped one; you ought not to waste time."
"O fair-faced one, it is because of you that my very life-breaths are being torn asunder.
For having obtained you, whether it be death or even a most terrible sin, I am yours; O timid one, accept me, your devotee who is utterly overwhelmed by love."
Having spoken thus to the maiden, the powerful one seized her by force with both arms; as she struggled against his will, he proceeded to violate her sexually.
Having committed that most terrible and dreadful crime, Daṇḍa—
She quickly proceeded toward the unsurpassed city of Madhumanta.
Even as she was weeping, Arajā waited not far from the hermitage, greatly terrified, for her father who resembled a god.
7.072.001a Having heard this after a moment, the celestial seer of immeasurable splendor,
surrounded by his disciples and afflicted by hunger, returned to his own hermitage. 7.072.002a There he saw Arajā, miserable and completely overwhelmed by dust.
Like the moonlight swallowed by Aruṇa at dawn, no longer shining,
his anger flared up— especially as he was afflicted by hunger—
as if burning the three worlds, and he spoke thus to his disciples:
Behold the terrible-looking calamity of this perverse man who does not know the Self,
like a blazing flame of fire; the destruction of this evil-minded and wicked-souled one, along with his followers, has arrived.
7.072.005c He who indeed desires to touch the blazing crest of a sacrificial fire—
7.072.006a because he has committed such an evil deed of terrible appearance, 7.072.006c therefore that dull-witted man shall reap the fruit of his sinful action.
Within seven nights, that evil-minded king, along with his servants, troops, and mounts, shall meet his death for his practice of sinful deeds;
and so too shall the territory of that wicked one, extending for a hundred yojanas in every direction.
Indra, the subduer of Pāka, will be scorched by a great rain of dust;
all beings here, whether stationary or moving,
will utterly perish through that great rain of dust.

"As far as the range of my staff extends, so far shall all this accumulation [of the world] become invisible, like dust, within seven nights. Having spoken thus, he who was consumed by anger addressed that resident of the hermitage.

"And he said, 'Let the people remain at the borders of the countryside. Having heard these words of the Silent One, that population residing in the hermitage departed from his domain and established their dwellings outside.
Having spoken thus to the sage, he said this to Arajā:
"O woman of dull intellect, dwell right here in this hermitage with a well-composed mind.
This lake, extending for a yojana, possesses a most beautiful radiance."

"O Arajā, free from fever, enjoy yourself; let the time for this be awaited. Furthermore, whatever beings shall dwell near you during that night, they will forever be incapable of being slain by a rain of dust."
Having spoken thus, the descendant of Bhṛgu departed to dwell elsewhere. After seven days, that territory of his was reduced to ashes, just as the knower of Brahman had declared,
upon the ridges of the Vindhya and Śaivala mountains.
7.072.017c Because he had previously committed an act contrary to dharma, he was cursed by that brahmin seer.
7.072.018a From that time forth, O descendant of Kakutstha, it has been called the Daṇḍaka forest. 7.072.018c Since ascetics dwell there, it has also become known as Janasthāna.
"O Rāghava, O hero, I have related all this to you that you asked me;
for the time to perform the twilight devotions has indeed passed. Here are all these great seers with full water-pots on every side."
7.072.020c Having performed the water-libations, O tiger among men, he sat in worship of the sun.
7.072.021a Urged by those sages, the best of Brahmins, who were gathered together, 7.072.021c the sun set, O Rāma; go and perform the ritual ablution with water.
Having understood the words of the seer, Rāma proceeded toward a sacred lake frequented by Apsarases in order to perform the evening twilight devotions (saṃdhyā). There,
having touched the water and performed the western twilight rites, he sat down.
Rāma entered the hermitage of the high-souled Agastya, the pot-born sage. For his meal, Agastya prepared for him fruits and roots of manifold virtues, as well as medicinal herbs and pure vegetables.
Having eaten that food, which was like nectar, that best of men,
pleased and fully satisfied, spent the night there. Rising at dawn in the morning, the subduer of enemies performed his daily rites.
The best of the Raghus approached the seer to depart.
Having offered his salutations, Rāma spoke to the great seer born from a jar:
"I take my leave of you; I shall go. You should grant me permission."
"I am blessed; I am graced by the sight of the Great-Souled One.
I shall come here again to see you for the sake of purifying my own self.
While the descendant of Kakutstha was speaking these words of wondrous appearance, [the sage remained silent].
7.073.008c Uttering these words, the one whose eyes are dharma, whose wealth is asceticism, spoke with supreme joy:
7.073.009a "O Rāma, this speech of yours is most wonderful and composed of auspicious syllables.
7.073.009c You alone, O delight of the Raghus, are the purifier of all the worlds."
"O Rāma, those who behold you for even a moment— whatever beings they may be—
are purified, become as if they have attained heaven, and are honored in the celestial realm by the gods.
And those living beings on earth who gaze upon you with eyes of awe,"
They have been struck down by the rod of Yama and shall immediately go to hell.
Go now upon a safe path, unperturbed and free from fear on all sides;
rule the kingdom with righteousness, for you are the refuge of the world.
Thus addressed by the sage, the wise king, with palms joined in reverence and body bowed low,
paid homage to that seer of virtuous conduct. Having saluted the best of sages and all those ascetics rich in penance, he stood before them.
He ascended that gold-adorned Puṣpaka chariot with a steady mind.
As he departed, throngs of sages from all sides honored him— who shone like the great Indra— with blessings, just as the immortals honor the thousand-eyed god.
7.073.016a Rāma appeared healthy and composed in the gold-adorned Puṣpaka chariot,
7.073.016c like the moon situated near the clouds at the onset of the rainy season. 7.073.017a Then, when midday had arrived, he was being honored from here and there.
Having reached Ayodhyā, the descendant of Kakutstha descended from the celestial chariot. Then, having dismissed the beautiful Puṣpaka, which travels at will,
Rāma spoke these words to the gatekeeper stationed at the entrance of the inner courtyard:
"Go quickly to Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata; having informed them of my arrival, summon me without delay. Having heard those words of Rāma, whose actions are effortless, [they departed].
The doorkeeper, having summoned the two princes, announced them to Rāghava.
Upon seeing that his beloved Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa had arrived,
Rāghava embraced them and then spoke these words.

"O Raghavas, I have performed this unsurpassed service for the twice-born exactly as it should be done. Now, with you two acting as my very own selves, I desire to further establish the bridge of dharma by performing the unsurpassed Rājasūya sacrifice."
7.074.004c "I wish to sacrifice together with him, for therein lies eternal dharma.
7.074.005a Having sacrificed with the Rājasūya, Mitra, the destroyer of enemies, attained the status of Varuṇa through well-offered oblations and a well-performed sacrifice."
7.074.006 Having performed the Rājasūya sacrifice according to dharma, Soma, the knower of dharma,
attained fame and an eternal station among all the worlds. 7.074.007 On this day, let that which is beneficial be considered by you together with me.
"You ought to speak that which is beneficial, appropriate for the future, and consistent with your disciplined efforts.
Having heard these words of Rāghava,
Bharata, who was himself skilled in speech, joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words.
"O virtuous one, in you resides the highest dharma; in you, O mighty-armed one of immeasurable prowess, the entire earth is established, as is your fame.
And all the protectors of the earth look to you, just as the immortals look to Prajāpati."

The high-souled ones gaze upon the Lord of the World just as we do; O King of great strength, the subjects look upon you like a father. O Raghava, you have become the refuge for all living beings upon this earth.
"O King, how will you perform such a sacrifice,
in which the destruction of royal lineages on earth is foreseen?
And as for those men on earth, O King, who have attained manliness— "
7.074.013c Therein shall come the destruction of all, like that of the universal end.
7.074.014a Therefore, O tiger among men, you whose prowess is incomparable in its virtues,
7.074.014c you ought not to destroy the earth, for it remains under your control.
Having heard those words of Bharata, which were like nectar, Rāma, whose prowess is truth, experienced incomparable joy. And he spoke auspicious words to the one who increased Kaikeyī’s delight.
"I am pleased, I am thoroughly satisfied by your words today.
O tiger among men, these words you have uttered— unyielding and centered on dharma— are for the protection of the earth."

"Therefore, O knower of dharma, because of your well-spoken words, I turn you away from that intention— the Rājasūya, the highest of sacrifices. For kings, the protection of subjects is a duty equal to sacrifice."
"Therefore, I listen to your words, which are well-spoken and perfectly composed. When Rāma and the high-souled Bharata had spoken thus,
Lakṣmaṇa also addressed these auspicious words to the joy of the Raghus.
The horse sacrifice is a great rite that purifies all sins; may this invincible preeminent sacrifice, which is your purifier, be pleasing to you.
For it is heard that in ancient times, when the high-souled Vāsava [performed it], a great event occurred.

O mighty-armed one, it is said that in former times, during the conflict between the gods and the asuras, there was a great son of Diti named Vṛtra, who was honored by the world. Śakra, though enveloped by the sin of killing a Brahmin, was purified by the horse sacrifice.

It is broad for a hundred yojanas and three times as high; through its passion, it gazes upon the three worlds with affection from every side. It is a knower of dharma, grateful, and perfectly established in wisdom.
7.075.006c He ruled the entire earth with righteousness, being perfectly composed.
7.075.007a While he was governing, the earth yielded all desires; 7.075.007c it produced juices, roots, and fruits that were full of flavor.
For that great-souled one, the earth yielded crops without being ploughed and was perfectly abundant;
he enjoyed such a kingdom, prosperous and wonderful to behold. Then, a thought arose in him: "I shall perform unsurpassed austerity."

"Austerity is indeed the highest good; austerity is indeed the highest happiness. Having entrusted his eldest son, the supreme lord, to the citizens, he devoted himself to fierce austerity, scorching all the gods.
While Vṛtra was performing austerities, Vāsava, as if deeply distressed,
approached Viṣṇu and spoke these words:
"O mighty-armed one, the worlds have been conquered by Vṛtra through his ascetic penance."
"For he is powerful and righteous in soul; I shall not be able to obstruct him.
O Lord of the Gods, if he were to practice even more intense austerity, then for as long as the worlds endure, they would remain subject to his will."
"And yet you, O mighty one, look on with indifference toward this most noble being;
for in an instant, O Lord of the Gods, Vṛtra would cease to exist were you to be enraged. Indeed, O Viṣṇu, when he has entered into a bond of affection with you,"
From that time forward, you have attained the lordship over the worlds. O you of great renown, show favor toward the worlds;
for by your action, the entire world shall become peaceful and free from decay.
"O Viṣṇu, all these dwellers of heaven are indeed looking toward you;
grant them assistance through this great slaying of Vṛtra.
For you have always provided assistance to these high-souled ones."
"You are the refuge for those who have no other resort, and this task is unbearable for others.
Having heard those words of Lakṣmaṇa,
the slayer of enemies said to Lakṣmaṇa, "Relate the slaying of Vṛtra in its entirety."
Thus addressed by Rāghava, Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of Sumitrā’s joy, related once more that divine narrative,
having heard the words of the thousand-eyed Indra and of all the celestial dwellers.
7.076.003 Viṣṇu said this to all the gods, with Indra at their head:
7.076.004 "In former times, I was bound by friendship to the high-souled Vṛtra;
therefore, for the sake of your pleasure, I do not slay that great Asura."
