"Your supreme happiness must certainly be achieved;
therefore, I shall declare the means by which you will slay Vṛtra.
O best of gods, I shall divide myself into three forms."
By that [power], the thousand-eyed one will slay Vṛtra; of this there is no doubt.
One part shall go to Vāsava, the second to the thunderbolt itself, and the third to the surface of the earth; then Śakra will slay Vṛtra.
When the Lord of the Gods had spoken thus, the gods then addressed these words:
"It is even so, there is no doubt, just as you say, O slayer of Daityas!
May prosperity be yours; we shall go, desiring the slaughter of the Asura Vṛtra."
"By your own splendor, honor the most noble Vāsava.
Then all those high-souled ones, led by the thousand-eyed Indra,
proceeded to that forest where the great asura Vṛtra was located.
7.076.011 With their own splendor, they beheld that supreme asura blazing with heat,
as if drinking up the three worlds and as if consuming the very sky.
7.076.012 Upon merely seeing that best of asuras, the gods were struck with terror.
"How shall we slay him? How may there be no defeat?"—
as they were thus reflecting there, the thousand-eyed Purandara,
grasping his thunderbolt with both arms, hurled it at the head of Vṛtra.
As if scorched by the terrible fire of time, blazing with great flames,
the world fell into terror at the head of Vṛtra.
Then the lord of the gods [considered] the slaying of that Vṛtra to be impossible.
Reflecting thus, the highly illustrious one quickly went to the end of the world.
As Indra was departing, the sin of Brahman-slaughter swiftly followed him;
it fell upon his limbs, and grief entered into that Indra.
7.076.017 With their enemies slain and Indra lost, the gods, led by Agni, repeatedly worshipped Viṣṇu, the foremost in the three worlds.
7.076.018 "O God, you are our supreme refuge; you are the first-born, the Lord of the universe."
Assuming the nature of Viṣṇu for the sake of all beings,
you have slain this Vṛtra; yet now, O tiger among gods, the sin of killing a Brahmin afflicts Vāsava— declare the means of his liberation.
Having heard those words of the gods, Viṣṇu said:
"Let Śakra sacrifice to me alone; I shall purify the wielder of the thunderbolt. Having worshipped me with the meritorious horse-sacrifice, the subduer of Pāka [Indra] shall be cleansed."
"Free from fear from any quarter, he shall once again attain the sovereignty of the gods.
Having thus delivered this nectar-like message to the gods,
Viṣṇu, the lord of the deities, being praised, returned to the celestial realm of Triviṣṭapa.

Having thus related the entire slaughter of Vṛtra in its full detail, that Lakṣmaṇa, the best among men, proceeded with the remainder of the narrative. Then, when the immensely powerful Vṛtra, the terror of the gods, had been slain—

Enveloped by the sin of Brahman-slaughter, Śakra, the slayer of Vṛtra, lost his senses. Taking refuge at the edge of the worlds, deprived of consciousness and bewildered, he remained there for some time, writhing like a serpent.
Then, when the thousand-eyed one had vanished, the world became distressed;
the earth appeared devastated, devoid of moisture, and its forests were parched. The clouds ceased to flow with rain, as did the lakes and the rivers.
And there arose a great agitation among living beings caused by drought.
As this world was thus wasting away, the gods, their minds filled with anxiety,
brought forth that sacrifice which had been previously described by Viṣṇu.
Then all the hosts of gods, together with their preceptors and the sages,
went collectively to that place where Indra was bewildered by fear.
Having seen the thousand-eyed one stupefied by the slaughter of a Brahmin, they [approached].
Placing that Lord of the Gods at their head, they performed the horse sacrifice.
Then, O lord of men, the great horse sacrifice of the high-souled Mahendra increased in scale for the sake of purifying him from the sin of Brahman-slaughter.
Then, upon the completion of the sacrifice, the personified sin of Brahman-slaughter approached the Great-Souled One and spoke these words: "Where will you provide a place for me?
Thereupon, the gods, gratified and filled with joy, said to her:
"Divide yourself into four parts by yourself, O you who are difficult to approach!
Having heard the speech of the high-souled gods, the Brahman-slaughter,
finding no other place to stay, chose a difficult dwelling.
"With one portion I shall dwell indeed among rivers full of water;
with the second, among trees—this I tell you truly. As for this third portion of mine, it shall be among women in the bloom of youth."

"O bulls among the gods, I shall dwell for three nights among the Darpa-parṇās as the destroyer of pride; and those who intentionally kill Brahmins who have done them no wrong, I shall take refuge with them for a fourth part [of my life]."
Then the gods replied to her: "O Durvāsas, as you have spoken, so shall it all be;
accomplish whatever you desire.
Thereupon, filled with joy, the gods paid homage to the thousand-eyed Indra.
Vāsava became free from fever and cleansed of all sin;
and when the thousand-eyed one was established, the entire world became tranquil. Then Śakra paid homage to that sacrifice of wondrous appearance.
"Such indeed, O descendant of Raghu, is the power of the horse sacrifice.
Perform the great horse sacrifice, O highly fortunate king!
Having heard those words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, he who was skilled in speech [replied].
The highly effulgent Rāghava, smiling, replied with these words:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, best of men, it is exactly as you say;
[I know] the slaying of Vṛtra in its entirety, as well as the fruit of the horse-sacrifice."
7.078.003 O gentle one, it is heard that in ancient times there was a son of the patriarch Kardama, a glorious and highly virtuous lord of the Bāhlīkas named Ila.
7.078.004 That king of great fame, having brought the entire earth under his control, [ruled over it].
O tiger among men, he protected the kingdom like his own son,
along with the most noble gods, the Daityas, the great Asuras,
the Nāgas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, and the high-souled Yakṣas.
O gentle descendant of Raghu, he was constantly worshipped by those afflicted by fear;
indeed, the three worlds were terrified of that great-souled one when he was enraged.
For such was that king, firmly established in both righteousness and valor.
Most noble in intellect and highly renowned among the Bāhlīkas,
that mighty-armed one set out on a hunt in the delightful Caitra month, accompanied by his servants, troops, and vehicles, in a beautiful forest.

In the forest, that king slaughtered deer by the hundreds of thousands; yet, even after killing them, no satisfaction came to that high-souled monarch. Ten thousand various kinds of wild animals were being slain by that great-souled one.
He approached that region where Mahāsena was born.
There, Hara, the lord of the gods, took pleasure with the daughter of the king of mountains, accompanied by all his invincible attendants.
Having transformed himself into a woman, Umeshas, whose banner bears the bull,
desiring to do what was pleasing to the Goddess, [remained] at that mountain waterfall.
And whatever beings there were in that forest region who spoke with human voices—
And whatever else existed there, all of it came to be designated as "woman.
In the meantime, King Ila, the son of Kardama,
arrived at that region while slaying thousands of deer.
7.078.015a Having seen everything turned into women, including the wild beasts and birds, 7.078.015c and himself along with his followers likewise transformed into women, O descendant of Raghu,
7.078.016a he was filled with great sorrow upon seeing himself in such a state.
Having learned of that deed of the Lord of Umā, he was seized with terror;
then the king, together with his servants, forces, and vehicles, went for refuge to the high-souled god, the blue-throated one with matted hair.
Then, laughing, the highly illustrious giver of boons, together with the Goddess,
himself addressed these words to the son of Prajāpati:
"Arise, arise, O royal sage, O mighty son of Kardama!"
"O gentle one of noble vows, choose another boon, with the exception of manhood.
Then that king, afflicted by grief at being refused by the Great-Souled One,
did not accept any other boon from the supreme god, having become a woman.
Then, O King, with great sorrow, the monarch prostrated himself before the daughter of the mountain king, the Great Queen, with his whole inner soul:
"O beautiful lady, you are the sovereign of boons and the bestower of boons upon the worlds."
"O Goddess of unfailing vision, O gentle one, I worship you; let there be salutation to you!
Having understood the heart's desire of that royal sage in the presence of Hara, the Goddess, who is highly esteemed by Rudra, replied with these auspicious words.

"The God is the giver of half, and likewise I am the giver of the other half; therefore, take as much of the male and female portions as you desire. Having heard that most wonderful and unsurpassed boon from the Goddess, [he was filled with joy].
With a heart full of joy, the king then spoke these words:
"O Queen, if you are pleased with me— you who are peerless in beauty upon this earth—
then after serving as a woman for one month, may I become a man again for another month."
Having understood his desire, the goddess with the beautiful face replied with these auspicious words: "O King, having become a man, you shall not remember your state as a woman."
"And for another month, having become a woman, you shall not remember your manhood.
Thus that king Puru, the son of Kārtavīrya, having been a man,
then became the woman Ilā, beautiful in the three worlds, for one month.
Having heard that story concerning Ila, which was related by Rāma, both Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata were greatly amazed. With palms joined in reverence, they addressed Rāma regarding that high-souled king.
Then they asked again for a detailed account of that state:
"How did that king conduct himself while in the miserable condition of a woman?
And when he had become a man, what kind of livelihood did he lead?"
Having heard that speech of theirs, which was full of curiosity,
the descendant of Kakutstha related to the king exactly how it had happened:
"In that very first month, having become a woman, she who is the most beautiful in the world— "
Surrounded by those women who had previously been her attendants,
she, whose eyes were like lotus petals, having quickly entered that forest thick with trees, shrubs, and creepers, sported there on foot.
Having abandoned all her vehicles on every side,
Ilā then took her delight in that mountain-like cavity.
Then, in that forest region not far from the mountain—
She beheld that lake, which was as radiant as the sun and filled with flocks of various birds;
and there, within it, she saw Budha, the son of Soma,
blazing with his own splendor like the risen full moon.

She, filled with wonder, agitated that entire reservoir of water where he was performing intense and difficult penance amidst the waters— he who was a lake of fame, moving at will, and established in the prime of youth.
O descendant of Raghu, along with those men who had become women,
Budha, upon merely beholding her, was tormented by the arrows of love;
he could no longer control himself and trembled within the water.
Beholding Ilā, who was more auspicious than anything in the three worlds, he fell into deep reflection: "Who could this be? She surpasses even the foremost goddesses.
She was not among the goddesses, nor the daughters of the nāgas, nor the asuras, nor the apsarases.
"I have previously seen someone adorned with such beauty;
she would be a match for me, were she not already taken by another. Having formed this thought, he emerged from the water onto dry land.
Having arrived at the hermitage, that righteous-souled one then summoned the four women; they bowed down to him, and he,
the virtuous one, asked them, "To whom does this woman belong, who is the most beautiful in the world?"
"For what purpose have you come here? Tell us the truth without delay.
Having heard those auspicious words of his, sweet and composed of melodious syllables, all those women replied with sweet voices.

"7.079.019a This woman of beautiful hips always exercises authority over us; 7.079.019c though she has no husband, she wanders with us through the edges of the forest. 7.079.020a But having heard those words of the women, whose syllables were indistinct—
That twice-born man recited the holy *Āvartanī* spell.
Having understood the king's entire situation exactly as it had occurred,
that bull among sages spoke to all those women.
"Are there auspicious men here who have dwelt on this mountain slope? Will you dwell on this mountain? Let a place be prepared for you;
you shall all subsist forever on roots, tubers, and fruits."
"You shall obtain husbands named Kimpuruṣas.
Having heard these words of the son of Soma, those many women were transformed into Kimpuruṣīs and then,
in various ways, took up their residence upon the mountain.
Having heard of the origin of the Kimpuruṣas, both Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata then said to Rāma, the lord of men, "It is a marvel! Then the highly illustrious Rāma began this story once again.
The righteous-souled one recounted [the story] of the son of Prajāpati.
Seeing that all those kinnarīs had fled, the best of sages spoke to that woman endowed with beauty, as if smiling:
"O lady of radiant countenance, I am Soma’s dearly beloved son.
O woman of excellent hips, accept me with devotion and a loving glance.
Having heard those words of his, she was alone in that desolate place, deprived of her kinsmen.
Ilā replied to that great planet, who was as radiant as the sun:
"O gentle one, I am a fulfiller of your desires and remain under your control. Command me, O son of Soma; do as you wish."

Having heard that wondrous report of hers, the son of the Moon, filled with joy and full of desire, took his delight with her. For Budha, that month of Mādhava passed while he was with that Ilā of the beautiful countenance.

As he, full of desire, was thus excessively delighting her, a month passed by as if it were a single moment. Then, when the month was complete, the glorious son of Prajāpati, whose face resembled the full moon, awoke upon his bed.
There he saw the son of Soma performing austerities in that pool of water, with his arms raised and without support; the king addressed him:
"O Blessed One, I have entered this difficult mountain range together with my followers."
"I do not see that army; where indeed have my men gone?
Hearing these words of the royal sage who had lost his senses, he replied with auspicious speech, consoling him with a supreme voice:
By a great rain of stones, your servants were struck down;
you, however, were sleeping in the hermitage, afflicted by the fear of wind and rain. Take heart—blessings be upon you—you are now fearless and free from distress.
"O hero, subsisting on fruits and roots, dwell here at your pleasure. At these words, that highly illustrious king was comforted;
yet, distressed by the destruction of his servants, he replied with these auspicious words:
"I shall renounce my own kingdom; deprived of my servants, O Brahmin, I cannot endure to live for even a moment. You ought to grant me permission.
My eldest son, O Brahmin, is devoted to dharma and possesses great fame."
"He who is known as Śaśabindu shall obtain my kingdom;
for I shall not be able, O one of great splendor, to go before my servants and wife who are enjoying happiness and address even a single unpleasant word to them."
When the lord of kings had spoken thus, Budha said this most wonderful thing in a conciliatory manner:
"O mighty son of Kārdama, you should not feel any distress; let your dwelling be here."
"Once you have dwelt here for a year, I shall bring about what is for your benefit.
Having heard those words of Budha, whose actions are untiring,
she set her mind on making a dwelling, just as had been instructed by the teacher of the Veda.
For one month she became a beautiful woman and delighted him incessantly;
for one month he remained in the form of a man and fixed his mind upon dharma.
Then, in the ninth month, Ilā [gave birth to] the son of Soma’s daughter.
The fair-hipped woman gave birth to her son Purūravas.
As soon as he was born, the fair-hipped woman placed the mighty son of Ilā— who resembled Budha in complexion— into his father’s hands.
7.080.025a Even the wise Budha, having consoled the king who had become a woman,
7.080.025c delighted him with stories endowed with righteousness, for he was self-possessed.
7.081.001a When Rāma had spoken thus, [he told] that wonderful account of his birth.

7.081.001 Lakṣmaṇa and the highly illustrious Bharata spoke again: 7.081.002 "O best of men, she who was the beloved of the Moon’s son and dwelt with him for a year—what did she do? You ought to tell us that."
7.081.003 Having heard that sweetness of speech from the two who were questioning him,
Rāma again spoke this story concerning the daughters of Prajāpati.
7.081.004 When the hero had attained manhood, Budha, possessed of supreme intelligence, [approached them].
The highly illustrious one summoned Saṃvarta, who is most noble,
as well as Cyavana, the son of Bhṛgu, the sage Ariṣṭanemi,
Pramodana, Modakara, and then the sage Durvāsas.
Having brought all these together— those who were skilled in speech and seers of truth— he,
being well-composed through fortitude, spoke to all his friends:
"This mighty-armed king is the son of Ila and Kardama."
"Know him as he truly is, so that what is for his ultimate good may be ordained.
While they were thus conversing,
Kardama, endowed with great splendor, arrived at that hermitage together with high-souled brahmins.
Pulastya, Kratu, and likewise Vaṣaṭkāra,
as well as the highly effulgent Oṃkāra, approached that hermitage.
With joyful minds, they all gathered together in mutual assembly.
Then those well-wishers spoke their individual words to the lord of Bāhlīka.
Kardama, however, spoke these words for the supreme benefit of his son:
"O twice-born ones, listen to my words regarding what is indeed for the welfare of the king."
7.081.012a I see no other remedy except for the one whose banner bears the bull;
7.081.012c there is no sacrifice superior to the horse-sacrifice, and it is indeed dear to that Great-Souled One.
7.081.013a Therefore, let us all perform this difficult-to-attain sacrifice for the sake of the king.
7.081.013c Thus addressed by Kardama, all those bulls among the twice-born 7.081.013e approved that sacrifice for the purpose of propitiating Rudra.
7.081.014a Now, the royal sage Saṃvarta had a disciple who was a conqueror of enemy cities.
The one renowned as Marutta brought that sacrifice to completion.
Then a great sacrifice took place in the vicinity of Budha’s hermitage,
and the highly illustrious Rudra attained supreme satisfaction.
Then, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the Lord of Umā, delighted with supreme joy, spoke these words to all the twice-born regarding Ilā:
"O best of the twice-born, I am pleased with this horse-sacrifice and with your devotion."
"What pleasing and auspicious service may I perform for this lord of the Bāhlikas?
While the Lord of the Gods was speaking thus, those well-composed twice-born ones propitiated the Lord of the Gods so that Ilā might become a man.

Then, with a delighted mind, Rudra of great splendor restored manhood to Ilā; having granted it, he vanished from sight. When the horse sacrifice had concluded and Hari had departed, he became invisible.
7.081.020c All those far-sighted twice-born men departed as they had come.
7.081.021a But the king, having abandoned Bāhlīka, established in the Middle Country the illustrious city of Pratiṣṭhāna, which was unsurpassed.
Śaśabindu was the king of Bāhlīka, a conqueror of enemy cities.
Ila, the powerful son of Prajāpati, was the king of Pratiṣṭhāna.
In due time, that Ila attained the unsurpassed world of Brahmā.
King Purūravas, the son of Ila, attained a firm foundation [of sovereignty].
Such indeed, O bulls among men, is the power of the Aśvamedha:
that even one who has become a woman regained manhood, as well as whatever else is difficult to obtain.
Having related this to his two brothers, the Kakutstha of immeasurable splendor spoke again these words, consistent with dharma, to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, and Kaśyapa..."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, having summoned all these twice-born men of the most eminent lineages who have been honored with the Aśvamedha sacrifice, and having consulted with them,
I shall release the horse endowed with auspicious marks according to the prescribed ritual."
Having heard those words spoken by Rāghava, he of swift prowess summoned all the twice-born and presented Rāghava to them. Seeing him, who resembled a god, they performed the salutation of his feet.
They honored the invincible Rāghava with blessings. Then,
with palms joined in reverence, Rāghava addressed those most excellent of the twice-born with words consistent with dharma concerning the horse sacrifice.

Having heard those words of the foremost of the twice-born, which were wonderful to behold and centered upon the horse sacrifice, he then became exceedingly pleased. Having understood their intention, Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"O mighty-armed one, dispatch a message to the high-souled Sugrīva.
Let him come quickly with many great monkeys and bears who depend upon him; may prosperity be yours, so that he may join you in enjoying this supreme sacrifice."
And Vibhīṣaṇa, surrounded by many Rākṣasas who travel at will,
let that mighty-armed one of swift prowess reach the horse sacrifice.
And those kings, O tiger among men, who desire to do what is pleasing to me—
"Let them, along with their followers, come quickly to this unsurpassed sacrificial ground.
And as for those twice-born ones devoted to dharma who have gone to other lands,
invite them all, O Lakṣmaṇa, for the horse sacrifice."
"O mighty-armed one, let the sages whose wealth is asceticism be summoned—
those great seers who have gone to other lands along with their wives—
and let a very large sacrificial enclosure be prepared on the banks of the Gomatī in the Naimiṣa forest."
"O mighty-armed one, let that which is most meritorious be commanded.
Let a hundred thousand loads of beautiful rice grains,
and ten thousand loads of sesame and mung beans, go before you, O one of great strength."
"Let the high-minded Bharata go at the head, preceded by many millions of gold pieces and hundreds more of silver. Let him lead the way,
with all the market stalls and rows of shops, and all the actors and dancers."
He summoned the merchants, the young and the old, and the twice-born who were well-composed; the skilled laborers and the highly learned artisans;
and all my mothers, as well as the princes and the women of the inner apartments.

"Let the high-minded Bharata go at the head, placing my golden wife— who is worthy of initiation for the sacrificial rite— in front of him. Having quickly dispatched all of that without omission, the elder brother of Bharata [set forth].
He released the horse, endowed with auspicious marks and black-spotted like a black antelope. Having assigned Lakṣmaṇa together with the officiating priests to attend to the horse,
that descendant of Kakutstha then proceeded toward Naimiṣa accompanied by his army.
Having seen that most wonderful sacrificial enclosure,
the illustrious and mighty-armed one experienced incomparable joy and spoke thus:
"All the lords of men [are present] for him as he dwells in Naimiṣa."
They arrived from all the kingdoms, and Rāma honored them in return. That best of men, possessed of great splendor, assigned costly residences for those high-souled kings and their followers.
Then Bharata, together with Śatrughna, quickly provided food, drink, and clothing for those great-souled ones and their followers;
and so too did the high-souled monkeys, together with Sugrīva.
All of them, bowing down, performed the service of serving the brahmins.
And Vibhīṣaṇa, surrounded by many garlanded rākṣasas,
stood in attendance as a servant to the sages of fierce asceticism.
Thus well-arranged, the horse sacrifice proceeded;
and protected by Lakṣmaṇa, the horse’s course was set forth.
No other sound arose there at the sacrifice of that high-souled one.
"Give with confidence according to your own will, as long as the supplicants remain satisfied.
Then it was seen that the monkeys and rākṣasas gave accordingly;
there was no one there who was soiled, miserable, or even emaciated.
In that excellent sacrifice of the king, crowded with joyful and well-fed people,
even those high-souled sages who have lived for long periods did not recall a sacrifice so adorned by a flood of gifts.
Of silver, gold, jewels, and garments,
no end is seen even as they are being given away incessantly;
not even that of Śakra, nor Soma, nor Yama, nor Varuṇa.
"Never before has such a sight been seen," thus spoke those whose wealth is asceticism.
Monkeys stood everywhere, and likewise, Rākṣasas stood everywhere;
with hands full of riches, they gave garments and wealth abundantly to those who desired them.
7.083.016a Such was the sacrifice of that lion among kings, endowed with every excellence;
7.083.016c it proceeded for more than a year and did not diminish.
7.084.001a While that supreme and wonderful sacrifice was thus proceeding,
Accompanied by his disciples, Vālmīki, the bull among sages, arrived quickly.
Having seen that sacrifice, which resembled the divine and was wonderful to behold,
he constructed auspicious huts for the dwellings of the sages in a secluded spot.
7.084.003a He, being confident, said to his two disciples: "Go, with concentrated minds,
7.084.003c and sing the entire poem of the Rāmāyaṇa with supreme joy 7.084.004a in the holy hermitages of the sages and in the dwellings of the brahmins."
In the streets, on the royal highways, and in the houses of kings;
at the gate of Rāma’s palace where the ritual work is performed;
and especially in the presence of the officiating priests—it is there that the song should be sung.

"And here are these various sweet fruits grown upon the mountain peaks; having tasted them again and again, you may sing. By eating these fruits, my dear children, you will surely not suffer from fatigue."
"And you shall depart from the city with your roots thoroughly cleansed.
If Rāma, the lord of the earth, should summon you to hear [the recital],
then let the song proceed while the sages are seated."
On each day, twenty cantos should indeed be sung with supreme joy,
according to the many measures previously specified by me;
nor should even the slightest greed be entertained out of a desire for wealth.
7.084.010c What need have those dwelling in the hermitage, who subsist on fruits and roots, for wealth?
7.084.011a If that descendant of Kakutstha should ask, "Whose children are you two? 7.084.011c Then you must say to the lord of men, "We are indeed the disciples of Vālmīki."
"Having tuned these very sweet strings to the pitch previously shown, let the two of you,
free from anxiety, sing most melodiously. The song should begin from the very start, and you must not show disrespect toward the king."
"For by law, the king is the father of all beings. Therefore,
with joyful hearts, both of you shall sing sweetly tomorrow at dawn, with concentration, a song accompanied by the rhythm of stringed instruments."
Having thus instructed him many times, the sage Vālmīki, son of Pracetas, most noble and highly renowned, then remained silent. Those two princes kept that wondrous thing in their hearts.
Having fixed their minds upon the auspicious words spoken by the seers,
those two, eager and refined by the conduct of Bhārgava, passed the night in happiness, like the two Aśvins.
When the night had turned to dawn, having bathed and offered oblations into the fire,
those two sang here and there according to what the sage had previously instructed. Kākutstha heard that ancient song from various places.
Having heard that unprecedented style of recitation, adorned with song,
composed according to many metrical measures, and accompanied by the rhythm of the lute strings,
Rāghava became filled with great curiosity.
Then, during an interval between rituals, the king— a tiger among men— summoned the great sages, as well as other kings, learned men,
and citizens; those versed in the Purāṇas, experts in grammar, and the elder twice-born.
Having brought all these together, he seated the two singers.
There, the throngs of sages and the kings of great prowess were filled with joy,
as if drinking in the king and those two singers with their very eyes.
Then they all spoke to one another at once:
"Both of them resemble Rāma as if two reflections had been drawn from a single image;
were it not for their matted hair and their garments of bark."
"We perceive no difference between the singing of Rāghava and [that of the other].
While the listeners were thus conversing, increasing their joy,
those two young sages there began to sing the song.
Then there began a sweet, superhuman performance of music;
and all the listeners did not reach satiety through the excellence of the singing. It had proceeded from the very beginning, prior to the section concerning the vision of Nārada.
From that point onward, they sang the cantos up to the twentieth.
Then, at the time of afternoon, Rāghava,
who is devoted to his brother, spoke to Bharata after he had heard those twenty cantos.
"O descendant of Kakutstha, give eighteen thousand pieces of gold for these two noble youths quickly; let there be no fruitless labor.
But as that gold was being offered, Kuśa and Lava would not accept it."
And the two high-souled ones, filled with wonder, said: "What is the use of this?
We forest-dwellers shall subsist on wild fruits and roots;
what shall we do with gold and bullion in the forest?"
While the two of them were speaking thus, the listeners, filled with curiosity, as well as Rāma himself, were all utterly amazed;
and Rāma was eager to hear the account of that poem’s origin.
The one of great splendor questioned those two young sages:
"What is the extent of this poem? What is the status of that high-souled one?
And who is that bull among sages, the author of this great poem?"
To Rāghava, who was questioning them, the two sons of the sage spoke these words:
"The venerable Vālmīki, the author, has arrived at the vicinity of the sacrifice;
by him this entire life-story has been fully revealed to you."
O Indra among kings, from the very beginning there have been five hundred creations;
O King, as long as one's life is established, so long do good and evil persist.
O great car-warrior, O King, if your mind is set upon hearing this, [then listen].
"Listen, along with your younger brother, to how Kṣaṇa was summoned during the course of the ritual.
"Very well," Rāma replied; and having taken leave of the descendant of Raghu, the two of them, greatly delighted, went to the dwelling where that bull among sages resided.
7.085.023a Rāma, together with the sages and the high-souled kings,
7.085.023c having heard that sweetness of song, went to the workshop.
7.086.001a For many days, Rāma listened to that most wonderful song.
7.086.001 He heard [the song] together with the sages, the kings, and the monkeys.
7.086.002 Having recognized Kuśa and Lava as the two sons of Sītā while that song was being sung,
Rāma spoke these words in the midst of that assembly.
"Go to the presence of the Blessed One and speak my words:
'Whether her conduct has been pure or whether she is free from stain, let her perform purification here, having obtained the consent of the Great Sage.'"
"Having understood the intention of the Sage and the thought within Sītā's mind,
tell me quickly so that she may give proof of her desire;
tomorrow at dawn, Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, shall take an oath."
"Let him perform this in the midst of the assembly for my purification here.
Having heard these most extraordinary words of the descendant of Raghu,
the messengers set out for the grove where the bull among sages resided.
Having bowed down to that great-souled one, who was blazing with immeasurable splendor,
they spoke words that were gentle and sweet to Rāma.
Having heard their speech and what was in Rāma’s mind, [he understood].
Having understood this, the sage of great splendor then spoke these words:
"So be it; may prosperity be yours, for Sītā shall act in such a way as to please Rāghava, for a husband is indeed the deity of a woman."
7.086.011a Thus addressed by the sage, all those messengers of Rāma, possessed of great prowess,
7.086.011c returned to Rāghava and related the words of the sage to him all together.
7.086.012a Then Kākutstha was overjoyed upon hearing the words of the high-souled one.
He addressed the sages assembled there, as well as the kings:
"O venerable ones, together with your disciples and the lords of men with their followers,
behold Sītā’s oath, and whatever else anyone else desires."
Having heard those words of the high-souled Rāghava,
a great cry of "Excellent! arose from all the foremost sages,
and the high-souled kings also praised Rāghava.
"O best of men, this is appropriate for you alone on earth and not for anyone else.
Having thus reached this conclusion, Rāghava,
the slayer of enemies, dismissed them all when the next day had dawned.
When that night had dawned, the king, the highly effulgent descendant of Raghu, having gone to the sacrificial enclosure, summoned all the sages:
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, and Kāśyapa.
Viśvāmitra, Dīrghatapas, and Durvāsas of great asceticism; Agastya, as well as Āśakti, Bhārgava Vāmana,
the long-lived Mārkaṇḍeya, and Maudgalya of great asceticism.
Bhārgava and Cyavana, Śatānanda who knows the dharma,
the radiant Bharadvāja, and the brilliant Agniputra—
these and many other sages of rigid vows [were there].
All the kings, those tigers among men, have assembled together;
as have the Rākṣasas of great heroism and the Vānaras of great strength—
all these high-souled ones have gathered out of curiosity.

7.087.007 Thousands of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras all gathered together for the purpose of witnessing Sītā’s oath. 7.087.008 Thus the entire assembly was gathered, as motionless as a mountain, appearing like a mass of horses.
Upon hearing this, the best of sages quickly approached him together with Sītā. Following behind that ṛṣi, Sītā went along with her face cast downward,
her hands joined in reverence and her throat choked with tears, keeping Rāma in her heart.
Seeing Sītā following behind Vālmīki like the goddess Śrī approaching Brahmā, a great cry of "Well done! arose;
then, a tumultuous roar of acclaim broke out from everyone.
With their souls agitated by a vast sorrow born of grief, some cried out, "O Sītā, well done! while others cried, "O Rāma, well done!
Still others there exclaimed, "Well done! Well done! for both of them.
Then, having entered the midst of the throngs of people, Vālmīki, the bull among sages, accompanied by Sītā, spoke thus to the descendant of Raghu:
"O son of Daśaratha, this is Sītā, who is firm in her vows and a practitioner of dharma."

"O Rāma of great vows, those sinless ones were abandoned by you in the vicinity of my hermitage out of fear of public scandal; Sītā will provide proof of her purity, and you ought to grant her permission to depart."
"These two sons of Janaka, both born as twins, are indeed your own sons, O invincible one; I tell you this truth. I am the tenth son of Pracetas, O delighter of the Raghus."
"I do not recall ever having spoken an untruth, and these two sons of yours [are proof]. For many thousands of years, I have practiced ascetic penance;
may I enjoy the fruit of that only if the princess of Mithilā is found sinless."
"O Rāghava, having reflected upon Sītā as pure among the five elements with the mind as the sixth, I accepted her at the forest waterfall.
She is one of pure conduct, sinless, and devoted to her husband."
"Out of fear of public scandal, he will provide proof for you.
When Vālmīki had spoken thus, Rāghava replied with palms joined in reverence before the assembly, beholding that woman who resembled a goddess.
7.088.002 "It is exactly so, O illustrious one, just as you say, you who know the Dharma. For I have gained conviction, O Brahmin, through your stainless words.
7.088.003 Indeed, conviction was previously given by Vaidehī in the presence of the gods."
"O Brahmin, knowing her to be sinless despite the fear of the world, I abandoned Sītā; therefore, you ought to forgive me. Furthermore, I know these two twin-born sons of mine, Kuśa and Lava."
"May my love for Maithilī, who is pure in the midst of the world, endure.
Having understood Rāma’s intention, all the best of the gods assembled together, placing the Grandfather (Brahmā) at their head.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts;
the two Aśvins, the Ṛṣis, the Gandharvas, and likewise the hosts of Apsarases;
all the Sādhyas and all the supreme Ṛṣis.
Then a pure, auspicious, divine-scented, and delightful wind blew;
that best of gods gladdened that multitude of people from every side.
With concentrated minds, they gazed upon that wondrous and inconceivable sight.
As in the Kṛta age, men from all kingdoms had gathered there as of old.
Seeing them all assembled, Sītā, dressed in saffron robes,
spoke these words with joined palms, her gaze cast downward and her face turned away.
“As surely as I do not think of anyone other than Rāghava even in my mind,
so may the lady Mādhavī grant me an opening. While Vaidehī was thus swearing her oath, that miracle appeared.
A divine and unsurpassed lion-throne rose up from the ground,
supported by the heads of nāgas of immeasurable prowess,
celestial in form and adorned with every kind of jewel.
Then the goddess Dharaṇī, taking Maithilī by both her arms,
greeted her with a welcome and seated her upon a throne.
Seeing her seated on the throne as she entered the subterranean realm (rasātala), [he spoke].
A divine rain of merit fell incessantly upon Sītā, and a great cry of "Excellent! suddenly arose from the gods:
"Excellent, excellent, O Sītā, you whose character is such as this!"
Thus, having witnessed Sītā’s entry, the gods stationed in the intermediate space, their hearts filled with joy, uttered many kinds of words;
and all those sages who had gone to the sacrificial enclosure likewise spoke.
And the kings, those tigers among men, could not cease from their amazement;
nor could all beings, both stationary and moving, in the sky and on the earth,
nor the massive-bodied Dānavas, nor the lords of the serpents in the netherworld.
Some cried out in great joy, while others were absorbed in meditation;
some gazed upon Rāma, and some, unconscious of their surroundings, looked toward Sītā.
Upon seeing Sītā’s entry, there arose a collective gathering among them.
For that brief moment, the entire world was utterly bewildered. Then, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, Rāma, deeply distressed in mind and not seeing Vaidehī, considered this world to be empty.
Overwhelmed by grief, he found no peace of mind.
Having dismissed all the kings— the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas—
he sent away the throng of people, including the foremost of the brahmins, with wealth in abundance.
Then, having dismissed them all, the lotus-eyed Rāma,
keeping Sītā in his heart, entered Ayodhyā;
that joy of the Raghus chose no wife other than Sītā.
In every sacrifice, a golden image of Janaki served as the sacrificial consort.
For ten thousand years, he performed the horse sacrifice (vājimedha),
as well as the vājapeya sacrifices tenfold and those involving abundant gold.
7.089.006 With the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices, with Gosavas involving great wealth, and with other rites accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, that illustrious king performed his worship.
7.089.007 In this manner, a very long period of time passed while that high-souled one remained established in his kingdom.
While Rāghava was thus striving in righteousness,
the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas remained obedient to Rāma’s command;
day after day, the kings grew increasingly devoted to the descendant of Raghu.

The rain-cloud pours at the proper time, the quarters of the sky are clear, and there is an abundance of food; likewise, both the city and the countryside are filled with people who are joyful and well-nourished.
At that time, no one dies prematurely, nor do living beings suffer from disease.
While Rāma was ruling the kingdom, no unrighteousness whatsoever occurred.
Then, after a long time had passed, the illustrious mother of Rāma,
surrounded by her sons and grandsons, met the law of time.

Sumitrā and the illustrious Kaikeyī also followed [the path]; having performed many kinds of righteous deeds, they are established in the third heaven. All of them, along with King Daśaratha, are firmly established in heaven.
7.089.013c Those highly fortunate women, having come together, received their share of the dharma. 7.089.014a Rāma bestowed great gifts upon them from time to time,
without distinction among his mothers, as well as upon the Brahmins and ascetics.

The righteous Rāma performed ancestral rites involving many jewels and sacrifices most difficult to accomplish, thereby increasing the merit of his ancestors and the gods. Then, after some time, King Yudhājit of Kekaya—
He dispatched his own guru, Gārgya— the son of Aṅgiras, a Brahman-sage of immeasurable splendor— to the high-souled Rāghava;
and he gave ten thousand horses as an unsurpassed gift of affection.
The king presented Rāma with woolen blankets, jewels, excellent variegated garments, and many ornaments. Upon hearing that the great seer Gārgya had arrived, Rāghava [received him].

Having gone out for the distance of a *krośa* with his followers to meet the beloved messenger who had arrived from his maternal uncle Aśvapati, the descendant of Kakutstha honored Gārgya and accepted the wealth he brought.
Having inquired after all the pleasant news regarding his maternal uncle’s welfare,
Rāma proceeded to question the illustrious one who was seated there:
"What words did my maternal uncle say, for which purpose the Blessed One has come here?"
"O best among those who know the art of speech, you have arrived like Bṛhaspati himself.
Having heard Rāma's words regarding the details of the matter, the Brahmarṣi began to speak to the descendant of Raghu about that which was of wondrous appearance.

"O mighty-armed bull among men, your maternal uncle Yudhājit has spoken these words filled with affection; listen to them, if it pleases you. This is the realm of the Gandharvas, adorned with fruits and roots."
On both sides of the ocean lies a most beautiful region;
there, the Gandharvas—armed and skilled in combat—protect it.
These heroic sons of Śailūṣa are three crores in number and possess great strength.
"O Kakutstha, having completely conquered them, O mighty-armed one, establish two cities with great concentration in that auspicious Gandharva territory.
No other person has access there, and this region is exceedingly beautiful."
"May it please you, O mighty-armed one; I shall not speak untruth to you.
Hearing that from his maternal uncle, Rāghava was delighted, and like a sage, he said "So be it," and looked toward Bharata.
7.090.015a Delighted, Rāghava, with his hands joined in reverence, spoke to the twice-born:
7.090.015c "O Brahman-sage, these two princes shall conquer that region—
7.090.016a the two heroic sons of Bharata, Takṣa and Puṣkala."
Well-protected by their maternal uncle and established in righteousness,
those two princes, placing Bharata at their head and accompanied by their armies and followers,
will slay the sons of the Gandharva and divide the two cities between them.
"Having established his two sons in that best of cities and having settled them there,
that most righteous one will come back to my presence again.
Having thus spoken to the Brahmarṣi, he [dismissed] Bharata along with his army and followers.
Then he gave his command and consecrated the two princes; and under an auspicious constellation, having placed the son of Aṅgiras at their head,
Bharata set forth with his army and the two princes.
Then that army, followed by Rāghava, set out from the human world like the host of Śakra; it was difficult for even gods and asuras to overcome,
and it included flesh-eating beings and very large rākṣasas.
And many hosts of most dreadful beings, who feed on flesh and thirst for blood, followed Bharata by the thousands,
desiring to eat the flesh of the Gandharva’s sons.
Many thousands of lions, tigers, jackals, and birds that fly through the sky marched at the front of the army.
Having remained on the road for a month and a half, the army was free from affliction.
Teeming with joyful and well-fed people, he arrived at Kekaya.
Hearing that the commander-in-chief Bharata had arrived accompanied by Gārgya, Yudhājit, the lord of Kekaya, experienced the highest delight.
7.091.002a That lord of the Kekayas set forth with a vast multitude of people;
7.091.002c hurrying, he advanced against the Gandharvas who possessed the forms of gods.
7.091.003a Both Bharata and Yudhājit, moving together with swift prowess, [proceeded].
Having reached the city of the Gandharvas with their army and followers,
they heard that Bharata had arrived; those immensely powerful Gandharvas then gathered together, roaring on all sides, desiring to fight.
Then there occurred a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end;
it was most terrifying for seven nights, yet victory belonged to neither side.
Then Rāma’s younger brother, filled with rage, [discharged] the most dreadful weapon of Time.
Bharata employed against the Gandharvas one named Saṃvarta.
Bound by the noose of Time and torn apart by Saṃvarta,
three crores were struck down there in an instant by that high-souled one.

The inhabitants of heaven do not even remember that terrible slaughter, for such great-souled ones [perish] in the mere twinkling of an eye. When those heroes had been slain, Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, [acted].
Then he established two most prosperous and excellent cities:
Takṣa at Takṣaśilā and Puṣkara at Puṣkarāvatī. That was the beautiful Gandharva country and the region of Gāndhāra.
For five years it was crowded with districts and likewise with city-dwellers; it was filled with floods of wealth and jewels and graced by groves,
where there was a mutual rivalry born of competition in the expansion of virtues.
Both cities were exceedingly beautiful to behold through their stainless public affairs; both were filled with throngs of garden carriages and possessed well-arranged marketplaces.
Both excellent cities were delightful and graced by extensive grounds.
Adorned with magnificent and beautiful palaces of uniform splendor, and graced by extensive and lovely temples,
Bharata, the younger brother of Rāghava, completed the settlement in five years.

The mighty-armed son of Kaikeyī returned once more to Ayodhyā; there, the illustrious Bharata paid homage to the high-souled Rāghava, who was like Dharma incarnate, just as Vāsava pays homage to Brahmā.
And he related exactly what had happened regarding the supreme slaughter of the Gandharvas, as well as the settlement of that region; having heard this, Rāghava was pleased with him.
Having heard that, Rāghava, together with his brothers, attained great joy.
And Rāghava spoke these words, appearing most wonderful, to his brothers:
"O Saumitri, these two youths, Aṅgada and Candraketu, are experts in righteousness; they are worthy of sovereignty and possess firm bows."
"7.092.003a I shall consecrate these two in the kingdom; let a suitable region be prepared.

7.092.003c For it must be delightful and spacious, where these two archers may find pleasure. 7.092.004a It should be a place where there is no oppression from kings, nor any destruction of hermitages."
"O gentle one, let that region be seen so that we may not commit any offense.
When Rāma had spoken thus, Bharata replied:
"This region along the Kārāpatha is most delightful and free from danger."
"Let a city be established there for the high-souled Aṅgada,
and a beautiful, moon-like, and healthy one for Candraketu.
Rāghava accepted those words spoken by Bharata.
Having brought that region under his control, he established it for Aṅgada.
A beautiful city named Aṅgadīyā was settled there for Aṅgada by Rāma, whose deeds are effortless, a city both delightful and well-protected.
Candraketu, however, was settled by the Malla king in Mallabhūmi;
it is renowned as Candrakāntā, a divine city like that of heaven.
Then Rāma, as well as Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa, attained the highest joy.
Those invincible warriors went forth to battle and performed the consecration ceremony.
Having consecrated the two princes and dispatched them with their armies and followers— sending Aṅgada to the western region and Candraketu toward the north— [they departed].
Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, followed after Aṅgada;
Bharata, for his part, became the rear-guard for Candraketu.
Lakṣmaṇa then dwelt for one year in the service of Aṅgada.
While his son remained invincible, he returned once more to Ayodhyā. Bharata likewise stayed there for a year and more;
then, having returned again to Ayodhyā, he approached the feet of Rāma.
Both Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata, devoted to Rāma’s feet,
though supremely righteous, did not realize that time had passed because of their affection.
In this manner, ten thousand years then went by for them.
Always striving for righteousness in the affairs of the citizens,
having enjoyed the world with fulfilled hearts, they were encompassed by splendor and remained established on the supreme path of dharma.

7.092.017c Like three fires kindled with blazing luster, the three [brothers] were like those who have offered oblations into the fire at a great sacrifice. 7.093.001a Then, after some time had passed, while Rāma remained on the path of righteousness...
Kāla, in the guise of an ascetic, approached the palace gate.
He spoke these words to the steadfast and illustrious Lakṣmaṇa:
"Announce me to Rāma, for I have arrived on account of a matter of great importance."
"I am indeed the messenger of the great seer Atibala, who possesses immeasurable power. O mighty one, I have come with a purpose, desiring to see Rāma.
Having heard those words of his, the son of Sumitrā was filled with haste.
He reported to Rāma what the ascetic intended to say:
"Be victorious through righteousness, O King, in both worlds, O you of great splendor!
A messenger has come to see you—a practitioner of austerities, radiant as the sun."
Having heard those words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma said:
"O dear one, let that great-souled sage, who upholds his word, be ushered in. Then the son of Sumitrā, saying "So be it," ushered in that sage.
Blazing, as it were, with splendors and scorching, as it were, with rays—
approaching that best of the Raghus who was radiant with his own majesty,
the seer addressed Rāghava in a sweet voice, saying, "May you prosper!"

To him, the immensely radiant Rāma offered worship preceded by the traditional water-offering (arghya) and proceeded to inquire after his well-being with composure. And that best among eloquent men was questioned regarding his welfare by Rāma.
The highly illustrious one sat down upon a divine golden throne.
Then Rāma said to him, "Welcome to you, O great sage;
convey the words of the one from whom you have come as a messenger."
Urged by that lion among kings, the sage spoke these words:
"This must be spoken as a pair; the eye is not destroyed by speech.
O Rāghava, whoever hears or looks upon it shall be put to death by you."
"If you heed the words of the foremost of sages, it shall indeed be so.
Having promised "So be it," Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Stand at the gate, O mighty-armed one; dismiss the doorkeeper."

"O Saumitri, whoever should see or hear the conversation prompted by this dispute between the sage and me would surely deserve to be put to death by me. Having said this, the descendant of Kakutstha stationed Lakṣmaṇa at the entrance to guard it.
Rāghava spoke these words to the sage:
"Tell me what you desire to say, and that by which you are so composed; speak without hesitation, for it dwells within my heart as well."
"Listen, O mighty-armed Rāma, to the purpose for which I have been summoned.
O one of great strength, I have been sent by the divine Grandfather.
O conqueror of enemy cities, in my former state, I was your son."
"O hero, Time, manifested through illusion, is the gatherer of all things.
And the blessed Grandfather, the Lord and Master of the worlds, has said:
'O mighty-armed one, it is now your time to protect the heavenly realms.'"
Having previously withdrawn the worlds by your own power of illusion,
you yourself, lying upon the waters in the great ocean, first brought me forth;
then, the serpent Ananta, who possesses many coils and reclines upon the water.
Having created by means of your illusory power two beings of great strength,
Madhu and Kaiṭabha, this earth became covered with their heaps of bones and was thus made a great land crowded with mountains.
Having generated me as well from your navel within a divine lotus resembling the sun,
you have transferred all your Prajāpati-like duties onto me. Thus, having laid down my burden, I worship you, the Lord of the World.

"Provide protection among all beings; you are the maker of my splendor. Therefore, being yourself invincible due to that eternal state, you have assumed the form of Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting all beings."
7.094.010a A powerful son was born of Aditi, the increaser of his brothers' joy;
7.094.010c when tasks arise, you are capable of assisting the world. 7.094.011a Therefore, O best among those who move, while all creatures are being terrified, [you must act].
Desiring the slaughter of Rāvaṇa, you set your mind upon human beings;
for ten thousand years and ten hundred years,
you yourself previously established the duration of your own residence.

O best among the foremost of men, you are that mind-made son who has reached a full lifespan here among humans; it is now time for you to approach [your father]. O Great King, if you wish to serve your progeny once more.

"Or dwell here, O hero; may it be well with you," thus spoke the Grandfather. "Or if you desire to conquer the world of the gods, O Raghava, let the deities, having Viṣṇu as their protector, be freed from their feverish distress."
Having heard the words spoken by the Grandfather, which were uttered at the proper time,
Rāghava, smiling, spoke these words concerning the destruction of all:
"I have heard the most wonderful speech of the God of gods."
"Indeed, great joy has arisen from your arrival.
May it be well with you; I shall now depart for the very place from which I came.
For you have entered my heart and reached it; of this I have no doubt."
"For in all the affairs of the gods who exercise sovereign power,
I must remain present during the universal dissolution, just as the Grandfather has commanded.
While they were thus conversing, the venerable sage Durvāsas arrived.
Desiring a sight of Rāma, he approached the palace gate.
Having arrived there, that best of sages said to the son of Sumitrā:
"Show Rāma to me quickly; my purpose will expire before long."
Having heard the speech of the sage, Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, saluted the high-souled one and spoke these words:
"Tell me, O Blessed One, what is to be done? What is the purpose? What shall I do?"
"For Rāghava is indeed busy, O Brahmin; wait for but a moment.
Having heard that, the tiger among sages, turbid with anger, spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa as if burning him with his eyes.
"O son of Sumitrā, at this very moment inform Rāma of my presence;
otherwise, I shall curse your realm, your city, and likewise Rāghava,
Bharata, O son of Sumitrā, and whatever progeny you may have."
"Indeed, I shall not be able to hold this anger within my heart any longer.
Having heard those words of such terrible appearance from that great-souled one,
he reflected in his mind upon the meaning of those words.

"Let there be death for me alone; let there not be the destruction of all," having resolved thus in his mind, he announced it to Rāghava. Having heard Lakṣmaṇa’s words, Rāma, setting aside the [proper] time, [acted].

7.095.010c Having rushed out in haste, the king beheld the son of Atri. 7.095.011a Having saluted that high-souled one who was blazing, as it were, with spiritual luster, the descendant of Kakutstha spoke with joined palms: "What is to be done?"
Having heard those words spoken by Rāghava, the powerful and eminent sage Durvāsas replied to Rāma: "Listen, O lover of dharma!
Today marks the completion of my thousand-year vow, O Rāghava."
"O sinless one, I desire food prepared according to your own means.
Hearing those words, Rāma was filled with great joy and served the meal prepared as it was to the chief of sages.
Having eaten that food, which was like nectar, that best of sages said,
"Well done, Rāma," and returned to his own hermitage.
When he had departed, the highly effulgent Rāghava was delighted in heart.
7.095.016c Recalling those words concerning the time, he then fell into sorrow. 7.095.017a Tormented by that grief and remembering that terrible sight,
he hung his head, dejected in mind, and was unable to speak.
Then, having deliberated with his intellect upon the words regarding the time, the highly illustrious Rāghava said, "This is not so," and remained silent. Then,
seeing him dejected with his face cast downward, like the moon eclipsed, [he spoke].
7.096.001c Delighted, Lakṣmaṇa spoke these sweet words to Rāghava:
7.096.002a "O mighty-armed one, you ought not to feel distress on my account;
7.096.002c for such is the course of Time, bound by its prior destiny."
"O gentle one, kill me with confidence; fulfill your promise. O descendant of Kakutstha, men who fail in their promise go to hell.
O great king, if you have affection for me, or if I am worthy of your favor,"
"Kill me without hesitation; increase your merit, O Rāghava.
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma’s senses were shaken;
he summoned his ministers as well as the family priest.
And in their midst, O lord of men, the king related everything as it had happened—
the arrival of Durvāsas and the vow of the ascetic.
Having heard that, all the ministers together with the preceptors summarized it.
Then Vasiṣṭha, of great splendor, spoke these words:
"O mighty-armed one, this destruction of yours, which causes the hair to stand on end, has been foreseen;
as has your separation from Lakṣmaṇa, O highly illustrious Rāma."
"Let this powerful Time take him; do not make your vow in vain. For if your vow is destroyed, Dharma itself will surely go to ruin.
And when Dharma is destroyed, then the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile,"
7.096.010c Everything, including the hosts of gods and sages, would undoubtedly perish.
7.096.011a Therefore, O tiger among men, for the sake of protecting the three worlds, 7.096.011c restore the world to well-being today by slaying Lakṣmaṇa.
Having heard those words, consistent with dharma and worldly purpose, spoken by them as they gathered together in the midst of the assembly, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"I dismiss you, O son of Sumitrā; let there be no transgression of dharma."
"Either abandonment or death has been ordained for the virtuous; both are equal.
When these words were spoken by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, his eyes clouded with tears, departed in haste and did not enter his own home.
Having gone to the bank of the Sarayū and performed his ablutions, he stood with palms joined in reverence;
restraining all the openings of his senses, he did not release his breath. As he remained thus absorbed in yoga, not breathing, Indra together with the hosts of Apsarases [approached].
Then all the gods, together with the hosts of sages, scattered flowers [over him].
Holding the mighty Lakṣmaṇa— who was invisible to all his younger brothers yet possessed of a physical body— Śakra entered heaven.

7.096.018 Then, O best of gods, all of them, joyful and delighted, together with the sages, worshipped that portion of Viṣṇu which had arrived. 7.097.001 Having sent Lakṣmaṇa away, Rāma was overcome with pain and grief.
He spoke thus to the family priest, the ministers, and the merchants:
"Today I shall consecrate Bharata, who is devoted to righteousness, as the lord of Ayodhyā;
thereafter, O heroes, I shall depart for the forest."
"Bring together the necessary provisions so that there may be no delay;
this very day I shall go to the destination reached by Lakṣmaṇa.
Hearing those words spoken by Rāghava, all the subjects were deeply moved.
With their heads bowed to the ground, they became as if lifeless.
And Bharata, having heard Rāma’s speech, lost consciousness;
he reviled the kingdom and spoke this to the descendant of Raghu:
"By truth, O King, I swear that I do not desire even the heavenly world, nor indeed do I desire sovereignty without you, O delighter of the Raghus. O King,
lord of men, consecrate these two, Kuśa and Lava."
"Let messengers of swift prowess go to Kuśa among the Kosalas and likewise to Lava among the Northerners; let them announce our departure for heaven to Śatrughna without delay."
Having heard what was spoken by Bharata and seeing the citizens with their faces cast down, tormented by grief, Vasiṣṭha spoke these words:
"O child Rāma, behold these subjects who have come to the earth."
"Having understood their desired purpose, do not do anything that is displeasing to them.
Then, at the word of Vasiṣṭha, having roused the subjects, the descendant of Kakutstha spoke these words to them all: "What shall I do?"
Then all the subjects spoke these words to Rāma:
"We shall follow you as you depart, O Rāma, wherever you go.
This is our supreme joy; this is considered by us to be the highest duty."
7.097.013c A firm satisfaction has always resided in our hearts regarding the pursuit of you.

7.097.014a O descendant of Kakutstha, if you have affection for the citizens, and if your love for them is indeed supreme, 7.097.014c then let us go together upon the right path, along with our sons and wives.
"Whether it be a penance grove, a difficult pass, a river, or likewise the ocean—
if we are not to be abandoned by you, O Lord, lead us all there.
Having understood their resolve and having observed the inevitable end, [he departed].
And regarding the firm devotion of the citizens, he said, "So be it.
Having thus made his decision on that day, Rāghava [appointed] the hero Kuśa over the Kosalas and likewise Lava over the northern regions.
He consecrated both high-souled Kuśīlavas,
bestowing upon each of them three thousand chariots, ten thousand elephants,
and ten thousand horses as their wealth.
Having consecrated those two heroes and likewise dispatched them to their own city— [the city] filled with many jewels and much wealth, and teeming with joyful and well-nourished people—
he sent messengers to the high-souled Śatrughna.
Urged by Rāma’s words, those messengers of swift prowess departed quickly for Madhurā; they did not stop to rest along the way. Then, having reached Madhurā after three days and nights, they arrived.
They related everything exactly as it had happened to Śatrughna:
the abandonment of Lakṣmaṇa, the vow of Rāghava,
the consecration of his two sons, and likewise the citizens' following him.
On the slopes of the Vindhya mountains, there was a beautiful city belonging to Kuśa;
it was named Kuśāvatī by the wise Rāma. And that lovely city was made known as Śrāvatī to Lava.
"The city of Ayodhyā is indeed deserted, and Bharata is following Rāghava. Having thus quickly reported all this to the high-souled Śatrughna,
those messengers then ceased speaking, saying, "Hurry, O King!"
Having heard of that impending destruction of the lineage, which was terrible in appearance,
the joy of the Raghus summoned his ministers and his golden-hued family priest; having related everything exactly as it had occurred to them, he spoke.
He foresaw his own downfall along with his brothers.
Then that heroic lord of men consecrated his two sons:
Subāhu obtained Madhurā, and Śatrughna, the slayer of enemies, obtained Vaidiśa.
Having divided that army into two parts for his two sons,
he established the two princes, endowed with wealth and grain, as rulers.
Then, having dispatched the king, the slayer of enemies, to Vaidiśa...
Rāghava traveled swiftly to Ayodhyā in a single chariot.
There he beheld the high-souled one, blazing like a fire,
wearing garments of fine linen, together with the imperishable sages.
Then, having saluted Rāma with joined palms and restrained senses,
he who knew the Dharma spoke these words, reflecting only upon righteousness:
"Having performed the consecration of my two sons, the descendants of Raghu, providing them with wealth as is fitting,"
"O King, know that I am resolved to follow you;
there is nothing else to be said here, for your command is difficult to transgress.
O hero, you ought not to abandon me, especially as I am so devoted."
Having recognized that resolute resolve of his, Rāma, the joy of the Raghus, said these words to Śatrughna: "So be it.
At the conclusion of those words, the monkeys, who could assume any form at will, [appeared].
And throngs of bears and rākṣasas rushed forward in great numbers;
likewise, sons of gods, sons of sages, and sons of gandharvas—
all of them having learned of Rāma’s destruction, gathered together.
Having all assembled together, they paid homage to Rāma and said:
"O King, O highly illustrious one, we have come to follow you.
O Rāma, O bull among men, if you should depart without us..."
"Raising it like the staff of Yama, you have struck them down.
Having heard these words of the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas,
he then spoke sweetly and gently to Vibhīṣaṇa.

"O Vibhīṣaṇa, O lord of Rākṣasas of great prowess, as long as living beings shall endure, so long shall you indeed remain in Laṅkā and sustain yourself. Protect the subjects with righteousness; you ought not to speak further."
Having spoken thus to Hanumān, the descendant of Kakutstha then said:
"O Lord of Monkeys, you have resolved to live; do not let your promise fail. My stories shall circulate throughout the world for as long as it endures."

"Maintaining your life-breaths for that long, you must uphold your promise. Having spoken thus to all those bears and monkeys, Rāghava, the descendant of Kakutstha, then said to them, "Depart with me."
When the night had turned to dawn, the broad-chested and highly illustrious Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, then spoke to the family priest:
"Let the *agnihotra* sacrifice proceed first, with clarified butter blazing in the fire."
And the parasol from the Vājapeya sacrifice beautified the great road.
Then the radiant Vasiṣṭha performed the entire righteous rite for the Great Departure according to the prescribed rules, leaving nothing undone.
Then, wearing garments of linen and reciting the supreme Veda,
he took up *kuśa* grass in both hands and set forth.
Along the path, he did not utter a single word, remaining motionless and free from worldly pleasure.
He emerged from that house, blazing like the sun;
on Rāma’s left side stood Padmā Śrī, perfectly composed,
while on his right was the large-eyed Hrī, and Vyavasāya stood before him.
Various kinds of arrows and a bow of immense form—
all these followed the descendant of Kakutstha in human form. The Vedas, in the form of Brahmins, and Sāvitrī, the protectress of all, were there as well.
Oṃkāra, Vaṣaṭkāra, and all [the deities] were devoted to Rāma; likewise,
the high-souled ṛṣis and all the brahmins followed the descendant of Kakutstha as he approached the gateway to heaven.
As he departed, the women of the inner apartments followed him,
accompanied by the elderly, children, female slaves, eunuchs, and servants.
And Bharata, together with Śatrughna, went forth along with the ladies of the inner apartments.
Having undertaken the vow of Rāma and remaining devotedly faithful to the descendant of Raghu,
the high-souled brahmins— concentrated in mind, maintaining their sacred fires, and accompanied by their sons and wives— then followed the great-minded Kākutstha.
The ministers and the groups of servants, along with their sons and kinsmen,
and all their followers, followed Rāghava with great joy. Then all the subjects, surrounded by people who were happy and well-fed, [followed].
Delighted by his virtues, they followed Rāghava as he departed.
All of them— bathed, joyful, thrilled, adorned with flowers, and unsurpassed—
were exultant with shouts of "Kilikila," for everyone was devoted to Rāma.
There was no one there who was dejected, ashamed, or sorrowful;
everyone became thrilled and exceedingly joyful in that most wonderful sight. Then the people of the countryside, desiring to see the king’s departure, came forth.
Having arrived, he too was seen by all his devoted followers—
bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas, as well as the people dwelling in the city—
who followed behind him with supreme devotion and great composure.
Having traveled one and a half yojanas, the joy of the Raghus beheld the Sarayū river of holy waters, which flows toward the west. Then,
at that very moment, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, appeared.
Surrounded by all the gods and the high-souled sages,
he arrived where the descendant of Kakutstha stood prepared for heaven,
encompassed by hundreds of millions of divine celestial chariots.
A rain of flowers, released by the wind like a great torrent, fell down.
Amidst that place filled with hundreds of musical instruments and crowded with Gandharvas and Apsarases,
Rāma stepped into the waters of the Sarayū on foot.
Then the Grandfather spoke these words from the sky:
"Come, Viṣṇu, blessings upon you; by good fortune you have arrived, O Rāghava.
Together with your brothers who resemble gods, enter your own body."
O one of great splendor, that Vaiṣṇavī [power] is that eternal space. For you, O God, are the refuge of the worlds; no one knows you except for Māyā, your ancient possession, O large-eyed one.
"You are the inconceivable, great being, imperishable, and the sustainer of all;
O you of great splendor, enter yourself into whichever form you desire.
Having heard the words of the Grandfather and having reached a firm decision, the high-minded one [acted].
7.100.010c With his body and his younger brother, he entered the splendor of Viṣṇu.
7.100.011a Then the deities worshipped the God who had gone into Viṣṇu— the Sādhyas, the hosts of Maruts, along with Indra and led by Agni.
And those divine hosts of sages, the gandharvas and apsarases,
the suparṇas, nāgas, yakṣas, daityas, dānavas, and rākṣasas—
all were thrilled and delighted; all had their desires fulfilled.
"Excellent! Excellent!"—thus all that [assembly], freed from impurity, ascended to the third heaven.
Then Viṣṇu, of great splendor, spoke to the Grandfather:
"O you of noble vows, it behooves you to grant worlds to these multitudes of people."

"For all these wise ones have followed me out of affection; they are devoted, they ought to be gratified, and they have surrendered their very selves for my sake. Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the lord and teacher of the world, [replied].
"These who have gathered here shall go to the worlds known as Sāntānika.
And whatever creature belonging to the animal realm shall give up its life while contemplating Rāma alone with devotion, it shall indeed dwell in the lineage [of the ancestors]."
Endowed with all virtues, they departed for the realm immediately adjacent to the world of Brahmā;
the monkeys and the bears likewise returned to their own origins,
from whichever gods and other sources they had originally emerged.
They sought refuge with those very sages, nāgas, and yakṣas.
When the Lord of Gods had spoken thus, they all approached Gopratāra and entered the Sarayū, overwhelmed with tears of joy.
Whichever living being, having plunged into the water, was filled with joy,
cast off its human body and ascended a celestial chariot (vimāna).
Even those belonging to the animal realm reached the waters of the Sarayū.
7.100.022a By means of their divine bodies, the gods appeared as if they were ablaze with light.
7.100.022c Having gone to the waters of the Sarayū, both the stationary and the moving beings,
7.100.023a having reached that moisture from the water, departed for the world of the gods.
7.100.023c Whatever was the origin of the gods— the monkeys, the ṛṣkas, and the rākṣasas—
7.100.024a they all entered that very [womb], having cast the gods into the waters.
7.100.024c Thus, having caused everyone to go to heaven, the Teacher of the World ascended to the sky.
The high-minded one, himself joyful, went forth together with the joyful gods.
